It is lighter and sharper and gives a paler sauce.
It gives the sauce wine depth and a little acidity.
It lacks the herbal scent, so the sauce is plainer.
It gives a brighter, more acidic sauce with less body than stock.

preparation/clarified-butter.is: Butter with its water and milk solids taken out. What is left is pure fat, which stands much more heat before it burns.

stands_in_for.caveat: It has no milk solids, so it stands far more heat before it burns. For the same reason it cannot thicken a sauce or brown to a nutty butter.
It tastes of butter and not of olive, and it stands high heat well. Brushed between phyllo it gives a crisp, buttery sheet.
It stands more heat than most fats and gives a clear buttery taste, with no milk solids to burn.

preparation/white-chicken-stock.is: A pale, clear stock made by simmering chicken bones and vegetables in water without browning anything, skimming as it goes.

stands_in_for.caveat: Homemade stock is unsalted and sets to a jelly, so season it and expect more body.
The sauce comes out paler and lighter, without the roasted depth.
It gives a savoury, lightly gelled base in place of plain water.
It has none of the sharpness or aroma of wine, so the sauce is rounder and sweeter. A little acid at the end brings some back.
It gives a milder, paler braise with less beefy depth.
Homemade stock is unsalted and sets to a jelly, so season it and expect more body.
It gives a lighter, paler sauce with no tannin or acidity, so it may need a splash of acid.

names.en: Seared chicken thighs with lemon butter pan sauce

steps.text: Pat the thighs dry and salt both sides. Lay them skin side down in the hot oil and leave them alone until the skin is deep golden and lifts off the pan by itself.
Turn the thighs, lower the heat and cook the other side. Check the thickest thigh against a trusted guide to doneness, then move them to a warm plate.
Pour off most of the fat and keep every brown bit. Stir the garlic in the pan just until it smells sweet.
Pour in the wine and scrape the pan with a wooden spoon until the brown bits have dissolved.
Let it boil until about half is left.
Take the pan off the heat. Whisk in the cold butter a few cubes at a time, then the juice of the lemon. The sauce turns glossy.
Taste, and add salt if it needs it. Pour the sauce into a warm jug.
Wilt the spinach in the same pan.
Plate the spinach with the chicken, skin side up, and spoon the sauce around it.
Crack the eggs into a bowl, add the salt and whisk until no streaks of white are left.

Melt most of the butter in a small pan over low heat until it foams, and keep the rest cold. Pour in the eggs and stir without stopping, scraping the bottom and the corners. Lift the pan off the heat whenever curds form too fast.
While the eggs still look wet and loose, take the pan off the heat and stir in the cold butter and the cream to stop the cooking. Serve at once on warm plates.
Crack the eggs into a bowl with the salt and the pepper, and whisk only until the streaks of white are gone.
Melt half the butter in the pan over medium heat. Turn the spinach in it until it collapses, then tip it onto a plate and press out the water.
Wipe the pan and melt the rest of the butter until it foams. Pour in the eggs and stir fast in small circles, shaking the pan, until they are mostly set and still wet on top.
Stop stirring and let the bottom firm for a moment. Scatter the spinach and the cheese down the middle.
Tilt the pan, fold the near edge over the filling and roll the omelette to the far lip. Turn it out onto a warm plate, seam side down.

en: add stock a ladle at a time

comes_after.why: The grains are coated in hot fat before any stock goes in.

cues.text: A spoon drawn across the pan leaves a trail that fills in slowly.
The grains are tender outside with a small firm centre, and the whole pan flows like a thick, loose cream.

technique/add-stock-gradually.does: Adds hot stock to rice a ladle at a time, stirring as each addition is taken up, so that the grains cook evenly and rub their starch off into a creamy sauce.
how: Keep the stock hot in a pot beside the pan, at a bare simmer, so that it never stops the rice from cooking.
Add enough stock to just cover the rice and stir. Keep the heat at a lively bubble.
When the pan is nearly dry and a spoon drawn across it leaves a trail, add the next ladle. Stir often and scrape the corners.
Taste along the way. Stop adding stock when the grains are tender with a small bite at the centre and the whole pan flows loosely when it is shaken.

mistakes.fix: Keep the stock at a bare simmer beside the pan.
mistakes.mistake: Using cold stock, which stops the cooking each time it goes in.

mistakes.fix: Add it a ladle at a time and stir.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring in all the stock at once, so that the rice boils and the sauce stays thin.

mistakes.fix: Add the next ladle as soon as the trail from the spoon stays open.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the pan dry out between ladles, so that the rice catches.

variant_of.differs: A pilaf takes all its hot stock at once and is covered and left alone. A risotto takes its stock in small lots and is stirred throughout, so that the starch is rubbed off the grains into a sauce.

cues.text: An even colour across the top, with the edges just darker than the middle.
A toasty smell that reaches the next room is the sign to check.

technique/bake.does: Cooks food with the dry, even heat of an oven.
how: Heat the oven fully before the food goes in.
Set the dish on the middle shelf, with space around it for the air to move.
Leave the door shut for the first part of the cooking.
Turn the dish if the oven browns one side faster, and check before the time is up.

mistakes.fix: Wait until the oven has reached its heat.
mistakes.mistake: Putting food into an oven that is still heating, so that it dries out before it colours.

mistakes.fix: Ovens run hot or cold. Learn yours, and judge by colour and feel as well as by time.
mistakes.mistake: Trusting the dial.

comes_after.why: The pie has to be layered and cut before it can be baked.

cues.text: The top is an even deep gold and the edges are dry and curled.
The pie crackles when the dish is moved, and the knife saws through a crisp top.

technique/bake-a-phyllo-pie.does: Bakes a pie of oiled phyllo sheets at a steady moderate heat until the layers dry out, turn golden and crackle, and the filling inside is set.
how: Heat the oven before the pie goes in, and set the dish on a rack in the middle.
Brush the top once more with fat just before baking, so that it browns evenly.
Bake at a steady moderate heat. A fierce heat browns the top before the layers underneath have dried.
Turn the dish round if one side browns faster than the other.
Bake until the top is deep golden and the sides pull in a little. Leave the pie to settle before cutting, so that the filling firms and the layers stay crisp.

mistakes.fix: Keep the heat moderate and bake for longer.
mistakes.mistake: Baking at a fierce heat, so that the top burns while the layers below are still pale and doughy.

mistakes.fix: Leave it to settle first.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting the pie straight from the oven, so that the filling runs and the layers go limp.

mistakes.fix: Leave it uncovered on a rack.
mistakes.mistake: Covering the pie while it cools, which steams the crust soft.

variant_of.differs: The food is sheets of dough brushed with fat, baked at a steady moderate heat until the layers dry and crackle around a moist filling, and rested before it is cut. A plain bake is for loaves and vegetables.

comes_after.why: A soufflé is a base with whipped whites folded in, so a cook has to be able to fold without knocking the air out.

cues.text: The soufflé stands well above the rim, with a deep gold top, and it trembles a little when the dish is moved.
The folded mixture is light and airy, and it falls from the spoon in a slow, soft mass.

technique/bake-a-souffle.does: Bakes a thick, flavoured base that has been lightened with whipped egg white, in a dish coated so that the mixture can climb. The trapped air swells in the oven and lifts the mixture high above the rim. It sinks soon after it comes out, so it is served at once.
how: Brush the dish all over with soft butter, using upward strokes so that the butter makes lines for the mixture to climb. Coat it with a dusting of grated cheese or flour and tip out the extra.
Warm the base and beat the egg yolks and the cheese into it. Season it boldly, because the whites will dilute it.
Whip the whites to firm, glossy peaks that are just short of dry.

Stir a spoonful of the whites into the base to loosen it, then fold in the rest in stages with a spatula, cutting down through the middle and lifting up the sides, until only a few streaks of white are left.
Fill the dish nearly to the rim, smooth the top and run a thumb around the inside edge, so that the mixture lifts clear of the dish.
Bake in the middle of a hot oven and keep the door shut until the soufflé has risen high and the top is deep gold. Take it to the table at once.

mistakes.fix: Keep the door shut until the soufflé has risen and browned.
mistakes.mistake: Opening the oven door early, so that the air chills and the soufflé collapses.

mistakes.fix: Stop when the peaks are glossy and just hold.
mistakes.mistake: Whipping the whites until they turn dry and grainy, so that they will not blend in.

mistakes.fix: Fold with a spatula, cutting down and lifting up, and stop while a few streaks show.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring the whites into the base, which beats the air out.

mistakes.fix: Butter the dish in upward strokes and coat it well.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the sides of the dish bare, so that the mixture sticks and rises crookedly.

variant_of.differs: The mixture is held up by trapped air, so it is baked in a coated dish, the oven door stays shut and the dish goes to the table at once, before the air cools and the mixture sinks.

comes_after.why: The apples cook in a caramel, so a cook must be able to take sugar to a deep amber without burning it.

cues.text: The caramel bubbles up thick and dark around the apples, and the pastry is deep gold and puffed.
A deep smell of caramel and baked apple.

technique/bake-a-tarte-tatin.does: Cooks apples in butter and caramel in a heavy ovenproof pan, covers them with a sheet of pastry and bakes the tart upside down. It is turned out onto a plate, so that the pastry becomes the base and the glossy caramelised apples are on top.
how: Cook the sugar in the pan to a deep amber caramel, take the pan off the heat and stir in the butter.
Pack the halved apples tightly into the caramel, rounded side down, in a ring and then a centre. They shrink as they cook, so they must be crowded.
Cook on the stove until the caramel is thick and the apples have begun to soften and take on colour.
Lay the rolled pastry over the apples and tuck the edge down around them inside the pan. Prick the pastry in a few places.
Bake until the pastry is puffed and deep gold.
Rest the tart for a short while so that the caramel thickens slightly. Lay a plate over the pan and turn both over together with care, because the caramel is very hot.

mistakes.fix: Cook the caramel to a deep amber, taking care that it does not burn.
mistakes.mistake: Stopping the caramel when it is pale, so that the tart tastes only sweet.

mistakes.fix: Crowd them tightly, because they will shrink.
mistakes.mistake: Packing the apples loosely, so that gaps open as they shrink.

mistakes.fix: Rest it briefly so that the caramel thickens, and turn it out over a plate with a deep rim.
mistakes.mistake: Turning the tart out at once, when the caramel is runny and still very hot.

variant_of.differs: The fruit goes in the pan first and the pastry on top, and the tart is baked upside down and turned out, so the pastry becomes the base.

cues.text: The crust is hard and dry all over, and it sounds hollow when it is tapped.

technique/bake-in-a-salt-crust.does: Seals food inside a shell of damp salt, so that it cooks in its own steam and is seasoned gently through its skin.
how: Mix coarse salt with enough egg white or water for it to feel like wet sand.
Spread a bed of the salt on a tray, lay the food on it with its skin on, and pack the rest of the salt over it until nothing shows.
Bake until the crust is hard and pale gold.
Push a thin probe through the crust into the thickest part and check it against a trusted guide to doneness.
Rest the food in its crust, then crack the shell, lift it off in pieces and brush away every loose grain before serving.

mistakes.fix: Leave the skin and the scales on. They keep the salt out.
mistakes.mistake: Scaling or skinning a fish first, so that the flesh takes up salt and turns harsh.

mistakes.fix: Patch every crack with more damp salt before it goes into the oven.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving a gap in the crust, so that the steam escapes and the food dries.

variant_of.differs: The food is shut inside a shell of salt and steams there. Nothing browns.

cues.text: The edges are set and the middle wobbles like jelly when the dish is nudged.

technique/bake-in-a-water-bath.does: Bakes a delicate mixture in a dish that stands in hot water, so that it sets softly and evenly.
how: Stand the filled dishes in a deep tin.
Pour hot water into the tin until it comes about half way up their sides.
Bake until the mixture is just set at the edges and still trembles in the middle.
Lift the dishes out of the water at once.

mistakes.fix: Take it out while it still wobbles. It goes on setting.
mistakes.mistake: Baking until the middle is firm, by which time the edges are rubbery and full of holes.

mistakes.fix: Fill the tin with hot water from the kettle.
mistakes.mistake: Starting with cold water, which slows everything down and gives an uneven result.

variant_of.differs: The dish stands in hot water, which shields it from the full heat of the oven, so that eggs and custards set gently.

cues.text: The parcel swells like a pillow and the paper browns lightly.
A burst of scented steam when the paper is cut.

technique/bake-in-parchment.does: Seals food in a paper parcel, so that it steams in its own juices in the oven.
how: Cut a large sheet of paper and fold it in half.
Lay the vegetables and then the fish on one side of the fold, with butter, seasoning and a splash of liquid.
Fold the paper over and crimp the edges in small, tight, overlapping folds.
Bake on a tray until the parcel puffs up.
Open it at the table, away from your face.

mistakes.fix: Make the folds small and tight, and twist the ends.
mistakes.mistake: A loose seal, so that the steam escapes and the fish dries out.

mistakes.fix: Cut them fine and soften them in butter first.
mistakes.mistake: Thick, raw vegetables under the fish, still hard when the fish is done.

variant_of.differs: The food is sealed in a paper parcel and cooks in its own steam.

comes_after.why: Basting with butter is how a sear ends, once the crust is already there.

cues.text: The surface glistens, and browns evenly from edge to edge.
The butter foams and hisses as it runs over the meat. When the foam dies down and darkens, stop.

technique/baste.does: Spoons hot fat or juices over food as it cooks, so that the top browns and stays moist.
how: Tilt the pan so that the fat pools at the near edge.
Scoop it up with a spoon and pour it over the food, again and again.
In a pan, add butter, garlic and thyme near the end and baste with the foaming butter.
For a roast, baste quickly and shut the oven door again.

mistakes.fix: Add the butter late, and take the pan off the heat when the foam subsides.
mistakes.mistake: Basting with butter that has turned dark, which leaves a bitter taste.

mistakes.fix: Take the tin out, baste, and put it straight back.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the oven door open while basting a roast, so that the oven loses its heat.

fr: tremper dans la pâte à frire

comes_after.why: A batter is mixed with a quick whisk, so a cook has to know how far to take it.

cues.text: The batter coats a spoon in a thin even film and runs off in a slow stream.
The coat sizzles at once and bubbles as it meets the oil.

technique/batter.does: Dips food in a thin, wet mixture of flour and cold liquid, so that it fries with a light, crisp, airy coat that is lighter than a crumb coat.
how: Stir the flour into cold liquid just until it is smooth enough to coat a spoon. A few lumps do no harm.
Keep the batter cold and use it soon after it is made.
Dry the food and dust it with a little flour so that the batter clings.
Dip the food, lift it and let the extra run off, then lower it into the hot oil away from you.
Fry in small batches so that the oil stays hot, and lift each piece out onto a rack.

mistakes.fix: Stir only until the flour has just gone in.
mistakes.mistake: Beating the batter smooth, which builds toughness into the coat.

mistakes.fix: Keep it cold and make it just before frying.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the batter stand warm for long, so that it turns heavy.

mistakes.fix: Fry a few at a time.
mistakes.mistake: Frying too many pieces at once, so that the oil cools and the coat turns greasy.

cues.text: The dough is sticky and soft, and stretches in a long strand without breaking.
Bubbles show on the surface and the dough no longer sticks in lumps to the bowl.

technique/beat-sfenj-dough.does: Mixes flour, warm water, yeast and salt into a very wet, sticky dough and beats it by hand in a bowl, with a wet hand, lifting and slapping it, until it turns stretchy and full of air. It is far too soft to knead on a board.
how: Stir the yeast into part of the warm water with the sugar and let it foam.
Put the flour and the salt in a large bowl and pour in the yeast water and the rest of the water.
Beat with a wet hand, lifting the dough high and letting it fall back, again and again.
Keep beating until the dough is smooth, elastic and bubbly, and drops from the hand in a slow rope.

mistakes.fix: Keep the dough wet and wet the hand instead.
mistakes.mistake: Adding more flour to stop the stickiness, which makes a dense doughnut.

mistakes.fix: Beat until it stretches and bubbles.
mistakes.mistake: Stopping too soon, which leaves a dough without air.

variant_of.differs: Kneading works a firm dough on a board with the heels of the hands. This dough is too wet for that: it is beaten in a bowl with a wet hand until it stretches, and it is never shaped until it goes into the oil.

comes_after.why: The sauce is beaten by hand until smooth, so a steady beating hand comes first.

cues.text: A pale, creamy, glossy sauce with no oil standing on top.
Stiff and tight after the lemon juice goes in, then silky and easy to stir as the water goes in.
Nutty and tart, with no bitter edge.

technique/beat-tahini-sauce.does: Beats tahini with lemon juice and cold water into a pale, smooth, pourable sauce. The paste stiffens and looks curdled when the first liquid goes in, then turns silky and loose as more water is beaten in.
how: Stir the tahini well first, as its oil rises to the top. If garlic is used, crush it with salt and stir it into the lemon juice.
Put the tahini in a bowl and stir in the lemon juice. The paste will seize and thicken, as it should.
Add cold water a spoonful at a time, beating hard after each, until the paste loosens, lightens and turns smooth.
Stop at the texture the dish wants: thick as cream for a dip, thinner for pouring over fish or falafel.
Taste, and adjust the lemon juice and the salt.

mistakes.fix: Add it a spoonful at a time and beat after each.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring in all the water at once, so that the sauce splits into oil and a watery paste.

mistakes.fix: Keep beating and keep adding water. It loosens.
mistakes.mistake: Giving up when the paste seizes, thinking it has gone wrong.

mistakes.fix: Stir the jar well before measuring.
mistakes.mistake: Using tahini from the top of the jar, where the oil has risen, so that the sauce is thin and oily.

variant_of.differs: No oil is added. The oil already in the tahini is spread through lemon juice and water by beating, and the paste first seizes and then loosens.

comes_after.why: The edges are bevelled after the food is cut into pieces.

cues.text: The pieces have smooth, rounded corners and no sharp edges.
The pieces are smooth in the hand and do not catch.

technique/bevel-edges.does: Shaves the sharp corners from cut pieces of a firm vegetable, so that they hold their shape and do not break or cloud the liquid while they simmer.
how: Cut the vegetable into chunks.
Hold a chunk in one hand and run a knife around its sharp edges, taking off a thin sliver from each corner.
Work around every chunk, so that all the corners are rounded.
Rinse the pieces, if they are starchy, before they go into the pot.

mistakes.fix: Take off only a thin sliver.
mistakes.mistake: Taking off too much, which wastes the vegetable.

mistakes.fix: Bevel the edges of any piece that will simmer for long.
mistakes.mistake: Skipping it for long simmering, so that the corners break off and cloud the liquid.

cues.text: Green vegetables turn a vivid green. Bones come out clean, with the grey scum left behind in the water.

technique/blanch.does: Plunges food briefly into boiling water, to clean bones, loosen skins or set the colour of green vegetables.
how: For bones, cover them with cold water, bring it to a boil, then drain them and rinse off the scum.
For vegetables, drop them into fast-boiling salted water.
Lift them out as soon as the colour brightens.
Cool them at once in iced water.

mistakes.fix: Take them out early. They are cooked again later.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving vegetables in until they are tender, when they were only meant to be set.

variant_of.differs: The food stays in only briefly and is not cooked to the end.

cues.text: A dry, matt base with no grey, greasy patches, and edges of pale gold.

technique/blind-bake.does: Bakes an empty pastry case, so that a wet filling does not leave the base raw and soggy.
how: Line the tin with the pastry and chill it until firm.
Prick the base with a fork, cover it with paper and fill it with baking beans.
Bake until the edges are set, then lift out the paper and the beans.
Bake a little longer, until the base looks dry and pale gold.

mistakes.fix: Rest the lined tin in the fridge until the pastry is firm.
mistakes.mistake: Skipping the chill, so that the pastry shrinks down the sides of the tin.

mistakes.fix: Wait until the edges hold their shape.
mistakes.mistake: Taking the beans out too soon, so that the base puffs up.

variant_of.differs: A pastry case is baked empty and weighed down, before any filling goes in.

cues.text: Big bubbles that keep rolling even when you stir.
The tip of a knife slides into a vegetable with only slight resistance.

technique/boil.does: Cooks food in plenty of fast-bubbling salted water, so that it is done quickly and evenly.
how: Fill a large pot with far more water than the food needs.
Bring it to a rolling boil and salt it until it tastes pleasantly salty.
Add the food and bring the water back to the boil as fast as you can.
Test a piece often, and lift the food out the moment it is tender.

mistakes.fix: Use a bigger pot and more water, and cook in batches.
mistakes.mistake: Too little water, so it stops boiling when the food goes in and green vegetables turn dull.

mistakes.fix: Salt it well. Food boiled in plain water tastes flat, however it is seasoned later.
mistakes.mistake: Salting the water too lightly.

cues.text: For a soft egg, a set white and a yolk that runs. For a hard one, a yolk that is firm and still bright yellow.

technique/boil-an-egg.does: Cooks an egg in its shell in gently boiling water, to a runny, soft or firm yolk.
how: Bring a pan of water to a gentle boil.
Lower the eggs in on a spoon, straight from the fridge.
Start a timer at once. The time alone decides how far the yolk sets.
Lift the eggs out and cool them under cold running water to stop the cooking.

mistakes.fix: Time it, and cool it at once.
mistakes.mistake: Boiling a hard egg too long, which leaves a grey-green ring around the yolk and a smell of sulphur.

mistakes.fix: Lower them in on a spoon and keep the boil gentle.
mistakes.mistake: Dropping eggs into hard-boiling water, so that they crack on the bottom.

variant_of.differs: The egg stays in its shell, the water bubbles gently so that the shell does not crack, and only the clock tells when it is done.

cues.text: A strand has a clean, springy bite, with no hard core.
The noodles move freely, not stuck in a mass.

technique/boil-noodles.does: Cooks noodles in a large pot of rapidly boiling water, stirring them loose at the start, and lifts them out the moment they are tender, so that they are springy and not gummy.
how: Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Do not salt it for dry buckwheat noodles.
Fan the noodles into the water and stir with long chopsticks or tongs so that they do not clump.
If the water rises, add a splash of cold water to calm it.
Taste a strand for bite.
Drain the noodles right away into a colander and rinse them if they will be eaten cold.

mistakes.fix: Use a very large pot.
mistakes.mistake: Using too little water, so that the noodles stick together.

mistakes.fix: Lift them out as soon as they are tender.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the noodles in the water after they are done, so that they go soft.

variant_of.differs: The noodles are stirred loose at the start, lifted as soon as they have a clean bite and rinsed, which the boiling of vegetables and pasta does not need.

cues.text: A bitten piece is tender, with a small firm core that is neither chalky nor soft.
A piece snapped in half shows a faint pale dot at the very centre when it is a moment from ready.

technique/boil-pasta.does: Cooks pasta in a large pot of fast-bubbling water that is salted well, and stops while the heart of each piece still has a little bite. It is lifted out with some of its starchy water kept back, and goes to its sauce without rinsing.
how: Fill the biggest pot to hand with water, so that the pasta can move freely, and bring it to a rolling boil.
Salt the water generously once it boils. It should taste lightly of the sea, because this is the only chance to season the pasta itself.
Slide in the pasta and stir at once, so that it does not stick. Keep the water bubbling and stir now and then.
Start tasting a little before the packet says it is ready. Stop when the pasta is tender outside and has a small firm bite at the centre, which is called al dente.
Scoop out a mug of the cooking water, then drain the pasta. Do not rinse it, and do not leave it waiting: it goes into the sauce while it is still wet and hot.

mistakes.fix: Use a large pot with plenty of water and keep it bubbling.
mistakes.mistake: Using a small pot, so that the water falls off the boil and the pasta clumps and turns gluey.

mistakes.fix: Leave the oil out and stir well at the start.
mistakes.mistake: Adding oil to the water, which makes the pasta slippery so that the sauce slides off.

mistakes.fix: Drain it and move it straight to the sauce, keeping a little of the cooking water.
mistakes.mistake: Rinsing the pasta, which washes away the starch that helps the sauce cling.

mistakes.fix: Take it out a little early when it is to finish in the sauce.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking the pasta to the end before it meets the sauce, so that it turns soft as it finishes in the pan.

variant_of.differs: The water is salted much more heavily, the pasta is stopped while it still has bite, and some of the starchy water is kept to loosen the sauce. It is never cooled in cold water.

comes_after.why: A braise begins with a sear.
The fond of that sear is deglazed into the liquid the food braises in.
The whole of a braise is a simmer held for a long time.

cues.text: The liquid barely moves under the lid: a bubble now and then.
A fork slides in and out of the meat with no resistance, and the piece still holds its shape.
A deep, rounded smell, with no raw wine left in it.

technique/braise.does: Cooks food slowly in a little liquid in a covered pot, after browning it, until it is tender and the liquid has become its sauce.
how: Brown the meat well in the pot and take it out.
Soften the vegetables in the same pot, then loosen the fond with the wine or the stock.
Put the meat back and add liquid to come about half way up it, not to cover it.
Bring it to a bare simmer, cover, and cook in a low oven or over the lowest heat.
Turn the pieces now and then. It is ready when a fork meets no resistance.
Lift the meat out, skim off the fat, and boil the liquid down if it is thin.

mistakes.fix: Lower the heat, or move the pot to a low oven, where the heat is gentler and comes from all sides.
mistakes.mistake: Letting it boil, which tightens the meat into dry strings even as it sits in liquid.

mistakes.fix: Use less liquid. The top of the meat should stand clear of it.
mistakes.mistake: Drowning the meat, which gives a thin soup and no sauce.

mistakes.fix: Keep going. A tough cut turns tender only after a long time at a simmer.
mistakes.mistake: Stopping when the meat is cooked but still tough.

comes_after.why: The onion is softened in the oil first, so a cook has to be able to soften it without letting it colour.

cues.text: The oil and the juices have come together into a loose, glossy sauce at the bottom of the pan.
A piece gives way under the back of a spoon and still holds its shape.
The vegetables taste sweet and soft, and nothing squeaks between the teeth.

technique/braise-in-olive-oil.does: Cooks vegetables slowly under a lid in a generous amount of olive oil with only a little water and no browning first, until they are very soft and sweet and the oil and their own juices have become the sauce. The dish is eaten warm or at room temperature, never piping hot.
how: Soften the onion in the olive oil over a gentle heat until it is soft and has not taken colour.
Add the vegetables, and the tomato if there is any, and turn them in the oil until they shine. Season with salt, and add a little sugar if the vegetables or the tomato are sharp.
Pour in a small amount of water, so that it comes only part way up the vegetables. They give off water of their own.
Cover the pan and cook over the lowest heat. Shake the pan now and then and do not stir, so that the pieces stay whole.
Cook until the vegetables are very soft and give way under the back of a spoon. If much liquid is left, take off the lid for the last stretch until what remains is mostly glossy oil and juice.
Let the dish cool in the pan until it is warm or at room temperature. Finish with lemon juice if the dish is dull.

mistakes.fix: Keep the heat gentle and take the onion off as soon as it is soft.
mistakes.mistake: Browning the onion or the vegetables first, which gives a roasted taste in place of the soft, sweet taste of the dish.

mistakes.fix: Add only enough to come part way up them. They give off water of their own.
mistakes.mistake: Adding too much water, which boils the vegetables into a thin soup.

mistakes.fix: Shake the pan and turn the pieces gently.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring hard and often, which breaks the pieces apart.

mistakes.fix: Use a generous amount. The oil is part of the sauce, and it is meant to stay.
mistakes.mistake: Skimping on the oil, so that the vegetables catch and taste flat.

variant_of.differs: It is the Turkish zeytinyagli way. The fat is a generous amount of olive oil and not a stock or a wine, there is no browning and no meat, the water is only a splash, and the dish is served warm or at room temperature and not hot.

en: break the crust of a cassoulet

cues.text: A deep golden crust, thicker than a gratin, with the beans below it glossy and moist.
The spoon cracks through a crisp top into a thick, creamy mass of beans.

technique/break-the-crust.does: Presses the golden crust that forms on top of a slowly baked pot of beans and meat down into the pot, so that it soaks up the juices and thickens them, then lets a fresh crust form. It is done several times, and the last crust is left whole for the table.
how: Sprinkle a thick layer of crumbs over the beans and meat, with the liquid just below the top.
Bake at a low heat until a golden crust has formed on the top.
Press the crust down into the pot with the back of a spoon so that it sinks into the juices. If the pot looks dry, add a ladle of hot liquid.
Sprinkle on a little more crumbs if the top is bare, and bake until a fresh crust forms.
Do this several times over the baking. Leave the last crust whole.

mistakes.fix: Wait for a golden crust before each press.
mistakes.mistake: Breaking the crust before it has browned, so that the crumbs turn to a paste and it never forms again.

mistakes.fix: Add a ladle of hot liquid whenever the beans no longer shine.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the pot dry out under the crust.

variant_of.differs: A gratin is browned once under strong heat from above and eaten at once. Here the crust is pressed down into the pot several times during a long, low bake, so that it thickens the beans and a new crust takes its place.

comes_after.why: A brunoise is a julienne cut across, so the strips come first.

cues.text: Cubes so small and even that they look like coarse grains.
The pile stays dry on the board.

technique/brunoise.does: Cuts food into tiny, even cubes that melt into a sauce or sit as a neat garnish.
how: Cut the vegetable into thin slabs, then into julienne strips.
Gather the strips into a tight bundle.
Cut across the bundle at the same spacing as the strips are wide.
For a shallot, halve it, make fine cuts towards the root and a few flat cuts into it, then slice across.

mistakes.fix: Cut each piece once. If the cubes are too big, cut the strips thinner next time.
mistakes.mistake: Rocking the knife back over the pile to make it finer, which bruises it into a wet mash.

mistakes.fix: Sharpen the knife. A clean cut stays dry.
mistakes.mistake: A blunt knife crushes instead of cutting, so the shallot weeps and turns bitter.

variant_of.differs: Far smaller. The food is first cut into julienne, then across into cubes that cook in moments.

cues.text: The surface shines evenly, with no puddles and no dry patches.
The bristles glide and do not drag or tear at soft dough.

technique/brush.does: Paints a thin, even film of oil, melted butter or beaten egg onto a surface with a soft brush, so that it browns and shines in the heat, keeps from drying out, or does not stick.
how: Have the oil, butter or egg ready in a small bowl, and the food in front of you.
Dip only the tip of the brush, and press the extra off against the rim of the bowl.
Stroke the surface in one direction and then across, so that the film is thin and no part is missed.
Go lightly over folds and edges, where the liquid pools and burns.
Brush again part-way through cooking if the surface looks dry.

mistakes.fix: Dip the tip only and press the extra off on the rim.
mistakes.mistake: Loading the brush so full that the fat pools and the food turns greasy.

mistakes.fix: Use a light touch and a soft brush.
mistakes.mistake: Brushing a soft dough hard, so that it tears or loses its air.

variant_of.differs: The fat or glaze is painted on in a thin film with a brush, often before the food meets the heat, and not spooned over the food from the pan as it cooks.

comes_after.why: The custard has to be cold and firm before the sugar goes on, or the crust melts into it.
A cook who knows how sugar melts and darkens can judge the colour of the crust.

cues.text: The sugar melts to a clear syrup and darkens evenly to deep amber, with no black patch.
The hardened crust cracks with a light tap of a spoon.
Toasted and bittersweet. A sharp, acrid smell means it has burnt.

technique/burn-a-sugar-crust.does: Sprinkles a thin, even layer of sugar over a cold, set custard and melts it with strong heat from above until it turns into a thin, glassy, amber crust that cracks under a spoon, while the custard beneath stays cold. The Catalan word for it is cremar, to burn.
how: Have the custard cold and firm, with a dry surface. Get the torch lit or the grill very hot before the sugar goes on.
Scatter an even, thin layer of sugar over the surface, tilting the dish so that it reaches every corner, and tip off the extra.
Pass the flame slowly just above the sugar, or slide the dish close under a very hot grill, until the sugar melts and turns amber. Keep it moving so that it browns evenly and does not scorch.
Leave it a moment to harden into a glassy crust, and serve soon after.

mistakes.fix: Scatter a thin layer and tip off the extra.
mistakes.mistake: Using a thick layer of sugar, so that the crust is hard and gritty in places and still sugar in others.

mistakes.fix: Keep the flame moving in slow passes over the whole surface.
mistakes.mistake: Holding the flame still, which scorches one spot and leaves the rest pale.

mistakes.fix: Chill the custard until it is cold and firm first.
mistakes.mistake: Burning a warm custard, which softens and melts the crust.

mistakes.fix: Burn it just before the dish goes to the table.
mistakes.mistake: Burning the sugar long before serving, so that the crust draws moisture and goes soft.

variant_of.differs: The sugar is scattered dry in a thin layer over a cold custard and burned in place in moments by heat from above, so that it sets as a crust on the dish. A caramel is cooked in a pan to a syrup that is used apart.
The top that browns is sugar, not cheese or sauce, and it is burned for moments only so that the cold custard beneath stays cold. A gratin is browned on a hot dish that is eaten warm.

comes_after.why: The fish is scaled before it is opened, or the scales get everywhere.
The belly is already opened and cleaned when the fish is butterflied.

cues.text: Both sides lie open in one piece, joined by the skin down the back, with no backbone left.
No bone catches on a fingertip run over the flesh.

technique/butterfly.does: Cuts a small fish open along the belly, takes out the backbone and opens the flesh flat like a book, so that it cooks fast and evenly and takes a marinade, a paste or a stuffing on its whole inner face.
how: Scale and gut the fish, rinse the belly and pat it dry.
Open the belly from the gut cut to the tail with a small sharp knife and lay the fish open, skin side up, on the board.
Press along the middle of the back with the heel of the hand, so that the backbone loosens and lies flat.
Turn the fish over, lift the backbone from the head end and snip or cut it free at the tail, with the small bones that come with it.
Pull out any bones left in the flesh with the fingertips, and lay the fish flat, skin side down.

mistakes.fix: Keep the knife on the belly side and ease the bone out with the fingers.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting through the skin of the back, so that the halves part.

mistakes.fix: Lift it slowly from the head end, and cut it free at the tail.
mistakes.mistake: Pulling the backbone out fast, which tears the soft flesh.

variant_of.differs: A fillet is cut off the bone as a separate piece, a piece for each side. A butterflied fish stays whole, with both sides joined by the skin along the back, and only the bones are taken out.

comes_after.why: Onions sweat before they caramelize. The first stage is the same move.

cues.text: An even, deep amber, a fraction of the raw heap, with no black edges.
Sweet and nutty, like toast and caramel. A sharp, acrid smell means they are burning.
As sweet as jam, with no sharpness left.

technique/caramelize.does: Cooks onions slowly until their water is gone and their sugars turn deep brown, soft and sweet.
how: Sweat sliced onions in butter with a little salt until soft.
Take the lid off and keep the heat at medium-low.
Stir every little while, scraping up the brown film that forms on the bottom of the pan.
Add a spoonful of water whenever the film darkens faster than the onions.
Stop when they are the colour of dark honey all the way through.

mistakes.fix: Keep the heat low and give it the time it takes. There is no shortcut.
mistakes.mistake: Rushing with high heat, which burns the edges and leaves the middle pale and bitter.

mistakes.fix: Use the widest pan you have.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding a small pan, so that the onions steam and never brown.

comes_after.why: A roast is rested before it is carved.

cues.text: Clean slices with the skin still on, and joints that part where the knife finds them, without sawing.

technique/carve.does: Cuts a rested roast or bird into portions, following the joints and cutting across the grain.
how: Rest the meat first, and catch its juices for the sauce.
For a bird, cut through the skin between the leg and the body, bend the leg out and cut through the joint.
Cut down along one side of the breastbone and follow the ribs to free each breast, then slice it across.
For a joint, hold it with a fork and slice across the grain with long strokes of a sharp knife.

mistakes.fix: Wiggle the leg or the wing to find the joint, and cut through that.
mistakes.mistake: Sawing through bone when the joint is a finger away.

mistakes.fix: Look for the lines of the fibres and cut across them.
mistakes.mistake: Slicing with the grain, which makes tender meat chewy.

cues.text: The skin is blackened and blistered all over, and the vegetable has sagged.
A deep, smoky, sweet smell.
The flesh gives completely when pressed with the tongs.

technique/char.does: Burns the skin of a whole vegetable black over an open flame or a fierce heat, so that the flesh inside turns soft, smoky and sweet, and the charred skin can be peeled away.
how: Set the whole vegetable directly on a gas flame, on a hot grill or on a barbecue.
Turn it now and then with tongs, until the skin is blackened and blistered all over and the flesh has gone soft and collapsed.
Move it to a bowl and cover it, so that the steam loosens the skin.
When it is cool enough to handle, peel off the skin and lift out the stem and seeds. Do not rinse it, or the smoky taste is lost.
Drain off the juices, or keep them for the dish, as it asks.

mistakes.fix: Keep turning it until the skin is black all over and the vegetable has collapsed.
mistakes.mistake: Taking it off while the skin is only blistered in patches, so that the flesh stays firm and the skin clings.

mistakes.fix: Wipe or pull the skin off by hand.
mistakes.mistake: Rinsing the vegetable under the tap to remove the skin, which washes away the smoke.

mistakes.fix: Cover it while it steams and cools.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving it uncovered, so that the skin sticks.

variant_of.differs: The whole, unpeeled vegetable sits straight on the flame and its skin is burnt black on purpose, then peeled away, so that the smoky soft flesh is what is kept.

cues.text: The container is cold to the hand all over, with no warm core.

technique/chill.does: Brings hot food down to the cold of the fridge quickly, so that it keeps well and so that a cold dish is truly cold.
how: Move the hot food out of its pot into a wide, shallow container.
Stand the container in iced water and stir now and then.
Put it in the fridge, uncovered, once it has stopped steaming.
Cover it when it is cold. Taste a cold dish again before serving, because cold dulls salt.

mistakes.fix: Divide it into shallow containers and cool them in iced water.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving a large pot of stock to cool by itself on the stove, where its middle stays warm for a long time.

mistakes.fix: Taste it again when it is cold.
mistakes.mistake: Seasoning a soup while it is hot and serving it cold.

cues.text: Pieces of roughly one size, still dry and separate on the board.

technique/chop.does: Cuts food into small, uneven pieces, where the exact shape does not matter.
how: Gather the food into a low pile.
Hold the tip of the knife on the board with your free hand.
Rock the blade up and down while swinging it across the pile.
Scrape the pile back together and go over it again until it is as fine as you want.

mistakes.fix: Dry the herbs well first, and stop as soon as they are fine enough.
mistakes.mistake: Chopping wet herbs, which turns them to a dark paste.

mistakes.fix: Cut it by hand with a sharp knife: slices, then strips, then small cubes.
mistakes.mistake: Chopping meat for a tartare in a machine, which smears it.

comes_after.why: A stock is skimmed clean before it is clarified. Clarifying is the last and finest step.

cues.text: The liquid seen through the hole is as clear as tea.

technique/clarify.does: Clears a cloudy stock by simmering it with egg white and minced meat, which rise as a raft and trap what clouds it.
how: Mix egg white, minced lean meat and finely cut vegetables into a cold stock with no fat on it.
Heat slowly, stirring gently, until the mixture starts to rise and clump.
Stop stirring the moment a raft forms on top.
Make a small hole in the raft and simmer very gently, so that the liquid bubbles up through it.
Ladle the clear liquid out through the hole and strain it through a cloth.

mistakes.fix: Leave it alone and keep the heat very low.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring after the raft has formed, or letting it boil, which breaks the raft and clouds the stock again.

mistakes.fix: Chill the stock and lift off all the fat first.
mistakes.mistake: Starting with a warm or fatty stock.

cues.text: The shells are closed and clean, with no tufts left sticking out.
They smell fresh, of clean sea water.

technique/clean-mussels.does: Scrubs the shells of mussels and pulls off the tuft of fibres at the hinge, which is called the beard, so that nothing gritty reaches the pot. Mussels are cleaned just before they are cooked.
how: Tip the mussels into a bowl of cold water and lift them out by the handful, leaving the grit in the bottom of the bowl.
Tap any open shell on the side of the bowl. Leave out any that stays open.
Scrape off barnacles and dirt with the back of a knife.
Take the tuft of fibres at the hinge between a thumb and the knife blade and pull it firmly towards the hinge end until it comes away.
Rinse once more and keep the mussels cold until they go into the pot.

mistakes.fix: Rinse them quickly in cold water and cook them soon after.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the mussels to soak for a long time in fresh water, which weakens them.

mistakes.fix: Pull towards the hinge end.
mistakes.mistake: Pulling the beard the wrong way, towards the point of the shell, which can tear the mussel.

variant_of.differs: Clams are left to stand in salted water so that they give up their sand. Mussels hold little sand, so they are scrubbed, bearded and cooked soon after, and are never left to stand.

comes_after.why: The meat is seasoned first, because the coat shuts the seasoning off once it is on.

cues.text: An even coat of crumbs on every side, with no bare patch.
The crumbs hold when the piece is picked up and do not rain off.

technique/coat.does: Covers a piece of meat in a layer of breadcrumbs over a sticky coat of mustard or beaten egg, which turns into a crisp crust when the piece is cooked.
how: Pat the pieces dry and season them.
Brush a thin, even layer of mustard or beaten egg over every side, so that the crumbs have something to hold to.
Tip the crumbs into a shallow dish. Press each piece into them, turn it, and press again.
Shake off the loose crumbs and lay the pieces on a rack, so that the coat sets before cooking.

mistakes.fix: Brush on a thin, even layer.
mistakes.mistake: Brushing on a thick layer of mustard, which slides off with the crumbs.

mistakes.fix: Pat the meat dry first.
mistakes.mistake: Coating wet meat, so that the crumbs go soggy and fall off.

variant_of.differs: Dredging dusts the piece with dry flour. Here a wet coat of mustard or egg goes on first and crumbs are pressed into it, to make a thick crisp crust.

cues.text: The crust is an even layer of dry flakes with no bare spots.
The flakes cling when the piece is lifted and do not fall away.

technique/coat-in-panko.does: Covers a cutlet in layers, first flour, then beaten egg and then coarse panko flakes, which fry into a light, shaggy, golden crust that stays crisp.
how: Season the meat and pat it dry.
Set out trays in a row: flour, beaten egg and panko.
Dust the meat in flour and tap off the extra, so that only a thin film is left.
Draw it through the egg so that every side is wet, and let the extra drip off.
Lay it in the panko and press the flakes on lightly with a dry hand, covering the faces and the edges. Do not pack them down.
Shake off the loose flakes and fry soon, before the coat turns damp.

mistakes.fix: Press lightly and let the flakes stay loose.
mistakes.mistake: Pressing the panko down hard, which makes a dense, heavy crust.

mistakes.fix: Let the extra egg drip off before the flakes go on.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving thick egg on the meat, which makes a gummy coat.

mistakes.fix: Coat just before frying.
mistakes.mistake: Coating well ahead of the oil, so that the flakes soak up the egg and turn soft.

variant_of.differs: The crumbs are panko, coarse, dry flakes, and not fine breadcrumbs, and the coat is flour, then egg, then panko, with no mustard. It fries lighter and more shaggy and stays crisp longer.

cues.text: The coating is thin, dry and even, with no wet spots.
The piece crackles in the oil.

technique/coat-in-starch.does: Dusts a piece of food, often after it has been marinated, in a thin layer of potato starch or cornstarch just before frying. It fries to a crisp, light, pale crust.
how: Pat the food dry and shake off any marinade that is dripping.
Tip the starch into a tray and turn each piece in it, pressing lightly.
Tap off the loose starch, as too much turns pasty in the oil.
Fry straight away, before the starch dampens and turns gluey.

mistakes.fix: Shake off the loose starch.
mistakes.mistake: Coating too thickly, which turns gluey and heavy.

mistakes.fix: Coat right before the oil.
mistakes.mistake: Coating long before frying, so that the starch gets wet.

variant_of.differs: The coat is starch, not flour, so it fries thinner, crisper and paler.

cues.text: The fat shivers and gives off a bubble now and then. The food does not sizzle.
A knife or skewer slips into the thickest part with no resistance.

technique/confit.does: Cooks food slowly while it lies covered in fat held far below a simmer, so that it turns tender and silky and the fat takes up its flavour. The food is lifted out and the scented fat is kept.
how: Season or cure the food first if it needs it, and dry it well.
Choose a pot just big enough for the food to lie in one snug layer, with the fat covering it.
Warm the fat over the lowest heat, or in a low oven, until it shivers and gives only the odd bubble. It must never fry.
Add the food and keep the fat at that heat until a knife slips into the thickest part with no resistance. Garlic needs less time than a duck leg, and a piece of fish least.
Lift the food out with a slotted spoon and drain it. Keep the fat.

mistakes.fix: Use the lowest heat, and lift the pan off the heat for a moment if the fat bubbles.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the fat get hot enough to fry, which toughens fish and browns garlic bitter.

mistakes.fix: Use a smaller pot, so that the fat covers the food.
mistakes.mistake: Using too little fat, so that part of the food sticks out and dries.

variant_of.differs: The food lies under fat and not under water, at a heat low enough that the fat barely stirs, so it gives its juices to the fat and takes the fat's flavour in return.

comes_after.why: The rolled round has to be thin and even or it will not puff.

cues.text: Bubbles rise on the upper face, then the bread swells like a ball on the flame, with brown flecks.
The finished bread is soft and flexible, not stiff or leathery.
A warm, toasty scent of wheat rises, with no burnt smell.

technique/cook-a-chapati.does: Cooks a thin round of atta dough for a short time on each face on a dry, hot iron plate, then lays it straight on the open flame, where the steam inside swells it into a soft ball. The finished bread is brushed with ghee and kept soft under a cloth.
how: Heat the iron plate until it is hot all over. A dusting of flour dropped on it should brown at once.
Lay the rolled round on the hot plate. When small bubbles show on the top, turn it.
Cook the second face until it has pale brown spots.
Using tongs, lift the bread off the plate and lay it straight on the open flame. It puffs up in moments.
Turn it over for a moment, then take it off. Brush it with ghee if wanted and stack the finished breads in a cloth, so that they stay soft.

mistakes.fix: Turn it as soon as bubbles show, and keep each side short.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking it too long on the plate, so that it dries out and will not puff.

mistakes.fix: Heat the plate until a dusting of flour browns at once.
mistakes.mistake: Putting it on a plate that is not hot enough, so that it turns leathery.

mistakes.fix: Hold it there for moments only and turn it.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the bread on the flame, where it chars to ash.

variant_of.differs: After the dry plate the bread is lifted off and held directly on the open flame, where trapped steam puffs it into a ball. A griddled flat bread is left on the hot surface from start to end.

comes_after.why: The vegetables go into a masala base that has already been fried until its fat parts.

cues.text: The pieces are tender and coated in a thick, dry spice paste, with a little browned crust on some.
A piece breaks easily under a spoon and a fork goes in with no resistance.

technique/cook-a-dry-vegetable-dish.does: Cooks cut vegetables in spiced fat with no added water, under a lid over a low heat, so that they soften in their own steam and end up coated in a thick spiced paste, with no gravy left in the pan.
how: Cut the vegetables into pieces of an even size and pat them dry.
Start the pan with a tempering of whole spices and a masala base cooked until its fat parts.
Add the vegetables and stir until they are coated. Add salt.
Cover the pan and cook over a low heat, lifting the lid and stirring now and then, so that the steam from the vegetables does the cooking. Sprinkle in a spoonful of water only if the pan catches.
Take off the lid at the end and stir over a higher heat for a short time, until any moisture has gone and the spices cling to the pieces.

mistakes.fix: Trust their own moisture and add only a spoonful if the pan catches.
mistakes.mistake: Adding water at the start, so that the vegetables boil and the dish turns into a watery stew.

mistakes.fix: Stir gently and seldom, and use a wide pan.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring hard, so that soft vegetables break into mush.

mistakes.fix: Take the lid off for the end of the cooking and let the moisture cook away.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the lid on to the end, so that the dish is damp and not dry.

variant_of.differs: No liquid is added, and the pieces are not browned first. The vegetables cook in their own steam under a lid and the dish ends dry, with a coat of spices, and not in a sauce.

comes_after.why: The dough must be risen before it is stretched and cooked.

cues.text: Large bubbles lift across the top and the underside is speckled with brown, not black all over.
The naan is soft and bends without cracking when it is lifted.
A toasty, buttery smell as the ghee meets the hot bread.

technique/cook-a-naan.does: Stretches a rested ball of naan dough by hand into a teardrop, cooks it on a very hot iron plate until it puffs and blisters, then holds it for a moment over the open flame to char it in spots. The finished bread is brushed with ghee and kept soft under a cloth.
how: Divide the risen dough into equal balls, cover them, and let them rest for a short while.
Flatten a ball on a floured board, then pull and press it by hand into a teardrop, a little thicker than a chapati.
Heat the iron plate until a drop of water skips on it. Wet one face of the naan lightly and lay it on the plate wet side down, so that it sticks and steams.
Cook until bubbles rise across the top and the underside is spotted with brown.
Turn the naan with the tongs and hold the top over the open flame for a moment, until it is blistered in dark spots.
Brush at once with melted ghee and keep the naan wrapped in a cloth while the rest are cooked.

mistakes.fix: Let the plate heat well first and cook quickly.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking on a plate that is not hot enough, so that the naan dries and turns leathery before it puffs.

mistakes.fix: Keep it a little thick and stretch it by hand.
mistakes.mistake: Rolling the dough thin like a chapati, so that it does not puff or stay soft.

mistakes.fix: Hold it over the flame only for a moment, turning it with tongs.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving it on the flame too long, so that it chars to a cinder.

variant_of.differs: The dough is yeast and yogurt dough, stretched by hand into a teardrop and left thicker. It is laid wet side down on the plate so that it sticks and steams, and it is charred over the flame at the end and not puffed whole.

en: cook rice in a paella pan

comes_after.why: The broth and the base of a paella start from a sofrito.

cues.text: The bubbling gives way to a faint crackle as the last of the liquid goes and the bottom begins to toast.
A nutty, toasted smell. A burnt smell means the pan must come off the heat at once.
The rice lies in a thin, even layer with separate grains and no liquid standing.

technique/cook-a-paella.does: Cooks short-grain rice in a thin, even layer in a wide, shallow pan, in a well-flavoured broth, with no lid and no stirring, until the rice has taken the broth up and a thin toasted crust, the socarrat, forms on the bottom.
how: Bring the flavoured broth, which has already simmered with its meat and vegetables, to a lively boil in the paella pan. Taste it: it should taste a little strong, as the rice will soften it.
Scatter the rice evenly over the pan in one layer and stir once to spread it. Do not stir again.
Cook at a strong simmer, then turn the heat down once the rice has swollen. Turn the pan over the flame if it is bigger than the burner, so that all the rice cooks at one pace.
When the broth has almost gone and the rice is nearly tender, turn the heat up for a short while to toast the bottom.
Take the pan off the heat and let it rest, covered with a clean cloth, so that the rice finishes in its own steam.

mistakes.fix: Spread it once and then leave it alone.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring the rice, which releases starch and makes it creamy like a risotto and not loose.

mistakes.fix: Measure the broth against the rice and keep the layer thin.
mistakes.mistake: Too much broth or too deep a layer, which leaves the rice soft, wet and uneven.

mistakes.fix: Listen for the crackle, smell the pan, and take it off the heat when it smells toasty.
mistakes.mistake: Toasting the bottom too long, so that the crust burns.

variant_of.differs: The rice is cooked uncovered, in a thin layer in a wide pan and in a flavoured broth, with no stirring, and it is finished with a toasted crust on the bottom. Plain rice is cooked under a tight lid.

en: fry a paratha on the plate

comes_after.why: The layers are made by the folding, and the plate only sets them apart, so folding comes first.

cues.text: Golden brown spots spread over both faces and the layers lift a little at the edge.
The ghee sizzles softly at the edge of the bread and does not spit.
The bread is crisp at the surface, and the layers spring apart when it is pressed.

technique/cook-a-paratha.does: Cooks a folded and lightly rolled round of atta dough on a hot iron plate, spooning a little ghee over one face and then the other, until each face is golden in spots and the layers inside have set apart, flaky and soft. The bread stays on the plate from start to end.
how: Heat the iron plate until a sprinkle of flour dropped on it browns slowly.
Lay the bread on the plate and cook until the first face is dry in spots and the bread has turned pale and a little puffy.
Turn it, spoon ghee over the top and let it sink in at the edge.
Turn it again, spoon ghee on the other face and press the edges gently with the spatula, until both faces are golden brown in spots.
Lift it out and, while it is hot, crush it lightly between the palms so that the layers open.

mistakes.fix: Heat the plate first and spoon ghee on each face as it cooks.
mistakes.mistake: Using too little ghee or a plate that is not hot, so that the bread dries and turns leathery.

mistakes.fix: Press only gently at the edges, and crush it lightly after cooking.
mistakes.mistake: Pressing hard on the bread, which squeezes the layers together.

variant_of.differs: Ghee is spooned over each face as it cooks, so the bread browns in ghee and not on a dry or barely oiled plate, and the folded layers set apart inside.
The bread stays on the plate from start to end and is never lifted to puff on the open flame. A paratha is meant to be flaky and golden, and a chapati is meant to swell into a ball.

comes_after.why: The potato has to be soft before the egg goes round it, and it is cooked soft in oil first.
The cake is turned over in the same way as any food that must be turned while its top is still soft.

cues.text: The edge pulls from the pan and turns pale gold, and the top shrinks from wet to a soft, glossy skin.
The pan shakes freely and the cake slides on the oil.
A sweet, eggy smell. A sharp, burnt smell means the heat is too high.

technique/cook-a-tortilla.does: Sets a mix of beaten egg and soft cooked potato in a small pan into a thick, round cake, golden outside and tender or even creamy in the middle. It is turned over once with the help of a plate.
how: Heat a spoonful of the kept oil in a small non-stick pan over a medium heat, so that it coats the base and the sides.
Pour in the mix of egg and potato and press it level. It should hiss softly, not spit.
Cook gently. Shake the pan now and then and run a spatula round the edge to keep it neat and tucked in, until the underside is golden and the edge has set while the top is still wet.
Turn it over onto a flat plate and slide it back, as in the flip, then tuck the edges in and cook the other side briefly.
Slide it onto a plate and let it stand a while. The middle can be left soft or set firm, as the cook likes.

mistakes.fix: Cook it over a medium heat or lower, and give it time.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking it too hot, so that the outside burns before the egg in the middle has begun to set.

mistakes.fix: Wait until the edge is firm and the cake slides when the pan is shaken.
mistakes.mistake: Turning it before the underside has set, so that it tears and runs.

mistakes.fix: Use a small, deep pan, so that the cake is thick.
mistakes.mistake: Using a pan far too big, which leaves a thin, dry cake.

variant_of.differs: The egg is a thick flat cake with soft potato inside it and is never rolled. It is cooked slowly, turned over with a plate, and served warm or at room temperature, with the middle left soft or firm to taste. A rolled omelette is thin, quick and creamy.

en: cook in garlic and chilli oil

comes_after.why: The garlic has to be sliced evenly, so that all of it turns pale gold at the same moment.

cues.text: A steady, lively sizzle when the food goes in, which dies down to a gentle bubbling.
Sweet garlic, with no sharp or bitter edge.
The garlic is pale gold and the shrimp are curled and opaque, with the oil bubbling round them.

technique/cook-al-ajillo.does: Cooks small pieces of shellfish or mushroom for a short time in a generous pool of olive oil scented with sliced garlic and a piece of hot pepper, in a shallow earthenware dish. The oil becomes the sauce, and the food reaches the table still sizzling in it.
how: Put the olive oil, the sliced garlic and the pieces of hot pepper in a cold earthenware dish and set it over a medium heat, so that the garlic warms along with the oil.
Let the oil heat until the garlic starts to bubble gently and turns pale gold. Do not let it brown.
Add the dry, salted shrimp or mushrooms in one layer and turn the heat up. Shake the dish now and then so that they cook evenly in the oil.
As soon as the shrimp turn opaque and curl, or the mushrooms soften, take the dish off the heat. The hot dish keeps the oil sizzling.
Scatter chopped parsley over and take the dish straight to the table, with bread to mop up the oil.

mistakes.fix: Start it in cold oil, and add the food as soon as the garlic is pale gold.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the garlic brown, which turns the whole pool of oil bitter.

mistakes.fix: Take the dish off the heat the moment they turn opaque.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking the shrimp too long, so that they turn rubbery.

mistakes.fix: Pat them dry first.
mistakes.mistake: Adding wet shrimp, which spit and cool the oil.

variant_of.differs: The food lies in a deep pool of oil and not in a thin film, the garlic and the pepper are warmed in the oil first, and the dish goes to the table as it was cooked, oil and all. A sauté keeps small pieces moving in a hot pan with a little fat.

comes_after.why: The onion is softened in the fat before the grain goes in.

cues.text: Small steam holes show in the surface and no liquid is left in the pan.
The grains are plump and tender with a slight bite, and they fall apart when fluffed.
A nutty, savoury taste with the sweetness of the onion and paste.

technique/cook-bulgur-pilaf.does: Fries coarse bulgur in fat with softened onion and a spoon of paste until every grain is coated, then covers it with hot liquid and leaves it under a lid, without stirring, until the grains have swollen, drunk the liquid and stand apart.
how: Soften the onion in the fat, then stir in the pepper or tomato paste and fry it until the colour deepens.
Add the bulgur and stir for a short while until each grain is coated and smells toasty.
Pour in hot water or stock, a little more than the volume of the bulgur, and add salt. Bring it to a boil.
Cover and turn the heat to its lowest. Do not stir.
When the liquid has gone, take the pan off the heat, lay a cloth under the lid and leave it to stand.
Fluff the grains with a fork before serving.

mistakes.fix: Stir only when the grains are coated, and fluff at the end.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring while it cooks, which breaks the grains and turns them sticky.

mistakes.fix: Measure the liquid and use only a little more than the bulgur.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring in too much liquid, which leaves a wet porridge.

mistakes.fix: Let it stand under a cloth and lid first.
mistakes.mistake: Serving it straight from the heat, so that it is wet and clumped.

variant_of.differs: The grain is coarse bulgur, which is already steamed and dried, so it needs no washing or soaking and takes less liquid and less time than rice. A spoon of pepper or tomato paste goes in with the onion for colour and body.

comes_after.why: A tagine starts on a bed of softened onion, so a cook has to know how to soften onion in fat without colour.

cues.text: Only a few small bubbles stir at the edge of the sauce, and a little steam rises from the top of the cone.
The meat gives way to the side of a spoon without a pull.
The scent of the spices turns round and warm, with no sharp note of scorching.

technique/cook-in-a-tagine.does: Cooks meat or poultry slowly over low heat in a shallow earthenware dish under a tall cone lid, on a bed of sliced onion, fat and spices, with only a little water. The steam rises into the cone, cools and runs back down, so the food stews in its own juices and the sauce stays short and strong.
how: Spread sliced onion over the base of the dish with the fat and the spices, and pour in a little water, only enough to wet the base.
Lay the meat on top and season it. Do not brown it first.
Put on the lid and set the dish over the lowest heat, with a diffuser under it if the flame is fierce. Leave it alone and lift the lid as seldom as you can.
When the meat is tender, spread over it whatever finishes the dish, such as dried fruit, olives or vegetables, and cover again.
Cook on until the sauce has shrunk to a rich coat and the fat shines on top.

mistakes.fix: Start on the lowest heat, use a diffuser, and bring the heat up slowly.
mistakes.mistake: Setting the dish on a fierce heat, which scorches the base and can crack the clay.

mistakes.fix: Start with only a little. The lid sends the steam back down.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring in water to cover, which makes a thin soup and washes out the taste of the spices.

mistakes.fix: Leave it covered and check only near the end.
mistakes.mistake: Lifting the lid again and again, which lets the steam escape.

variant_of.differs: Braising browns the food first and cooks it in a measured amount of liquid. A tagine skips the browning, lays the meat on a bed of onion and spices and adds only a little water, because the cone lid sends the steam back down.

comes_after.why: The gravy is made on a masala base cooked until its fat parts, so the base comes first.

cues.text: The gravy is thick and glossy and clings to the pieces, with a little fat shining at the edge.
The pieces give easily under a spoon and are tender throughout.
The scent is round and full, with no raw spice in it.

technique/cook-in-masala-gravy.does: Simmers pieces of meat, bird or firm cheese in a gravy made from a fried masala base, with a little water or cream, until they are tender and the gravy has thickened and clings to them.
how: Start from a masala base cooked until its fat has parted.
Add the pieces, raw or already roasted or fried, and stir them into the base for a moment so that they are coated.
Add hot water or cream a little at a time, and bring the pan to a gentle simmer. Cover it partly.
Stir now and then and scrape the bottom. Add a little more liquid if the gravy dries out before the pieces are tender.
Stop when the pieces are tender and the gravy is thick enough to coat them, with a shine of fat on top.
Stir in the finishing touches, such as cream, dried fenugreek leaf or garam masala, off the heat or just before.

mistakes.fix: Add hot water, a little at a time.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring in cold water, which stops the cooking and thins the flavour.

mistakes.fix: Keep a gentle simmer and stir now and then.
mistakes.mistake: Boiling hard, so that the gravy splits and the pieces turn tough.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat for a moment, or lower the heat, before the cream goes in.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the cream or yogurt to a boiling pan, so that it splits.

variant_of.differs: The pieces are not browned first and there is no wine or stock. The liquid is water or cream added to a fried masala base, and the sauce is thick and clings to the pieces. It is cooked on the stove, covered only in part.

comes_after.why: The rice is soaked before it is cooked in the seasoned stock.

cues.text: A sweet, savoury steam rises from the pot.
The rice is evenly tinted by the seasoning, and the pieces are scattered on top.

technique/cook-mixed-rice.does: Cooks washed, soaked rice together with a seasoned stock and small pieces of vegetables, mushrooms or tofu, so that the taste cooks into every grain.
how: Put the washed, soaked, drained rice in the pot or the rice cooker and level it.
Pour in the seasoned stock, in place of plain water, up to the usual level. Stir once, then leave it still.
Scatter the cut pieces evenly over the top without stirring them in, and shut the lid.
Cook the rice as usual, then leave it to rest, covered.
Fold the pieces through the rice at the end.

mistakes.fix: Lay the pieces on top and fold them in afterwards.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring the pieces into the rice before cooking, which makes some of the rice cook unevenly.

mistakes.fix: Use the same amount of liquid as for plain rice, counting the seasonings as part of it.
mistakes.mistake: Adding too much stock and seasoning, so that the rice is soft and salty.

variant_of.differs: The rice cooks in seasoned stock together with its pieces of vegetable and tofu, and not in plain water, so the whole pot is flavoured.

comes_after.why: The dough has to be folded into layers before it is cooked.

cues.text: Both faces are golden and speckled, and the edges look layered.
The fat sizzles gently under the dough.
The bread is crisp on the outside and soft inside, and pulls apart in thin sheets.

technique/cook-msemen.does: Stretches a folded square of layered dough out thin again with oiled fingertips, lays it on a hot, lightly oiled griddle and cooks both faces until it is golden in speckles and its layers have set apart, so that it comes away in flaky sheets.
how: Heat a flat griddle or a wide pan over a medium heat and oil it lightly.
Press the folded square out with oiled fingertips, to a flat square that is still in layers.
Lay it on the griddle and cook until the underside is gold and speckled.
Turn it over once and cook the other side the same way.
Lift it out, clap it between the hands so that the layers open, and serve it hot.

mistakes.fix: Press it out with oiled fingertips.
mistakes.mistake: Rolling the square flat with a pin, which crushes the layers together.

mistakes.fix: Keep the heat moderate.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking on too high a heat, so that the outside burns and the layers inside stay doughy.

variant_of.differs: Griddling cooks flat breads that are already shaped. Here the dough is a folded square of many layers of fat and dough, pressed out thin by hand on the pan itself, turned once, and clapped open at the end.

cues.text: After the dips the arms curl into tight spirals and the purple skin is still on.
A knife slides into the thickest part of an arm as into a ripe pear, with no pull.
The cut rounds are glossy and keep their curl, with the skin still on the edge.

technique/cook-octopus.does: Cooks a whole octopus in plenty of water, first dipping it in and out of the boil several times so that the arms curl and the skin stays on, then lets it bubble steadily until the thickest part of an arm is tender. It is rested, then snipped into rounds with scissors.
how: Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Hold the octopus by the head with tongs and dip it in and out of the water, a few times, for a moment each time. The arms curl up.
Lower it in completely. When the water comes back to a boil, turn the heat down to a steady bubbling.
Cook until a knife slips into the thickest part of an arm with no pull. The time depends on the size of the animal, so test it often towards the end.
Lift it out onto a board, cover it with a cloth and let it rest while the potatoes cook in the same water. It goes on softening as it stands.
Snip the arms into rounds about as thick as a thumb with kitchen scissors, straight onto the serving dish. Cut the head into strips if it is used.

mistakes.fix: Dip it in and out of the boil first, to set the skin.
mistakes.mistake: Lowering the octopus straight in, so that the arms stay limp and the skin comes away.

mistakes.fix: Turn the heat down to a steady bubbling once it is in.
mistakes.mistake: Boiling it hard for the whole time, which toughens the outside before the middle has softened.

mistakes.fix: Snip them with scissors straight onto the dish.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting the rounds with a knife on a board, which squashes them and loses the juices.

variant_of.differs: The food is one whole animal and not many small pieces. It is dipped in and out of the boil first, then cooked at a steady bubbling, rested out of the water, and cut with scissors. Boiling cooks small pieces fast and evenly in fast-bubbling water.

en: seal the pot and cook slowly

comes_after.why: The rice goes into the pot only nearly cooked, so a cook has to be able to stop it at that point first.
The meat goes into the pot already marinated, and cooks in the steam without being browned.

cues.text: A rich scent of spice, saffron and ghee seeps out from under the lid when the pot is nearly ready.
A faint, steady hiss comes from the pot, with no hard bubbling.
The grains of rice on top are long, dry and separate, and the meat below is tender and coated in a thick gravy.

technique/cook-on-dum.does: Layers marinated meat and nearly cooked rice in a heavy pot, closes the lid tightly, often with a rope of dough, and finishes the dish in its own steam over a very low heat. Nothing is stirred, and the pot is opened at the table.
how: Spread the marinated meat in an even layer on the bottom of a heavy pot, with a little ghee.
Pile the nearly cooked rice over the meat in loose layers, with herbs, crisp fried onions and ghee between them. Do not press it down.
Sprinkle saffron steeped in warm milk over the top.
Seal the gap between the lid and the pot with a rope of firm dough, pressing it in all round. A heavy cloth under the lid works too.
Set the pot on a flat plate of iron over a medium heat for a short spell to build up steam, then turn the heat to its lowest and leave it undisturbed.
Rest the sealed pot off the heat before it is broken open. Fold the rice and the meat together from the bottom with a flat spoon, so the layers are kept.

mistakes.fix: Press the rope of dough into the join all round, and patch any gap at once.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the seal leak, so that the steam escapes and the rice on top stays hard.

mistakes.fix: Set the pot on a flat iron plate and turn the heat to its lowest once the steam builds.
mistakes.mistake: Keeping the heat too high, so that the bottom layer scorches.

mistakes.fix: Leave the pot shut until the end of the rest.
mistakes.mistake: Lifting the lid to look, which lets the steam out and breaks the slow cooking.

mistakes.fix: Dig down to the bottom with a flat spoon and lift the layers out whole.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring the layers together, so that the dish turns into a heap of mush.

variant_of.differs: The seal is for a pot on the stove, over a very low heat, and not for a long bake. The food is layered, half-cooked rice over marinated meat, and cooks in the steam and scent held in the pot, never stirred.
A pilaf cooks raw rice in a measured amount of stock. Here the rice is boiled nearly done first, laid over meat that has not been browned, and finished by steam alone.

comes_after.why: A pilaf begins by sweating onion.

cues.text: The grains are separate and dry, with small steam holes across the surface and no liquid left.

technique/cook-pilaf.does: Cooks rice by coating it in hot fat with sweated onion, then letting it absorb a measured amount of hot stock under a lid.
how: Sweat finely cut onion in butter without colour.
Stir in the rice until every grain is coated and turns glassy at the edges.
Pour in the hot stock all at once, add a bouquet garni and bring to a boil.
Cover closely with paper and a lid, and finish in the oven or over the lowest heat, without stirring.
Rest it off the heat, then fluff it with a fork and a little butter.

mistakes.fix: Leave it shut until the time is up.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring or lifting the lid while it cooks, which breaks the grains and lets the steam out.

mistakes.fix: Measure the rice by volume and the stock against it. With too much, it turns to porridge.
mistakes.mistake: Guessing the liquid.

cues.text: The polenta pulls away from the side of the pot in a mass as it is stirred.
A taste is soft and sweet, with no gritty or raw-flour bite.

technique/cook-polenta.does: Rains coarse maize meal in a thin stream into boiling salted water, stirring all the while, then cooks it for a long time over the lowest heat, stirring often, until it swells into a thick, smooth porridge that comes away from the sides of the pot. It is eaten soft and creamy, or poured out to set firm.
