how: Bring plenty of salted water to a boil in a heavy pot with a broad base.
Lower the heat so that the water is just bubbling. With one hand let the meal fall in a thin stream, and stir with the other, so that no lumps form.
Keep the heat very low. The porridge will pop and spit, so stir with a long wooden spoon and keep a hand clear of the pot.
Stir often, scraping the base and the corners, for a long time, adding hot water if it gets too stiff to stir, until it is thick and smooth and the grains are tender, with no raw taste.
Beat in butter and cheese off the heat if the dish asks for them. Serve it soft at once, or pour it onto a board and let it set.

mistakes.fix: Let it fall in a thin stream while stirring.
mistakes.mistake: Tipping the meal in all at once, which clumps into lumps that never soften.

mistakes.fix: Keep it at the lowest heat and stir often.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking it at a fierce heat, which scorches the base and leaves the grains hard.

mistakes.fix: Keep cooking and stirring until the grains are tender.
mistakes.mistake: Stopping as soon as it thickens, when the grains are still raw.

variant_of.differs: The meal is rained in a thin stream into boiling water and the porridge is stirred for a long time over a very low heat, until the grains are tender and the mass pulls away from the pot. A white sauce or a milk pudding is stirred only until it thickens.

comes_after.why: Washing takes off the loose starch that would make the rice gluey.

cues.text: The bubbling goes quiet and the pot starts to hiss softly once the water is used up.
Small steam holes show on the surface and no water is left at the edge.
The grains are plump and tender, and a short-grain rice clings in a mass.

technique/cook-rice.does: Cooks washed rice in a measured amount of water in a covered pot until all the water is taken up, then leaves it covered off the heat so that the grains finish plump, tender and separate, or lightly sticky for a short-grain kind.
how: Wash the rice in several changes of cold water, swirling it, until the water is much less cloudy. Drain it well.
Put it in a pot with a tight lid and add the measured water. A short-grain rice takes a little less water than a long-grain one.
Bring it to the boil uncovered or just covered, then turn the heat to its lowest and cover tightly.
Leave the lid on and do not stir, so that the steam stays in.
Take it off the heat when the water has gone, and let it stand covered. Then fluff it with a fork, or fold it with a paddle.

mistakes.fix: Leave the lid on from the moment the heat goes down until the rice has rested.
mistakes.mistake: Lifting the lid again and again, so that the steam escapes and the top stays hard.

mistakes.fix: Do not stir. Fluff it with a fork only at the end.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring, which releases starch and turns the rice gluey.

mistakes.fix: Measure the water against the rice, and use a little less for a short-grain kind.
mistakes.mistake: Using too much water, so that the rice turns soft and wet.

comes_after.why: The lentils are simmered first, and the rice goes into their pot.
Washing takes off the loose starch that would make the pot gluey.

cues.text: The liquid is gone and small steam holes show in the surface.
Both the rice and the lentils are tender, whole and separate.
The bubbling quietens to a soft hiss as the last liquid is taken up.

technique/cook-rice-with-lentils.does: Cooks rice in the pot where lentils have been simmering, so that the rice takes up the lentil water and its flavour, and the rice and the lentils finish together under one lid as a dish of tender grains and whole lentils.
how: Simmer the lentils in plenty of water until they are tender outside but still firm at the centre.
Wash the rice until the water is much less cloudy, and drain it.
Stir the rice into the pot with the lentils and add salt. If the liquid does not stand above them by about the depth of a finger, add hot water.
Bring to a boil, then turn the heat to its lowest, cover tightly and leave without stirring.
Rest it covered off the heat, then fluff it gently with a fork.

mistakes.fix: Take the lentils off when the centre is still firm. They finish with the rice.
mistakes.mistake: Simmering the lentils soft before the rice goes in, so that they fall apart.

mistakes.fix: Let the liquid stand only a finger above the grains.
mistakes.mistake: Adding too much water, so that the dish turns to porridge.

mistakes.fix: Stir once to settle the rice, then leave it alone.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring after the rice has gone in, which turns the starch gluey.

variant_of.differs: The rice goes into a pot of part-cooked lentils and takes up their liquid, so the rice and the lentils finish together. It is not cooked alone in measured water.

comes_after.why: The rice is first softened in water, as in plain rice cooking.

cues.text: The pudding is pale and creamy and coats the spoon, and the grains are swollen and soft.
The spoon drags a little on the base of the pan, and the pudding is looser than it should be when set.
Sweet and milky, with no hard centre in the grain.

technique/cook-sutlac.does: Simmers washed rice in water until it is soft, then in plenty of milk with sugar, stirring often, until the grains are very tender and the milk has thickened to a loose, creamy pudding that sets a little as it cools.
how: Wash the rice and simmer it in water until it is soft and has drunk most of the water.
Pour in the milk and stir in the sugar. Bring it back to a gentle simmer.
Stir often, scraping the base of the pan, until the rice is very soft and the milk has begun to thicken.
Stir in a smooth slurry of rice flour if the pudding needs more body, and simmer for a short while longer.
Pour the pudding into bowls while it is still runny, because it thickens as it cools.

mistakes.fix: Stir often and keep the heat gentle.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving it unstirred, so that the milk catches on the base of the pan and scorches.

mistakes.fix: Pour it into the bowls while it is still loose.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking it until it is stiff in the pan, so that it sets like glue when cool.

mistakes.fix: Soften the rice in water first.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the milk to hard rice, so that the grains stay firm in the thick milk.

variant_of.differs: The rice is cooked in a large amount of milk and stirred often, to a soft, thick pudding. Plain rice is cooked in a measured amount of water, left alone and kept in separate grains.

cues.text: An even, unbroken wall of flesh and no hard core or seeds left inside.
The inside is smooth to the touch.

technique/core.does: Takes out the hard centre, the seeds or the pith of a fruit or vegetable, or hollows it out, so that the flesh is left as an even wall that cooks evenly or holds a filling.
how: Cut off the top, or push the corer in from the stem end, keeping the wall of the flesh even.
Twist the corer, or run the tip of a small knife round the inside, and lift out the core and seeds.
Scoop out any pith or hard bits that are left, taking care not to cut through the wall.
Keep the scooped flesh if it is wanted for the filling.

mistakes.fix: Work slowly and keep the corer in the middle.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting through the wall, so that a filling leaks.

mistakes.fix: Scrape the inside clean with a spoon.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving pith or seeds behind, which turn bitter or hard.

mistakes.fix: Leave a wall of about the width of a finger.
mistakes.mistake: Scooping out too much flesh, so that the wall collapses as it cooks.

cues.text: Bubbles rise around the edge of the lid and the liquid reaches the top of the pieces.
The pieces keep their shape, and the liquid slowly turns glossy.

technique/cover-with-a-drop-lid.does: Lays a lid that is smaller than the pot straight on the food, so that the simmering liquid is pushed up and over every piece. The pieces cook evenly in a small amount of liquid and stay still.
how: Arrange the food in a single layer in a wide pot and add just enough liquid to come part of the way up.
Bring the liquid to a simmer.
Lay the drop lid on the food, inside the pot. Wet it first, so that nothing sticks to it.
Keep the liquid at a gentle simmer, so that it bubbles up around the edge of the lid.
Take the lid off for the last stretch if the liquid should reduce to a glaze.

mistakes.fix: Use a drop lid, or a round of baking paper cut to fit with a small hole in the middle.
mistakes.mistake: Using a plain lid that sits on the rim of the pot, so that the top pieces stay dry and uncooked.

mistakes.fix: Turn the heat down until it only bubbles gently.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the liquid boil hard under the lid, which knocks the pieces about.

variant_of.differs: The lid lies on the food itself, and not on the rim of the pot, so the liquid is held against every piece and little liquid is needed.

cues.text: A soft, steady hiss comes from under the lid.
Drops of steam gather on the inside of the lid and run back down.

technique/cover-with-a-lid.does: Puts a lid over a pot or a dish, so that steam and heat stay in and the food cooks gently in its own moisture.
how: Choose a lid that fits the pot or the dish well.
Put it on once the food is heated and the liquid is in.
Leave it on while the food cooks. Every time it is lifted, heat and steam escape.
Lift the lid away from you, so that the steam does not scald.

mistakes.fix: Leave it shut and trust the sound.
mistakes.mistake: Lifting the lid again and again to look, which lets the heat out.

mistakes.fix: Use a lid that sits snugly, or cover the dish tightly with foil.
mistakes.mistake: Using a lid that does not fit, so that the steam escapes.

cues.text: The garlic turns from pieces to a pale, glossy, wet paste.
A sharp, raw scent rises as soon as it breaks, and fades into the dressing.

technique/crush.does: Presses a clove of garlic flat under the blade of a knife, or under a pestle, and works it with salt into a damp, rough paste that melts into a dressing or a sauce.
how: Peel the clove and set it on a board with a little salt. The salt grips it and wears it down.
Lay the flat of a broad knife on the clove and press down with the heel of the hand until it splits.
Drag the blade over the pieces with the flat tilted, again and again, until the garlic is a damp paste with no lumps.
Scrape the paste into the dressing or the sauce and stir it in at once.

mistakes.fix: Add a little salt first, so that it grips.
mistakes.mistake: Crushing without salt, so that the garlic slides about under the blade and stays in pieces.

mistakes.fix: Stir it into the acid or the oil soon after it is done.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the paste on the board to turn bitter and harsh.

variant_of.differs: The garlic is pressed and dragged flat under a blade or a pestle for a few moments into a damp, rough paste, and not worked long in a mortar until it is smooth.

en: thicken a bean soup with its own beans

comes_after.why: The beans must be simmered tender before any of them can be crushed.

cues.text: The broth turns cloudy and creamy and a spoon leaves a trail in it.
Some beans still hold their shape when pressed, while others melt into the broth.

technique/crush-some-of-the-beans.does: Presses a few spoonfuls of cooked, tender beans or other pulses against the side of the pot, or lifts out a ladle of them with a little broth and crushes them, then stirs the paste back in, so that the soup turns creamy and thick without flour or cream while the rest of the beans stay whole.
how: Wait until the beans are completely tender, or they will not crush.
Lift a ladle of beans, with a little of their broth, into a bowl.
Crush them to a rough paste with the back of a spoon or a masher. Do not make them completely smooth.
Stir the paste back into the pot and let the soup bubble gently for a little while, until it has thickened.
Crush more if the soup is still thin. Thin it with hot water if it has grown too thick.

mistakes.fix: Cook them longer, until a bean crushes at a light touch.
mistakes.mistake: Crushing beans that are still firm, which leaves a gritty, thin soup.

mistakes.fix: Crush only a ladle or so and leave the rest whole.
mistakes.mistake: Crushing nearly all of them, so that the soup turns to paste.

variant_of.differs: Only a few beans are crushed, with no butter or milk, and the rest are left whole. The crushed beans thicken the soup they were cooked in.

cues.text: The cubes have clean, sharp corners and smooth sides.
The blade glides through with almost no pressure.

technique/cube-tofu.does: Cuts a block of soft tofu into neat cubes with a wet blade and a slicing motion, without pressing, so that the cubes keep their corners and do not break.
how: Lift the block out of its water and let it drain for a short while on a board.
Wet a thin, sharp knife.
Cut the block in slabs, then in sticks, then in cubes, drawing the blade through in one slow motion and never pressing down.
Slide the cubes into the dish on the flat of the knife or on a spoon, and do not stir them roughly.

mistakes.fix: Draw the blade through in a slicing motion.
mistakes.mistake: Pressing down with the knife, which crushes the block into crumbs.

mistakes.fix: Wet the blade.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting with a dry knife, so that the tofu drags and tears.

variant_of.differs: Soft tofu is too tender to be stacked and cut like a vegetable, so the block is cut slab by slab with a wet blade and no pressure, and the cubes are moved on a flat blade.

comes_after.why: Batons start as thick, even slices.

cues.text: Sticks with flat faces and square corners, all of one thickness, so that they cook in the same time.

technique/cut-into-batons.does: Cuts food into even, square-sided sticks.
how: Peel the vegetable and trim its sides flat to make a block.
Slice the block into slabs as thick as the sticks you want.
Stack a few slabs and cut them lengthwise into sticks as wide as the slabs are thick.
Keep the trimmings for a soup or a mash.

mistakes.fix: Trim the sides flat before you slice.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting from a round vegetable without squaring it first, so that the sticks come out as wedges.

mistakes.fix: Hold the knife straight and take the same width at every cut.
mistakes.mistake: Slabs of uneven thickness, so that thin sticks burn while thick ones stay raw.

cues.text: The pieces are blocky and about the same size.

technique/cut-into-chunks.does: Cuts a firm food into large, bite-sized pieces of about the same size, bigger and less exact than dice, so that they stay whole through a long simmer.
how: Peel the food if it needs peeling, and cut it in half or in long strips to get a flat base.
Cut across into thick pieces that fit one mouthful.
Keep the pieces about equal in size, so that they cook in the same time.
For a hard squash, rest the cut side down on the board so that it cannot slip.

mistakes.fix: Cut by eye to a single size.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting some pieces much smaller, so that they dissolve while the others are hard.

mistakes.fix: Cut it in halves on a steady board first.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting a hard squash held in the air, which slips.

variant_of.differs: The pieces are large and not cut to an exact cube, because they are meant to be eaten as chunks after a long simmer.

cues.text: The pieces are small and similar in size, and can be scattered with a spoon.

technique/cut-into-small-pieces.does: Cuts food into small, loose pieces, not exact cubes, so that they spread through rice, a filling or a sauce.
how: Trim the food, take out any bone or tough stem, and slice it first if it is wide.
Cut the slices across into small, rough pieces.
Try to keep the pieces about the same size, so that they cook together.
Gather the pieces in a bowl as you go.

mistakes.fix: Cut them about as small as a grain of rice.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting the pieces large, so that they cannot spread evenly through the rice.

mistakes.fix: Use a sharp knife and a clear board.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting soft food on a crowded board, so that it is squashed.

variant_of.differs: The pieces are small but cut by eye and not to an exact cube, since they only need to blend into rice or a filling.
The pieces are small and loose, cut to spread through rice, a filling or a sauce, so the exact shape still does not matter.

comes_after.why: Pasta is cut from a sheet that has first been rolled evenly thin.

cues.text: The strips are of even width, with clean edges, and they fall apart when shaken.
The sheet folds without sticking to itself.

technique/cut-pasta.does: Cuts a thin sheet of rolled pasta dough into ribbons, strips or squares of even size, so that they cook at the same speed.
how: Roll the dough out thin and let the sheet dry for a short while, until it feels leathery and no longer sticks.
Dust the sheet lightly with flour, then fold it loosely into a flat roll, or leave it as a sheet.
With a long, sharp knife cut straight across at the width the dish needs: narrow for ribbons, broad for short strips.
Shake the cut pieces loose, toss them in a little flour and lay them in loose heaps or nests on a floured tray.

mistakes.fix: Let it dry a little and dust it with flour.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting a sheet that is still sticky, so that the pieces glue together.

mistakes.fix: Cut with a long knife and a steady hand, in straight lines.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting strips of uneven width, so that the thin ones are soft before the wide ones are ready.

mistakes.fix: Toss it in flour and lay it loosely in nests.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving cut pasta in a damp heap, so that it sticks into a lump.

cues.text: A steady stream of small bubbles around each piece, slowing as the food dries and turns golden.
A lively, even crackle. A loud spit means water, and silence means the oil is too cool.

technique/deep-fry.does: Cooks food under hot oil, so that its surface dries to a crisp shell while the inside steams.
how: Dry the food well. Water makes hot oil spit and boil over.
Fill a deep, heavy pan no more than a third full of oil and heat it.
Lower in a small batch, so that the oil keeps its heat and the pieces do not stick together.
Lift the food out when it is crisp and golden, drain it on a rack and salt it at once.
For thick chips, fry once gently until soft and pale, rest them, then fry again in hotter oil until crisp.

mistakes.fix: Fry in small batches and let the oil come back to heat between them.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding the pan, so that the oil cools and the food soaks it up and turns greasy.

mistakes.fix: Pat everything dry first, and never fill the pan more than a third.
mistakes.mistake: Putting wet food into the oil, so that it spits and foams up.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat at once and let it cool.
mistakes.mistake: Oil that smokes. It tastes acrid and is close to catching fire.

variant_of.differs: The food is covered by the oil and floats in it. Nothing touches the pan.

comes_after.why: There is nothing to deglaze until a sear has left a fond.

cues.text: A sharp hiss and a burst of steam when the liquid hits the pan.
The bottom of the pan comes clean under the spoon and the liquid darkens.
The raw smell of the wine goes as it boils.

technique/deglaze.does: Dissolves the browned layer stuck to a hot pan with a splash of liquid, turning it into the base of a sauce.
how: Pour off the fat, and keep everything brown that sticks to the pan.
Soften a little shallot or garlic in the pan first, if the sauce calls for it.
Take the pan off the flame to add wine or spirits, then put it back.
Scrape the bottom with a wooden spoon as the liquid boils, until the pan is clean and the liquid has turned brown.

mistakes.fix: Taste a scrap of the fond first. If it is bitter, wipe the pan out and build the sauce without it.
mistakes.mistake: Deglazing a pan whose fond has burnt black, which makes a bitter sauce.

mistakes.fix: Pour the fat off first. The flavour is in the brown bits, not in the fat.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving all the fat in, so that the sauce is greasy and will not come together.

comes_after.why: The loose salt on the surface is rinsed off before the long soak.

cues.text: A flake from the thickest part tastes lightly salted, like seasoned fish and not like brine.
The flesh has swelled and gone soft and springy, where it was stiff and hard before.

technique/desalt.does: Draws most of the salt out of salt cod by leaving it in cold water that is changed again and again, so that the fish tastes of cod and not only of salt, and can be cooked on its own.
how: Rinse the surface salt off the pieces under cold water.
Lay the pieces skin side up in a deep dish and cover them with plenty of cold water. Keep the dish in the fridge.
Change the water several times, and leave thick pieces longer than thin ones.
Taste a small flake from the thickest part. Stop when it tastes lightly seasoned, and go on if it still tastes of brine.
Drain the pieces and pat them dry before they are cooked.

mistakes.fix: Soak it in the fridge and change the water often.
mistakes.mistake: Soaking at room temperature, where the fish spoils and turns slimy before it loses its salt.

mistakes.fix: Taste a flake from the thickest part.
mistakes.mistake: Tasting the thin end only, which loses its salt first.

mistakes.fix: Taste the fish and the sauce before adding any salt.
mistakes.mistake: Salting the dish as usual afterwards, so that it ends up far too salty.

variant_of.differs: The aim is to take salt out and not to swell the food. The water is changed again and again, and the cook tastes the thickest part to decide when it is done, not the clock.

comes_after.why: A dice is a slice cut again, lengthwise and across, so an even slice comes first.

cues.text: The cubes are all one size, with square edges.
The knife glides forward and down. Your knuckles guide the blade and your fingertips stay tucked behind them.

technique/dice.does: Cuts food into even cubes, so that every piece cooks at the same speed.
how: Trim the piece so that it has a flat side and sits still on the board.
Cut it into slabs as thick as the cube you want.
Stack the slabs and cut them into sticks of the same width.
Turn the sticks and cut across them into cubes.
For an onion, halve it through the root, cut towards the root without cutting through it, then slice across.

mistakes.fix: Set the thickness with the first cut. Every later cut copies it.
mistakes.mistake: Pieces of different sizes, so the small ones turn to mush before the large ones are tender.

mistakes.fix: Cut a thin slice off one side first and rest it on that flat.
mistakes.mistake: Chasing a round vegetable that rolls under the knife.

cues.text: The piece is damp on the surface and still firm when pressed. It does not bend limp.
The biscuit has darkened only at the surface and not all the way through.

technique/dip.does: Passes a dry, absorbent biscuit or slice through a liquid for a moment only, so that the outside takes up flavour and softens while the centre stays dry enough to hold the dish together.
how: Pour the liquid into a shallow dish wide enough to take a whole piece, and let it cool if it is hot.
Hold each piece flat and pass it through the liquid in one quick motion, turning it once.
Lift it out at once and lay it straight into the dish, before the next piece goes in.
Work in a steady rhythm, and try one piece first to judge the time.

mistakes.fix: Pass it through and lift it out at once.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the piece in the liquid, so that it turns to mush and falls apart.

mistakes.fix: Let the liquid cool first.
mistakes.mistake: Dipping into a hot liquid, which soaks the biscuit before it can be lifted.

variant_of.differs: The piece spends only a moment in the liquid, enough to dampen the outside and leave a dry heart. It is not left to take the liquid up all the way through.

cues.text: The egg covers the piece in a thin, glossy film with no thick drips.
A piece that is dipped from flour comes up with a smooth, even coat.

technique/dip-in-egg.does: Draws food through beaten egg, so that it takes a thin, even coat that browns in the pan, or holds a crumb or flour coat in place.
how: Beat the egg in a shallow dish with a little salt until the white and yolk are one.
Have the food ready, dry on the surface or just floured, and slightly firm.
Draw each piece through the egg and turn it, then lift it and let the extra drip off.
Go straight to the pan, or on to the next coat, before the egg runs off.

mistakes.fix: Draw it through briefly and lift it at once.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving a bread slice in the egg until it falls apart.

mistakes.fix: Let the extra run off before the piece goes in.
mistakes.mistake: Letting a thick coat of egg drip into the pan, where it scrambles into strands.

cues.text: The soup turns evenly cloudy and there are no lumps.
The miso scent is full and warm, and is not flat.

technique/dissolve-miso.does: Stirs miso smooth into a little warm liquid away from the main pot, and then stirs it into the pot at the end, so that it never clumps and its scent is not boiled away.
how: Heat the soup or stock and turn off the heat or lower it until the liquid only trembles.
Put the miso in a ladle or a small sieve and lower it into the liquid.
Work the miso loose with the back of a spoon or a whisk until it has all gone into the liquid.
Stir the pot once, taste, and serve before it cools. Never let it come back to a boil.

mistakes.fix: Dissolve it in a ladle of warm liquid first.
mistakes.mistake: Dropping the miso into the pot in a lump, so that it sinks and stays in clots.

mistakes.fix: Take it off the heat first and serve right away.
mistakes.mistake: Boiling the soup after the miso is in, which dulls its scent.

cues.text: The pieces crackle sharply in the second round of frying.
The first-round pieces are pale, and the second round turns them deep golden.

technique/double-fry.does: Fries food in rounds: first at a moderate heat to cook it, then a rest, and again in hotter oil to crisp and brown the outside. The result is tender inside and crunchy outside, and stays crisp longer.
how: Heat the oil to a moderate heat and fry the pieces until pale and just firm. Do not crowd the pot.
Lift them onto a rack and let them rest, so that the heat spreads to the middle.
Heat the oil much hotter and put the pieces back for a short time, until golden and crisp.
Lift out, drain on the rack and serve right away.

mistakes.fix: Rest the pieces on a rack between rounds.
mistakes.mistake: Skipping the rest, so that the outside browns before the middle is ready.

mistakes.fix: Fry in small batches.
mistakes.mistake: Frying too many pieces at once, which cools the oil.

variant_of.differs: The food is fried twice, with a rest in between, at a moderate heat first and a high heat after, instead of once at a single heat.

cues.text: No more drops fall from the food.
The food is no longer slippery with water, and fried pieces feel dry and light.

technique/drain.does: Lets water or oil run off food after it has been boiled, soaked, salted or fried, so that it is not watery or greasy when it meets the next step.
how: Tip boiled food into a colander set in the sink, and give it a good shake. Keep a ladleful of the cooking water if the dish will want it.
Leave soaked or salted food in a colander for a while, and press out the rest of the water with the hands or a cloth.
Lift fried food out with a slotted spoon and set it on a rack or on paper.
Shake or toss the food once to free the last of the liquid.

mistakes.fix: Set it on a rack, or on paper that is changed when it soaks through.
mistakes.mistake: Draining fried food flat on a plate, where it steams and goes soft.

mistakes.fix: Scoop out a ladleful first.
mistakes.mistake: Throwing away all the cooking water of pasta, when the dish needs it to loosen a sauce.

mistakes.fix: Shake it well, and press out what a cloth can take.
mistakes.mistake: Draining too little, so that the food waters down the dish.

cues.text: A thin, even, dusty coat, with the food still showing through it.

technique/dredge.does: Coats a piece of food in a thin layer of flour just before it is fried, so that it browns evenly and does not stick.
how: Dry the food and season it.
Lay it in a plate of flour and turn it to coat every side.
Lift it and tap off everything that does not cling.
Fry it straight away.

mistakes.fix: Flour at the last moment, when the fat is already hot.
mistakes.mistake: Flouring ahead of time, so that the coat turns to a damp paste and fries gummy.

mistakes.fix: Tap the piece well.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving a thick coat on, which falls off in the pan and burns.

comes_after.why: Boiled food is drained first, so that only the last water is left to steam away.

cues.text: The surface is matt, with no shine of water, and no steam rises from the pot.
The food feels dry to the touch. The skin of a boiled potato wrinkles.

technique/dry.does: Takes the wet off the surface of food so that it browns, crisps or clings instead of steaming. For food that has been boiled, it lets the last water steam away and leaves a dry skin.
how: For raw food, pat it all over with a clean cloth or paper, on every side, and let it stand a little in the air if it is still wet.
For food that has been boiled, drain it well, then return it to the empty, still-hot pot over a very low heat.
Shake the pot now and then until the steam stops and the surface looks dull and dry.
If the water was heavily salted, the dry skin is left with a thin white crust of salt.

mistakes.fix: Pat it dry on every side first.
mistakes.mistake: Putting wet food into hot fat, where it spits and steams instead of browning.

mistakes.fix: Dry it in the hot pot, over a very low heat.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving boiled food to dry on a cold plate, where the steam settles back into it.

comes_after.why: An emulsion is whisked the whole time, so a steady whisking hand comes first.

cues.text: The sauce is smooth, opaque and glossy, and thickens as more fat goes in.
The whisk meets more resistance with every addition.

technique/emulsify.does: Makes fat and a water-based liquid hold together as one smooth sauce, by breaking one into droplets too small to find each other again.
how: Start with the water-based part and whatever helps it hold: egg yolk, mustard, or a liquid boiled down until syrupy.
Add the fat very slowly at first, drop by drop, whisking all the time.
Once the sauce has thickened and holds, add the fat in a thin stream.
Thin it with a few drops of water or acid if it turns stiff and looks oily at the edges.

mistakes.fix: Stop. Start again with a fresh yolk or a spoonful of mustard, and whisk the broken sauce into it drop by drop.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the fat too fast at the start, so that the sauce stays thin and then separates into oil and liquid.

mistakes.fix: Let the egg, the mustard and the oil come to room temperature first.
mistakes.mistake: Ingredients at very different temperatures, which makes a cold emulsion refuse to take.

en: make a cream with pasta water

comes_after.why: The starchy water that binds the sauce comes from cooking the pasta.

cues.text: A smooth, glossy cream that coats the back of a spoon, with no lumps of cooked egg and no puddle of oil.
It flows like thin cream and clings to the pasta as it is tossed.
The pan has stopped sizzling before the egg goes in.

technique/emulsify-off-the-heat.does: Binds fat, egg and a hard cheese into one glossy cream with hot starchy water, off the heat. No fat is whisked in drop by drop: the starch in the water and the warmth of the pasta hold it together, and it splits or scrambles if the heat comes back.
how: Have everything ready before the pasta is done: the fat in the pan, the egg and cheese mixed in a bowl, and a mug of hot starchy cooking water.
Take the pan off the heat. Heat is what splits this kind of sauce.
Loosen the egg and cheese with a splash of the hot water, stirring, until it is a smooth pourable cream with no streaks.
Bring it together with the fat and the pasta, adding more water a splash at a time and tossing, until it turns glossy and clings.
Serve at once. It is at its best straight away and sets as it cools.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat before the egg goes in, and keep it off.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the pan on the heat, so that the egg scrambles into flecks.

mistakes.fix: Use hot water from the pasta pot, and add it a splash at a time.
mistakes.mistake: Using water that has gone cool or has no starch, so that the sauce stays thin and slides off.

mistakes.fix: Add it a splash at a time and stop when it is glossy.
mistakes.mistake: Adding all the water at once, so that the sauce turns watery.

variant_of.differs: No fat is added drop by drop. The sauce is bound with hot starchy water, off the heat, and it splits or scrambles if the heat returns.

cues.text: A whole fillet with smooth edges, and a skeleton with almost no flesh left on it.
The blade rides on the bones the whole way.

technique/fillet.does: Cuts the flesh of a fish away from its bones in whole, clean pieces.
how: Lay the fish flat. Cut behind the head and the fin, down to the backbone.
Turn the blade flat and run it along the backbone toward the tail in long strokes, keeping it against the bones.
Lift the fillet away, turn the fish over and do the same on the other side.
Run a finger down each fillet and pull out the small bones it finds.
Keep the bones and the head for a stock.

mistakes.fix: Use a sharp, flexible blade and long, light strokes.
mistakes.mistake: Sawing with a dull or stiff knife, which tears the flesh.

mistakes.fix: Keep the flat of the blade pressed against the backbone.
mistakes.mistake: Lifting the blade away from the bones, which leaves flesh behind.

cues.text: Blue flames that rise, then sink and go out within moments.
The sharp smell of raw spirit gives way to a warm, sweet one.

technique/flambe.does: Sets light to a spirit poured over hot food. The flame burns away its harshness and leaves its flavour. Some of the alcohol stays in the dish.
how: Take the pan off the heat and clear the space above it.
Pour in the spirit from a ladle or a small glass, never from the bottle.
Put the pan back on the heat, lean back, and touch a long match to its edge.
Shake the pan gently until the flames die on their own.

mistakes.fix: Measure the spirit into a ladle or a glass first.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring from the bottle, so that the flame can run up the stream.

mistakes.fix: Have the pan hot, and warm the spirit if need be.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the spirit to a pan that is too cool, so that it will not light and the dish tastes of raw alcohol.

mistakes.fix: Clear the space above the pan before you light it.
mistakes.mistake: Lighting it under a low shelf or a running fan.

comes_after.why: Sinew and skin are cut away first, or they shrink and curl when the meat is beaten flat.

cues.text: The slice is an even sheet with no thick middle and no holes.
Under the pan the meat gives evenly and no longer springs back.

technique/flatten.does: Beats a slice of meat to an even, thin sheet between layers of paper, so that it cooks in moments and stays tender.
how: Trim away any sinew or skin from the slice, and nick the edge in a few places so that it does not curl.
Lay the slice between sheets of parchment paper.
Beat it from the middle outwards with the flat of a heavy pan, in even blows, turning it as you go.
Stop when the sheet is the same thickness from edge to edge, before it tears.

mistakes.fix: Use the flat of the pan, with steady, even weight.
mistakes.mistake: Beating with hard, sharp blows that tear the meat into holes.

mistakes.fix: Start in the middle and work outwards.
mistakes.mistake: Beating the edges thin and leaving the middle thick, so that it cooks unevenly.

comes_after.why: Turning at the right moment depends on reading the underside of food in a pan, which pan-frying teaches.

cues.text: The edges are set and dry, and the underside is a rich brown when the corner is lifted.
The food slides when the pan is shaken, and does not cling.

technique/flip.does: Turns food over in the pan or on the griddle at the right moment, so that its other side cooks and browns while the first side has set enough to hold together.
how: Wait until the underside has set and browned, and the food moves freely when the pan is shaken.
Slide a wide spatula fully under the food, so that none of it hangs over the edge.
Lift and turn in one quick, confident motion, close to the pan.
For a large, soft cake, slide it onto a plate, set the pan upside down over it and turn both over together, then slide it back.
Press gently to settle it, and cook the other side.

mistakes.fix: Wait until the edges are set and it moves freely.
mistakes.mistake: Flipping too early, so that the food is still soft and breaks.

mistakes.fix: Use a wide spatula, or slide the food onto a plate first.
mistakes.mistake: Using a narrow spatula, so that the food folds as it is lifted.

mistakes.fix: Turn it in one quick motion, close to the pan.
mistakes.mistake: Hesitating in mid-air, which tears or splashes.

comes_after.why: Couscous is fluffed once it has drunk its liquid, so a cook has to be able to bring the grains to that point first.
Rice is fluffed once it has taken up its water, so a cook has to be able to cook it to that point first.

cues.text: The grains lie loose, each with its own outline, and the heap holds no wet patches.
The fork meets no resistance and the grains fall away from it.

technique/fluff.does: Loosens cooked grains with a fork or the fingertips, lifting and separating them, so that the steam escapes and each grain stands apart instead of sitting in a block.
how: Wait until the grains have taken up their liquid and the steam is no longer heavy.
Add a little butter or a trickle of oil, so that the grains stay loose.
Run a fork, or the fingertips, lightly through the grains, lifting from the bottom and letting them fall. Do not press and do not stir.
Rub any lumps between the fingertips to break them.
Cover with a cloth until it is time to serve, so that the grains stay warm without drying.

mistakes.fix: Lift and let fall, with light strokes.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring hard, which breaks the grains and turns them to paste.

mistakes.fix: Leave them covered until the liquid has gone.
mistakes.mistake: Fluffing while the grains are still wet, which smears them.

mistakes.fix: Fluff them once more just before serving.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the grains in a heap without airing them, so that they set into a block.

comes_after.why: There is nothing to fold until something has been whipped.

cues.text: An even, light mixture that still stands in soft mounds and has lost little of its volume.

technique/fold.does: Combines a light, airy mixture with a heavier one while keeping as much of the air as possible.
how: Stir a small part of the whipped mixture into the heavy one to loosen it.
Tip the rest on top.
Cut down through the middle with a spatula, sweep along the bottom, and bring it up and over.
Turn the bowl a little and repeat, stopping when only a few streaks remain.

mistakes.fix: Cut, lift and turn. Stop early: a few streaks do less harm than more folding.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring in circles, which knocks the air out and leaves a flat batter.

comes_after.why: The dough must be rolled thin and even before it can be folded over a filling.

cues.text: The parcel is a flat half moon with an even bump of filling and a neat, thin rim.
The rim is pressed thin and sticks to itself, with no gap.

technique/fold-a-gozleme.does: Scatters a filling over one half of a thin round of dough, folds the other half over it and presses the edges shut, so that the filling is held in a flat parcel that cooks on a dry griddle.
how: Roll the dough out into a thin, even round and brush off the loose flour.
Scatter a thin layer of filling over one half, leaving a clear rim at the edge.
Lift the clear half over the filling and press the rim with the fingertips until it is sealed all the way round.
Carry the parcel to the hot griddle without letting it stretch.

mistakes.fix: Spread the filling in a thin layer.
mistakes.mistake: Overfilling, so that the parcel bursts on the griddle.

mistakes.fix: Squeeze or drain a wet filling first.
mistakes.mistake: Using a wet filling, which soaks the dough and makes it soggy.

mistakes.fix: Brush the rim clean before pressing it shut.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving flour on the rim, so that it will not stick.

variant_of.differs: The dough is folded once over a filling to make a flat sealed parcel, with no layers built up. Folding dough in the layered way stacks sheets over fat.

comes_after.why: The folds start from a round of dough that is rolled even, so a cook has to be able to roll one first.

cues.text: The cut edge of the folded triangle shows thin stripes of dough and ghee.
The triangle rolls out smoothly and the layers do not slide apart.

technique/fold-a-paratha.does: Brushes a rolled round of atta dough with ghee, dusts it with a little flour, and folds it over on itself into a half-moon and then a triangle, so that the dough is stacked in thin layers with ghee between them. The folded piece is then rolled out again, lightly.
how: Brush the whole rolled round with soft ghee and dust it with a little dry flour.
Fold the round in half to a half-moon, brush the top with ghee again and dust it lightly.
Fold the half-moon in half once more, into a triangle with its layers stacked inside.
Press the edges gently so that the layers stay together, and roll the triangle out lightly with even strokes.

mistakes.fix: Roll lightly and evenly, and stop as soon as the triangle is the size of the plate.
mistakes.mistake: Rolling hard after folding, so that the ghee is pressed out and the layers fuse into one.

mistakes.fix: Brush every fold with ghee, right to the edges.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the dough dry between the folds, so that the finished bread is tough and not flaky.

variant_of.differs: The dough is a soft atta dough that is not rested between folds, the fat is ghee brushed on by hand, and it is folded once or twice into a half-moon or triangle and rolled out again lightly. It is not a pastry that is turned and rolled many times.

cues.text: Each pastry is a neat triangle with no filling showing at the corners.
The sealed flap holds without sticking and the triangle is firm and flat.

technique/fold-briouats.does: Cuts sheets of warqa into long strips, puts a spoonful of filling at one end of each strip and folds the end over it again and again, corner to corner, into a small neat triangle, with the loose end sealed down with a dab of fat.
how: Keep the warqa under a damp cloth. Cut a sheet into strips as wide as a hand, and brush each strip lightly with melted butter.
Put a small spoonful of filling at one end, a little in from the corner.
Fold the corner over the filling to make a triangle, then fold the triangle over on itself along the strip, again and again, as one folds a flag.
Seal the last flap with a dab of butter and tuck it under.
Lay the triangles on a tray and cover them until they are fried.

mistakes.fix: Use only a small spoonful.
mistakes.mistake: Overfilling, which splits the thin sheet and leaks in the oil.

mistakes.fix: Cut only a few at a time and keep the rest under a damp cloth.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the strips dry out, so that they crack when folded.

variant_of.differs: Wrapping encloses a filling in a leaf, caul fat or a thin omelette. Here the wrapper is a paper-thin sheet cut in strips, and the filling is folded up in a series of triangle folds along the strip.

comes_after.why: A dough is rolled or stretched into an even sheet before it is folded.

cues.text: The layers show along a cut edge as fine, even lines.
The dough is supple and springs back slowly, and tears only when it is pulled hard.

technique/fold-dough.does: Folds a sheet or a round of dough over itself, from the sides and into a square or a letter, so that it stacks into layers or gains strength, and so that any fat or oil brushed between the layers stays shut in them.
how: Rest the dough first, so that it relaxes and does not spring back.
Stretch or roll it into an even sheet on a lightly oiled or floured surface.
Brush or sprinkle the surface with the fat or the dusting the dish asks for, right to the edges.
Lift one edge and fold it over towards the middle, then bring the opposite edge over it, as when folding a letter. For a square, fold the other sides in as well.
Press the folded shape lightly, turn it, and rest it before it is rolled or stretched again.

mistakes.fix: Let it rest until it relaxes.
mistakes.mistake: Folding dough that is still tense, which tears and shrinks back.

mistakes.fix: Brush the fat right to the edges.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the corners and edges bare, so that the layers weld together there.

comes_after.why: The crust must be on the meat before it goes into the oil.

cues.text: A steady, lively sizzle that softens as the cutlet browns.
An even, deep gold crust, with the bubbles around it slowing down.

technique/fry-a-cutlet.does: Fries a crumbed cutlet whole in deep oil, turning it once, until the crust is deep gold. It is then stood upright to drain, rested a little and cut across in strips, so that the crust stays crisp.
how: Heat deep oil in a heavy pan to a moderate heat, enough to cover the cutlet.
Test it with a few flakes of panko, which should sink briefly and then rise in a stream of fine bubbles.
Lower in one cutlet at a time, so that the oil keeps its heat, and leave it alone until the crust has set.
Turn it once and fry until the crust is deep gold on both sides.
Lift it out and stand it upright against a rack, so that the oil drains from the crust instead of pooling under it.
Rest it for a short while, then cut across in strips with a sharp knife, sawing lightly so that the crust does not shatter.

mistakes.fix: Keep the heat moderate and test with a few flakes of panko.
mistakes.mistake: Frying in oil that is too hot, so that the crust browns before the meat is ready.

mistakes.fix: Stand it upright against a rack.
mistakes.mistake: Laying the fried cutlet flat on a plate, where it steams and the crust goes soft.

mistakes.fix: Let it rest for a short while first.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting at once, so that the juice runs out and the crust goes limp.

variant_of.differs: One thick, crumbed piece of meat is fried whole at a moderate heat and turned once, then stood upright to drain, rested and cut across, where deep-frying works on small pieces and is salted at once.

en: fry in ghee and soak in syrup

comes_after.why: The balls are made from khoya dough, so the dough comes first.

cues.text: The balls swell, rise and turn an even, deep reddish brown, with no pale patches.
A soaked ball is soft and spongy, and gives under the spoon without breaking.

technique/fry-and-soak-in-syrup.does: Fries balls of dough slowly in ghee over a gentle heat until they are deep brown and cooked to the middle, then drops them into warm sugar syrup, which they drink up until they are soft, swollen and sweet to the centre.
how: Make the syrup first and keep it warm. It should be thin and sticky, not thick.
Heat the ghee or oil gently. A test ball should rise slowly, with a few bubbles, and not brown at once.
Slide in a few balls and shake the pan so that they turn. Keep the heat low, so that they swell and colour slowly.
Fry until they are deep, even brown all over. Lift them out with a slotted spoon and let the extra fat drip off.
Drop the hot balls into the warm syrup and leave them to soak, turning once, until they swell and are soft all the way through.

mistakes.fix: Test with one ball and keep the heat low.
mistakes.mistake: Frying in fat that is too hot, so that the outside darkens while the middle stays raw and dense.

mistakes.fix: Keep the syrup warm and thin.
mistakes.mistake: Putting the balls into cold or boiling syrup, so that they stay hard or fall apart.

mistakes.fix: Boil it just until it turns sticky.
mistakes.mistake: Making the syrup too thick, so that it sits on the surface and does not soak in.

variant_of.differs: The fat is held low and gentle, so that the balls swell and colour slowly and the middle cooks. It is not a hot fry meant to crisp a thin crust, and the fried balls are not drained dry, they go into syrup.
The soaking is done in warm sugar syrup, straight after frying, so that the fried balls drink it up as they cool.

comes_after.why: The pastries must be folded and sealed before they go into the oil.

cues.text: The pastry is a deep, even gold and the layers show a fine blister.
The oil sizzles quietly and steadily, with no spitting.
The honey coat is thin and glossy, and the pastry still crackles under it.

technique/fry-briouats.does: Fries small folded pastries in a good depth of hot oil, turning them until they are golden and crisp, then dips them while hot in warm honey scented with orange blossom water and scatters them with toasted sesame seeds.
how: Warm the honey gently with a spoonful of water and the orange blossom water, and keep it at the side of the stove.
Heat the oil in a wide pan to about a finger deep, until a scrap of warqa sizzles at once.
Fry the pastries a few at a time, turning them, until they are golden on every side.
Lift them out and let the oil run off for a moment.
Dip each one into the warm honey, turn it over, lift it out and set it on a rack. Scatter with toasted sesame seeds.

mistakes.fix: Test the oil with a scrap of warqa first.
mistakes.mistake: Frying in oil that is too cool, which leaves the pastry greasy and pale.

mistakes.fix: Dip them for a moment only and set them on a rack.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the pastries in the honey, which turns them soggy.

mistakes.fix: Warm it gently and keep it just hot.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the honey boil, which makes it bitter and hard.

variant_of.differs: Pan-frying cooks a flat piece in a thin layer of fat and turns it once. Here small filled triangles fry in oil about a finger deep, are turned until gold on every side, and are then dipped hot into warm honey.

comes_after.why: There is nothing to fry until the croquetas are shaped and coated.

cues.text: A sharp, steady sizzle when they go in, which quietens as the shell sets.
The shell is an even deep gold, with no cracks.
The croquetas are light for their size and the shell feels firm when pressed.

technique/fry-croquetas.does: Fries coated croquetas in a few at a time in hot oil deep enough to cover them, turning them until the shell is deep golden all round and the paste inside has melted soft.
how: Heat plenty of oil in a deep, heavy pan. A crumb dropped in should sizzle at once and rise.
Lower a few croquetas in with a slotted spoon. Do not crowd the pan, or the oil cools and the shells go greasy.
Turn them gently until they are deep golden all round.
Lift them out onto a rack and let the oil run off. Serve at once, while the shell is crisp and the middle is soft.

mistakes.fix: Wait until a crumb sizzles at once, and fry only a few at a time.
mistakes.mistake: Frying in oil that is not hot enough, so that the shell soaks up oil and the paste leaks out.

mistakes.fix: Fry in small batches and let the oil heat up again between them.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding the pan, which cools the oil.

mistakes.fix: Turn them with a slotted spoon.
mistakes.mistake: Piercing the shell with a fork while turning.

variant_of.differs: The food is a soft paste in a fragile shell that has to set in the first moments, so the oil must be hot at once and only a few go in each time. A firm food such as a potato is fried to cook it and then fried again to crisp it.

cues.text: A lively crackle as the egg goes in, which settles to a steady sizzle.
The white is set and frilled, golden and lacy at the edge, and the yolk is still glossy and wobbly.

technique/fry-eggs.does: Cooks eggs in a generous depth of hot olive oil, so that the whites puff, bubble and turn lacy and crisp at the edges while the yolks stay soft.
how: Heat a good depth of olive oil in a small, deep frying pan until a breadcrumb dropped in sizzles at once.
Break each egg into a small bowl first, so that a broken yolk or a shell is found before the pan.
Slide the egg in from close to the oil at the side of the pan, so that the white curls round the yolk.
Tilt the pan and spoon hot oil over the white until it is set and frilled, while the yolk stays soft.
Lift the egg out with a slotted spoon, drain it on paper and salt it at the end.

mistakes.fix: Heat the oil until a breadcrumb sizzles at once.
mistakes.mistake: The oil is too cool, so that the egg spreads thin and greasy with a pale, limp white.

mistakes.fix: Lower the heat a little and spoon the oil over the white.
mistakes.mistake: The oil is too hot, so that the white turns brown and leathery before the yolk is warm.

mistakes.fix: Break the egg into a small bowl first and slide it in low.
mistakes.mistake: Breaking the yolk as the egg goes in.

variant_of.differs: The egg swims in a generous depth of hot olive oil and not in a thin film of fat, so the white frills and crisps at the edge. Nothing is turned, and the oil is spooned over the white.

cues.text: A steady, lively sizzle. A roar means the oil is too hot, and silence means it is too cool.
The edges turn lacy and golden before the middle sets.

technique/fry-fritters.does: Drops spoonfuls of a thick mixture of grated vegetable, egg, cheese and a little flour into hot oil, flattens them lightly and turns them once, so that each fritter is crisp and golden outside and soft inside.
how: Make the mixture thick enough to sit on a spoon. If it runs, stir in a little more flour. If it is stiff and dry, loosen it with a spoonful of water.
Warm a shallow layer of oil in a wide pan until a crumb of the mixture sizzles at once.
Drop in spoonfuls with room between them, and press each to a flat round with the back of the spoon.
Leave them alone until the underside is deep golden and the edges look set, then turn each once.
Lift them onto a rack or paper to drain. Fry the rest in lots, and wipe the pan if bits of the mixture scorch.

mistakes.fix: Wait for the sizzle before the first spoonful goes in.
mistakes.mistake: Frying in oil that is too cool, so that the fritters soak it up and turn greasy.

mistakes.fix: Fry a few at a time, with room between them.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding the pan, so that the fritters steam and join together.

mistakes.fix: Wait until the underside is golden and the edges are set.
mistakes.mistake: Turning too soon, so that the fritter tears.

variant_of.differs: A fritter mixture has no shape of its own, so it is dropped in by the spoonful and flattened, in more oil than a cut of meat or fish would be fried in, and it is turned only once it has set.

comes_after.why: The base is built on a paste of ginger, garlic and spices, so a cook has to be able to make one first.

cues.text: The paste turns a deeper colour and shiny fat parts from it and gathers at the edge of the pan.
The raw sharp smell of garlic and spice is gone, replaced by a rounded, roasted scent.
The spoon leaves a clean track across the paste on the pan.

technique/fry-masala-base.does: Cooks onion, ginger and garlic, ground spices and tomato in fat over a medium heat, stirring often and sprinkling a little water when the pan dries, until the water of the vegetables is gone and the fat parts from the paste and shines on its edge. This is the base of a gravy.
how: Heat the fat and cook the sliced or chopped onion until it is soft and golden.
Add the ginger and garlic paste or the spice paste and stir until the raw smell goes.
Add the ground spices and stir for a few moments. Sprinkle in a little water if they catch.
Add the tomato, mash it down with the spoon and cook, stirring, until it has collapsed into a thick paste.
Go on until the fat separates from the paste and gathers in a bright pool at the edge. Add a spoonful of water and scrape the pan whenever the paste sticks.

mistakes.fix: Wait until the fat shines at the edge of the paste.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the liquid too soon, before the fat has parted, so that the gravy tastes raw and thin.

mistakes.fix: Keep the heat moderate, sprinkle in a little water when the pan dries, and add the tomato soon after the spices.
mistakes.mistake: Burning the ground spices by frying them in dry, hot fat.

mistakes.fix: Keep a medium heat and be patient. The wait is the point.
mistakes.mistake: Rushing it over a high heat, which scorches the paste.

variant_of.differs: A sofrito is cooked slowly in olive oil to a sweet, jammy paste. Here ground spices and a spice paste go in as well, with a splash of water whenever the pan dries, and the cook stops when the fat parts from the paste.

comes_after.why: The noodles must be pulled apart before they go into the pan.

cues.text: The sauce smells sweet and tangy as it hits the hot pan.
The strands are evenly brown, separate, and there is no wet pool in the pan.

technique/fry-noodles-in-sauce.does: Tosses loosened noodles in a very hot pan with meat and vegetables that are already cooked, and pours a sweet, tangy sauce round the edge of the pan, until the noodles are coated, lightly browned in places and still separate.
how: Have the noodles loosened, the sauce mixed and everything else cut and at hand.
Cook the meat and the firmest vegetables first in a hot pan with a little oil, then add the leaves and sprouts for a short time.
Add the noodles and toss them with tongs, lifting from the bottom, until they are hot.
Pour the sauce round the edge of the pan, so that it sizzles on the metal before it is tossed in.
Toss until the sauce is taken up, and serve at once, before the noodles soften.

mistakes.fix: Loosen them first.
mistakes.mistake: Adding noodles that are still in a clump, so that they tear and cook unevenly.

mistakes.fix: Pour it round the edge of the hot pan.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring the sauce on top of the noodles, so that they stew and turn soft.

mistakes.fix: Use a wide pan, or cook in batches.
mistakes.mistake: Packing too much into the pan, so that the food steams.

variant_of.differs: The main food is noodles and not rice or vegetables. They are loosened first and added late, and the sauce is poured round the edge of the pan so that it sizzles before it coats them.

comes_after.why: Even slices brown at one pace, so a cook who can slice evenly fries better onions.

cues.text: A deep, even brown with a few darker tips, and no black.
A loud bubbling at the start that calms to a quiet sizzle as the water leaves the onions.
A piece lifted out and cooled snaps when it is pressed.

technique/fry-onions-dark.does: Fries thinly sliced onions in a generous layer of hot oil until they turn deep brown and crisp at the edges, then lifts them out to drain. They bring a bittersweet crunch to rice and lentils, and the oil they leave behind is full of their flavour.
how: Slice the onions thin and evenly, so that they brown at one pace.
Heat a good depth of oil in a wide, heavy pan until a slice sizzles the moment it goes in.
Add the onions in a loose layer, in batches if need be. Stir often at first, then less often as they darken.
Lower the heat once the edges go dark, and keep frying until the onions are a deep brown. They crisp further as they cool.
Lift them out with a slotted spoon onto a rack or paper, and salt them lightly. Keep the oil.

mistakes.fix: Fry in batches, in the widest pan you have.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding the pan, so that the onions steam, turn limp and never crisp.

mistakes.fix: Stay by the pan and lift them out as soon as they are deep brown.
mistakes.mistake: Looking away at the end, when the onions go from brown to bitter black in moments.

mistakes.fix: Wait until a slice sizzles at once.
mistakes.mistake: Starting in cool oil, which soaks into the onions and leaves them greasy.

variant_of.differs: The onions are cut thin and fried in plenty of hot oil until dark and crisp at the edges, and not coaxed slowly in a little fat until soft and sweet.

comes_after.why: Slices of an even width brown together, so the cook has to be able to slice onions evenly first.

cues.text: The slices pass from limp and pale to amber and then deep brown, with the edges darkest.
The sizzle is loud while the onions are wet and fades to a quiet crackle as the water goes.
A slice lifted out and left to cool snaps between the fingers.

technique/fry-onions-deep-brown.does: Fries thinly sliced onions in a generous amount of fat until their water has gone and they turn deep brown and crisp, then lifts them out to drain. They are crushed into a marinade, layered into rice, scattered on top, or stirred into a gravy.
how: Slice the onions thin and even, so that they brown together. Spread them out to dry a little if they are wet.
Heat plenty of fat in a wide pan until a slice sizzles at once, then add the onions in a loose layer.
Stir often at a steady medium heat. They go limp, then pale gold, then amber.
Lower the heat as the colour deepens. The last stage takes only moments, so stay at the pan.
Lift them out with a slotted spoon the moment they are deep brown, and spread them on paper to drain. They crisp as they cool.

mistakes.fix: Fry in a wide pan, in a thin layer, or in batches.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding the pan, so that the onions steam and stay limp and pale.

mistakes.fix: Lift them out while they are a shade lighter than wanted. They go on darkening in the fat they carry.
mistakes.mistake: Walking away at the end, when the onions turn from brown to bitter black in moments.

mistakes.fix: Lift them out and spread them on paper at once.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving them in the hot fat to cool, so that they go soft and greasy.

variant_of.differs: Caramelising keeps the onions soft and sticky, in little fat and over a low heat. Here the slices swim in a generous amount of fat at a steady medium heat until they dry out, turn deep brown and crisp, and are lifted out and drained, to be used as a topping, a layer or a flavouring.

comes_after.why: There is nothing to fry until the balls are shaped, coated and chilled.

cues.text: A sharp, steady sizzle as they go in, which quietens as the shell sets.
An even deep gold all round, with no cracks in the shell.
A ball is light for its size and the shell feels firm and dry when pressed.

technique/fry-rice-balls.does: Fries coated, filled rice balls a few at a time in hot oil deep enough to cover them, turning them until the shell is deep golden all round and the filling inside is hot and soft.
how: Heat plenty of oil in a deep, heavy pan and hold it steady. A crumb dropped in should sizzle at once and rise.
Lower a few balls in with a slotted spoon. Do not crowd the pan, or the oil cools and the shells go greasy.
Turn them gently until they are deep golden all round. Keep the heat moderate, so that the warmth reaches the filling before the shell gets too dark.
Lift them out onto a rack and let the oil run off. Rest them briefly before serving, because the middle stays very hot.

mistakes.fix: Keep the oil at a steady, moderate heat and use a thermometer.
mistakes.mistake: Frying in oil that is too hot, so that the shell turns dark while the filling is still cold.

mistakes.fix: Wait until a crumb sizzles at once, and fry only a few at a time.
mistakes.mistake: Frying in oil that is not hot enough, so that the shell soaks up oil and splits.

mistakes.fix: Fry in small batches and let the oil heat up again between them.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding the pan, which cools the oil.

variant_of.differs: The food is a filled ball of rice in a crumb shell, and the filling has to be hot all through when the shell is done, so the oil is held steady and moderate and only a few go in each time.
The balls are larger and hold a filling in a firm rice wall, and not a soft paste, so they stay in the oil a little longer at a slightly gentler heat for the middle to warm.

comes_after.why: The dough must have risen until it is light and full of gas before it goes into the oil.

cues.text: The ring floats, swells and turns an even gold on both sides.
The oil sizzles steadily and not wildly.
A finished ring is light for its size and springs back when pressed.

technique/fry-sfenj.does: Shapes lumps of very soft, risen dough into rings with a wet hand and drops them into hot oil, turning them once, until they puff up golden with a thin crisp crust and a light, chewy crumb. They are lifted out at once, drained and tossed in sugar.
how: Heat the oil until a scrap of dough dropped in sizzles and rises at once.
Wet one hand and a plate. Pull off a lump of dough, flatten it, and poke a hole through the middle with a wet thumb.
Slide the ring into the oil and fry only a few at a time, so that the oil stays hot.
Turn each ring once with a skewer or the handle of a spoon when it has puffed and coloured underneath.
Lift the rings out when golden on both sides, drain them well and toss them in sugar while they are warm.

mistakes.fix: Test the oil with a scrap of dough first.
mistakes.mistake: Frying in oil that is too cool, which makes greasy, heavy rings.

mistakes.fix: Fry a few at a time.
mistakes.mistake: Putting in too many at once, which cools the oil.

mistakes.fix: Wet the hand each time.
mistakes.mistake: Handling the dough with dry hands, which sticks and tears it.

variant_of.differs: Deep-frying cooks food that is firm or coated. Here the food is a sticky raw dough that is shaped in the hand moments before it goes in, and the oil is what makes it puff.

cues.text: The garnish sits on top of the food, in a light scatter.
A fresh scent rises as the garnish meets the heat.

technique/garnish.does: Adds a small, fresh or crisp finishing touch just before serving, such as a herb, a seed, a flake or a shaving, for scent, colour or crunch.
how: Keep the garnish ready at the side, cut or measured.
Add it as the last step, when the food is hot or just plated.
Scatter or place a little where it will be seen, and do not cover the food.
Add the delicate ones at the table.

mistakes.fix: Add it at the last moment.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the garnish too early, so that it wilts or sinks.

mistakes.fix: Use only a small amount.
mistakes.mistake: Using too much, so that it hides the food.

cues.text: No liquid is left: a shiny film coats each piece and the pan.
The bubbling turns to a sizzle as the last of the water goes.

technique/glaze.does: Cooks small vegetables in a little water, butter and sugar until the water has gone and they are left tender and coated in a shiny syrup.
how: Put the vegetables in a wide pan in a single layer.
Add water to come half way up them, with butter, a little sugar and salt.
Cover with a round of paper and simmer until the vegetables are nearly tender.
Take the paper off and boil away the last of the liquid, rolling the vegetables in the syrup as it forms.
Stop there for a pale glaze, or go on a moment for a golden one.

mistakes.fix: Use less, and pour some off if they are tender before the glaze forms.
mistakes.mistake: Too much water, so that the vegetables are overcooked before it has gone.

mistakes.fix: Stay, and keep them rolling.
mistakes.mistake: Walking away at the end, when the syrup burns.

cues.text: Loose, separate shreds that do not clump.

technique/grate.does: Rubs firm food against a rough surface to turn it into fine shreds.
how: Chill a soft cheese first, so that it shreds and does not smear.
Hold the grater steady on the board or over a bowl.
Push the food down the grater in long strokes with the flat of your hand.
Stop while there is still enough left to hold.

mistakes.fix: Stop early and chop the end with a knife.
mistakes.mistake: Grating the last small piece and catching a knuckle.

cues.text: The grated daikon is a soft, wet, white mound.
The taste is fresh, juicy and a little sharp.

technique/grate-daikon.does: Grates a daikon on a fine grater into a wet, light, snowy mound, which is eaten raw beside rich or grilled food to freshen the mouth.
how: Peel the daikon, or leave the skin on if it is tender, and cut it into a piece that is easy to hold.
Grate it with firm, even strokes on the finest side of the grater, in one direction.
Let the juice drain away a little in a sieve, but do not press it dry.
Shape the mound with a spoon and serve it straight away.

mistakes.fix: Grate it just before serving.
mistakes.mistake: Grating long ahead, so that it turns bitter and watery.

mistakes.fix: Drain it lightly only.
mistakes.mistake: Squeezing it dry, which leaves it harsh.

variant_of.differs: It is grated very fine and wet, kept juicy and loose and served as a raw mound, not dried or used to flavour a dish.

cues.text: A blistered, golden-brown crust that bubbles at the rim.
Toasted cheese. A sharp, bitter smell means it has gone too far.

technique/gratinate.does: Browns the top of a dish under strong heat from above, until it forms a golden crust.
how: Cover the dish with what will brown: cheese, crumbs, or a sauce rich in butter or cream.
Set it on a high shelf, under a grill that is already hot.
Stay beside it. The crust goes from pale to burnt very fast.
Turn the dish for an even colour, and take it out when it is golden and bubbling at the edges.

mistakes.fix: Watch it the whole time, with the oven door ajar.
mistakes.mistake: Walking away from the grill.

mistakes.fix: Warm the dish in the oven first, then brown the top.
mistakes.mistake: Grilling a dish that is cold in the middle, so that the top burns before the inside is hot.

cues.text: Brown speckles on the underside, and bubbles or puffing on the top.
A toasty, bready smell, and not a burnt one.
A quiet sizzle when the food touches down.

technique/griddle.does: Cooks flat foods on a wide, flat, heavy surface that is dry or only lightly oiled, so that they brown in speckles and spots on each face and stay soft within, without being fried in a pool of fat.
how: Heat the griddle well in advance, until it is evenly hot all over and a drop of water skips off it.
Wipe it with a thin film of oil, or leave it dry for a dough that holds its own fat.
Lay the food down flat and leave it still until the underside is spotted brown and it lifts easily.
Turn it and cook the other face, pressing lightly if it puffs.
Stack the finished pieces in a cloth so that they stay soft.

mistakes.fix: Preheat it until it is evenly hot.
mistakes.mistake: Putting the food on before the griddle is hot, so that it dries out and turns stiff.

mistakes.fix: Wipe on only a thin film.
mistakes.mistake: Using too much oil, which fries the food and turns it greasy.

mistakes.fix: Stack it in a cloth to keep it soft.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the finished food open to the air, where it dries and stiffens.

variant_of.differs: The food lies on a flat surface that is dry or barely oiled and browns in speckles, where pan-frying cooks in a film of fat.

cues.text: An evenly browned or blistered surface, with no black, bitter patches.
A smell of toasting, not of burning.

technique/grill.does: Cooks food close to fierce, direct heat, so that its surface colours and chars lightly while the inside stays moist.
how: Heat the grill until it is very hot before the food goes near it.
Dry the food, oil it lightly and season it.
Set it close to the heat and leave it until the surface has coloured, then turn it once.
Move a thick piece further from the heat once it has coloured, so that the inside can catch up.
For cheese on toast, set it a little further from the heat and take it out when the cheese has softened and browned on top.

mistakes.fix: Let it lose its chill first.
mistakes.mistake: Grilling food straight from the fridge, so that the outside burns before the inside is warm.

mistakes.fix: Leave it alone until it has coloured, then turn it once.
mistakes.mistake: Turning it again and again, so that it never colours.

comes_after.why: The meat has to be held on a skewer before it can be turned over the coals.

cues.text: The meat is browned and speckled with dark spots on every side, with no black patch.
A smoky, meaty scent rises from the coals.
The meat springs back when pressed, instead of giving way.

technique/grill-over-charcoal.does: Cooks skewered minced meat over glowing coals, turning it often, so that the outside takes a smoky crust while the inside stays juicy.
how: Let the coals burn down until they are covered in grey ash and glow evenly, with no tall flame.
Lay the skewers across the coals, close enough to sizzle at once.
Turn the skewers often, so that they colour on every side and no side burns.
Fan the coals if they fade, and move the skewers aside if fat drips and flares.
Take the skewers off when they are browned all over and the meat feels firm.

mistakes.fix: Wait until the coals glow under grey ash.
mistakes.mistake: Grilling over open flame, which blackens the outside before the middle is ready.

mistakes.fix: Turn them often.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the skewers in one place, so that one side burns.

mistakes.fix: Leave it alone between turns.
mistakes.mistake: Pressing the meat flat on the grate, which squeezes out the juice.

variant_of.differs: Grilling cooks close to a fierce, direct heat, often from above. Here the heat is glowing charcoal underneath, the food lies across the coals on skewers, and it is turned constantly.

comes_after.why: Spices and nuts are toasted first so that they grind to a finer, more fragrant powder.

cues.text: The food falls into an even powder or paste with no whole pieces left.
Spices turn sharply fragrant as they break.
A ground paste holds together when pressed between the fingers.

technique/grind.does: Breaks hard or firm food down to a powder, a coarse meal or a paste, by crushing it in a mortar, milling it in a grinder or running it through a blade, so that it blends into a dish or binds into a dough.
how: Dry whole spices lightly in a warm pan first, so that they grind finer and smell stronger, then let them cool.
Soak dried pulses and drain them well before grinding them, and cut meat into strips and chill it first.
Grind in short bursts or with steady circles, a small amount at a time, so that the heat of the blade does not cook the food.
For a paste, add a very little liquid, a spoonful at a time, to keep the blades turning.
Stop when it has the texture the dish asks for, and scrape down the sides once.

mistakes.fix: Grind a little at a time.
mistakes.mistake: Grinding a large amount at once, so that some is dust and some is whole.

mistakes.fix: Work in short bursts and let it rest.
mistakes.mistake: Running a machine for long, so that the heat dulls the scent or cooks the food.

mistakes.fix: Add a spoonful at a time and stop as soon as it turns.
mistakes.mistake: Adding too much liquid to a paste, which turns it to soup.

cues.text: The paste is moist and coarse, with a slow ribbon when it falls from the spoon.
Fresh, mild and sweet from the coconut, with a sharp warmth from the chilli and a clean finish.

technique/grind-a-chutney.does: Grinds fresh coconut or fresh herbs with green chilli, ginger, salt and a little cold water in a blender or on a stone into a coarse, moist paste, which is served raw as a fresh relish.
how: Put the coconut or the herbs in the blender with the green chilli, the ginger, the salt and any thickener, such as roasted split chickpeas.
Add a little cold water to start. Pulse and scrape down the sides.
Add more water a spoonful at a time, until the blades catch and the paste turns over and over.
Stop when the paste is coarse and moist, thick enough to hold on a spoon, and not a smooth purée.
Taste and adjust the salt and the chilli. It is served the same day, often with a hot tempering poured over it.

mistakes.fix: Add the water a spoonful at a time.
mistakes.mistake: Adding all the water at once, so that the chutney is thin and bland.

mistakes.fix: Pulse in short bursts and stop while it is still coarse.
mistakes.mistake: Grinding too long, so that the paste turns warm and pasty.

mistakes.fix: Use cold water.
mistakes.mistake: Using warm water, which turns the herbs dark and the coconut sour sooner.

variant_of.differs: The food is ground fresh and wet to a coarse, moist paste and served raw, not dried and ground to a powder. A little cold water is added slowly so that the blades catch.

cues.text: A deep, nutty, warm scent rises from the bowl.
The mixture turns into a damp, oily paste with some seeds left whole.

technique/grind-sesame.does: Toasts sesame seeds until they are fragrant, then grinds them in a ridged bowl to a rough, oily paste with some seeds left half whole, ready to coat vegetables or to thicken a dressing.
how: Toast the seeds in a dry pan, shaking them, until they smell nutty and begin to pop.
Tip them into the ridged bowl while they are still warm.
Grind them with a circular motion, pressing against the ridges, until they are half crushed and oily.
Stir in the other seasonings and use the paste right away, as its scent fades.

mistakes.fix: Toast them first.
mistakes.mistake: Grinding raw seeds, which gives a pale, flat taste.

mistakes.fix: Stop while the seeds are still half whole.
mistakes.mistake: Grinding too long, which turns the paste greasy and pasty.

variant_of.differs: The seeds are ground only until half crushed, in a ridged bowl, so that the paste stays rough and oily instead of becoming fine powder.

comes_after.why: A fish is scaled first, so that loose scales do not stick to the flesh when the belly is opened.

cues.text: The cavity is pale and clean, with no dark blood left along the backbone.
A clean fish smells of the sea and of nothing sour or sharp.

technique/gut-a-fish.does: Opens the belly of a whole fish and takes out the guts and the gills, then rinses the cavity, so that the fish can be cooked whole or filleted without a bitter taste.
how: Lay the fish on a board with the belly towards you.
Slide the tip of the knife in at the vent near the tail and slit the belly up to the gills, shallow, with the blade pointing up so that the guts are not pierced.
Reach in, loosen the guts at the throat and pull them out in one piece.
Lift the gill cover and cut the gills away at both ends. They taste bitter if they are left in.
Rinse the cavity under cold running water, rubbing away the dark blood along the backbone, and pat the fish dry.

mistakes.fix: Cut shallow, with the tip of the knife pointing up.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting too deep and piercing the guts, which taints the flesh with bitterness.

mistakes.fix: Cut them out at both ends and rinse the cavity.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the gills in, which turn a stock or a sauce bitter.

cues.text: The liquid smells clearly of the flavouring when you bend over the pan.
Saffron turns the liquid a deep gold, and the threads go pale.

technique/infuse.does: Lets a flavouring steep in a warm liquid until the liquid has taken on its scent, colour and taste, and then lifts or strains the flavouring out. It is the reverse of soaking, where the food takes up the liquid.
how: Warm the liquid until it steams. Do not let it boil hard, which dulls a delicate scent and makes milk climb the pan.
Add the flavouring, such as strips of peel, a stick of cinnamon, a split vanilla pod, threads of saffron or herbs, and take the pan off the heat.
Cover and leave it to steep until the liquid smells strongly of the flavouring.
Strain, or lift the flavouring out, before the liquid is used. Press it gently to give up the last of its taste.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat before the flavouring goes in.
