mistakes.mistake: Boiling the liquid with the flavouring in it, which turns peel and saffron harsh and bitter.

mistakes.fix: Taste it, and leave it longer if it is weak.
mistakes.mistake: Straining too soon, so that the liquid is only faintly flavoured.

comes_after.why: A julienne starts as thin, even slices.

cues.text: Fine strips of one length that bend without snapping and fall apart from each other.

technique/julienne.does: Cuts food into fine, even strips the length of a matchstick.
how: Cut the vegetable into lengths as long as the strips you want.
Slice each length into thin, flat sheets.
Stack a few sheets and slice them lengthwise into strips as wide as the sheets are thick.
For a leek, split a length open, lay the layers flat and slice along the grain.

mistakes.fix: Stack only a few sheets at a time and keep the pile flat.
mistakes.mistake: Stacking too many sheets, so the pile slides and the strips come out as wedges.

cues.text: A piece lifted out is still steaming hot, with no steam rushing off.
The liquid barely moves.

technique/keep-warm.does: Holds finished food at a gentle heat, below a simmer, so that it stays hot and goes on taking up flavour until it is served.
how: Take the pot off the strong heat and turn the flame as low as it goes, or move the food to a warm place.
Keep the food covered so that it does not dry or skin over.
Stir or turn it now and then, so that the bottom does not catch.
Serve from the pot. Do not leave it for a very long time.

mistakes.fix: Lower the heat until the liquid is still.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the food on a simmer, which cooks it past tender.

mistakes.fix: Cover it.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving it uncovered, so that a skin forms or it dries.

cues.text: A dough turns from rough and tacky to smooth and elastic, and springs back slowly when it is pressed.
A kneaded mince or bulgur mixture holds together when pressed into a ball and does not crumble.
The surface of a kneaded dough is smooth and satiny, with no dry patches.

technique/knead.does: Works a dough, or a loose mixture such as minced meat or soaked bulgur, with the heels of the hands, pressing and turning it until it comes together and holds its shape. In a dough this builds the stretch that gives bread its chew. In a mixture it binds the pieces so that they do not fall apart in the pan.
how: Bring the mixture together in a wide bowl or on a clean surface, with just enough liquid to make it hold.
Press a dough away from you with the heel of the hand, fold it back over itself, give it a quarter turn and press again.
Keep a steady rhythm. Dust a dough that sticks with a little flour, and wet one that cracks with a little water.
Work minced meat or bulgur with wet hands, squeezing and pressing, until it turns sticky and holds when pressed into a ball.
Stop when a dough is smooth and springs back, or when a mixture sticks to itself and not to the bowl, then let it rest.

mistakes.fix: Keep the dough a little tacky, and dust the surface only as needed.
mistakes.mistake: Working in too much flour, so that the dough turns dry and heavy.

mistakes.fix: Keep going until it is smooth and springs back when pressed.
mistakes.mistake: Stopping early, so that the dough tears when it is stretched and bakes dense.

mistakes.fix: Keep the meat cold, and stop as soon as the mixture turns sticky.
mistakes.mistake: Working minced meat for long with warm hands, so that the fat smears.

comes_after.why: Laminating starts with a dough rolled out thin and even.
Laminating is folding a dough over fat again and again.

cues.text: A cut edge shows fine, even layers, each one shining with fat.
The cooked dough pulls apart in thin, crisp sheets.

technique/laminate.does: Builds a dough into many thin layers with fat between them, by rolling or stretching it out, spreading it with fat, folding it over and repeating, so that in the heat each layer cooks apart from the next and the finished bread or pastry comes away in flaky sheets.
how: Start from a smooth dough that has rested and is soft enough to stretch thin.
Roll or stretch it out as thin as it will go without tearing.
Brush the whole sheet with melted fat or oil, or lay a slab of cold butter on it. For some breads, sprinkle fine semolina over the fat, so that the layers do not weld.
Fold the sheet over the fat, as a letter or into a square, so that the fat is sealed inside.
Rest the dough between folds: cold for a dough with butter, covered at room warmth for an oiled one.
Repeat the rolling and folding until the dough has as many layers as the dish needs, then shape it and cook it.

mistakes.fix: Chill the dough between folds and keep the butter cold.
mistakes.mistake: Letting butter warm and melt into the dough, so that the bread is not flaky.

mistakes.fix: Roll with an even, light pressure and rest the dough when it fights back.
mistakes.mistake: Rolling so hard that the fat tears through the layers.

cues.text: A level top, and layers of the same thickness when the dish is cut.

technique/layer.does: Builds a dish in even layers, so that it cooks evenly and holds together when it is served.
how: Have every part ready and within reach before you start.
Spread each layer to the edges, in one even thickness.
Season lightly between the layers, not only on top.
Finish with the layer that should brown.

mistakes.fix: Take a moment to level each layer.
mistakes.mistake: Thick and thin patches, which cook at different speeds.

mistakes.fix: Season lightly as you go.
mistakes.mistake: Seasoning only the top, which leaves the inside bland.

comes_after.why: The biscuits must be dipped before they are laid down, or they stay dry.
The cream goes between the layers, so it is made first.

cues.text: The layers are flat and even, and show as stripes where a square is cut out.
A knife cuts through without the cream running, and the biscuits are soft right through.

technique/layer-a-cold-dessert.does: Builds a dessert without baking it, from dipped biscuits and a soft cream laid in even layers in a dish, dusts the top and chills it for long enough that the layers soften into each other and the whole can be cut in squares.
how: Have the dipped biscuits and the cream within reach before the first layer goes down.
Lay a single layer of biscuits side by side in the dish, close together with no gaps.
Spread half the cream over them in an even layer, right to the corners, and smooth it with a spatula.
Lay a second layer of biscuits, then spread the rest of the cream and smooth the top.
Sift cocoa over the top just before serving, so that it stays dry and dark.
Cover the dish and chill it until the layers have melded and the cream is firm enough to cut cleanly.

mistakes.fix: Leave it to chill until it is firm, ideally overnight.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting the dessert after only a short chill, so that the cream runs and the layers slide.

mistakes.fix: Dust it on just before serving.
mistakes.mistake: Dusting the cocoa on before chilling, so that it dissolves into a damp, patchy top.

variant_of.differs: Nothing is baked. The layers are built cold and soften together as they chill, so the dessert needs a long rest before it is cut.

cues.text: Every sheet shines evenly with fat, and none is left dry at the edges.
The baked pie crackles under the knife and the top breaks into fine flakes.

technique/layer-phyllo.does: Builds a pie from paper-thin sheets of phyllo laid one on another, each brushed with oil or melted butter, so that the baked pie is made of many crisp, flaky layers around its filling.
how: Keep the stack of sheets under a barely damp cloth and lift out only the sheet in hand, because open sheets dry and crack within moments.
Brush the dish lightly with fat. Lay a sheet in, let the edges hang over the sides, and brush the whole sheet with fat right to the edges.
Add the next sheet at a slight turn, so that the hanging edges reach all round the dish, and brush it in the same way. Go on until the base is thick enough to hold the filling.
Spread the filling in an even layer and fold the hanging edges back over it.
Lay the top sheets one at a time, brushing each with fat. Tuck the edges down inside the dish and brush the top.
Cut through the top layers into portions before the pie goes in the oven. A baked crust shatters under the knife.

mistakes.fix: Keep them under a barely damp cloth and take out one sheet at a time.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the stack uncovered, so that the sheets dry out, crack and crumble.

mistakes.fix: Brush a thin, even coat on every sheet, right to the edges.
mistakes.mistake: Brushing too lightly, so that the sheets stick together and bake leathery, or too heavily, so that the pie turns greasy.

mistakes.fix: Drain the filling well and let it cool before it goes in.
mistakes.mistake: Putting a wet filling on the base sheets, which turns them soggy.

mistakes.fix: Cut through the top layers before baking.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting the pie only after it is baked, so that the crust shatters.

variant_of.differs: The layers are the dough itself, paper-thin sheets each brushed with fat so that they bake crisp and stay apart, and the filling is closed between them. A plain layer stacks cooked food in turn with its sauce.

cues.text: The strands are separate and glossy.
The strands slide apart with no tearing.

technique/loosen-noodles.does: Pulls apart a clump of steamed, oiled noodles, with a splash of water or a short warming in the pan, until each strand is free and ready to be stir-fried.
how: Put the clump in a hot pan or in a bowl, and add a splash of water.
Cover for a very short time to steam, so that the strands relax.
Pull the strands apart with chopsticks or tongs, working gently from the edge to the middle.
Drain off any water and use the noodles at once.

mistakes.fix: Warm it first so that it relaxes.
mistakes.mistake: Tearing the clump while it is cold, which breaks the strands.

mistakes.fix: Use only a splash.
mistakes.mistake: Adding too much water, so that the noodles are soggy.

comes_after.why: The yolks are first whisked over gentle heat to a ribbon, as in a sabayon, before the butter goes in.

cues.text: The yolks leave a ribbon on the surface, and the finished sauce is glossy and thick enough to coat a spoon.
Sharp at first, then rounded by the butter, with a clear note of tarragon.

technique/make-a-bearnaise.does: Makes a warm sauce of egg yolk and butter, as a hollandaise is made, but sharpened with a strong reduction of vinegar, white wine, shallot and tarragon in place of lemon juice, and finished with chopped tarragon.
how: Put the vinegar, the wine, the chopped shallot and part of the tarragon in a small pan and boil them down until only a few spoonfuls of strong, sharp liquid are left.
Strain the reduction and let it cool a little.
Melt the butter gently and keep it warm.
Whisk the yolks with the reduction in a bowl over a pan of barely trembling water until they are pale, thick and leave a ribbon. Lift the bowl away from the heat as soon as it gets too hot to touch.
Off the heat, whisk in the warm butter, a drop at a time at first and then in a thin stream, leaving the milky part in the pan.
Season, stir in the rest of the tarragon, chopped, and keep the sauce warm, never hot, until it is served.

mistakes.fix: Lift the bowl off the heat often and keep whisking.
mistakes.mistake: Heating the yolks too long or too hot, so that they scramble.

mistakes.fix: Start a drop at a time. If it splits, whisk the split sauce into a fresh yolk slowly.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the butter too fast, so that the sauce splits.

mistakes.fix: Stop when a few spoonfuls of syrupy liquid are left.
mistakes.mistake: Reducing the vinegar too little, so that the sauce is sour and thin, or too far, so that it is harsh.

mistakes.fix: Keep it in a warm bowl, away from direct heat.
mistakes.mistake: Keeping the sauce too hot while it waits, so that it separates.

variant_of.differs: A hollandaise takes its sharpness from lemon juice. A béarnaise starts with a strong reduction of vinegar, wine, shallot and tarragon, which is strained into the yolks, and ends with fresh tarragon.

comes_after.why: A béchamel begins with a pale roux, so a cook has to be able to cook flour in fat without lumps or colour.

cues.text: The sauce is smooth and ivory, and runs off the spoon in a slow, even ribbon.
The smell of raw flour has gone and a gentle smell of milk and nutmeg remains.

technique/make-a-bechamel.does: Cooks a pale roux, whisks warm milk into it a little at a time and simmers it to a smooth white sauce seasoned with nutmeg. Thin, it coats food. Thick, it holds a baked dish together.
how: Warm the milk in a second pan until it is hot but not boiling.
Melt the butter in a saucepan, stir in an equal weight of flour and cook it, stirring, only until it smells like biscuit and has taken no colour.
Take the pan off the heat and whisk in a ladle of milk until the paste is smooth. Add the rest a ladle at a time, whisking each one smooth.
Set the pan back on a low heat and simmer gently, stirring into the corners, until the raw taste of flour has gone and the sauce coats a spoon.
Season with salt and a grating of nutmeg. For a baked dish, cook it thicker. For coating, leave it looser.
If it must wait, press a piece of buttered paper onto its surface so that no skin forms.

mistakes.fix: Add it a ladle at a time and whisk each one smooth. A lumpy sauce can be rescued through a sieve.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring in all the milk at once, which leaves lumps.

mistakes.fix: Stir into the corners all the while and keep the heat low.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the sauce unstirred on the heat, so that it catches on the base of the pan.

mistakes.fix: Simmer it gently until it tastes of milk and not of flour.
mistakes.mistake: Serving it before the flour is cooked out, so that it tastes pasty.

cues.text: A clear, deep amber, like dark honey. Smoke means it has gone too far.
Toasted sugar. An acrid smell means a bitter caramel.

technique/make-a-caramel.does: Cooks sugar until it melts and browns to an amber syrup with a bittersweet taste.
how: Put the sugar in a clean, heavy, pale pan with just enough water to wet it.
Heat it without stirring. Swirl the pan if it colours unevenly.
Watch as it turns from clear to straw to amber.
Stop it the moment it is the colour of dark honey, by adding the liquid the recipe calls for, standing well back.
For a sweet and sour base, stop it with vinegar and boil until syrupy.

mistakes.fix: Leave it alone and swirl the pan.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring the sugar as it melts, which makes it seize into crystals.

mistakes.fix: Stay with it, and have the liquid ready beside the stove.
mistakes.mistake: Walking away. Caramel goes from amber to burnt in moments.

comes_after.why: The yolks and the sugar are whisked first.

cues.text: It coats the back of the spoon, and a finger drawn through the coating leaves a clear line that does not close.
The spoon moves through something a little heavier than milk.

technique/make-a-custard.does: Thickens sweetened milk with egg yolks over gentle heat, stirring until it coats a spoon and before the yolks scramble.
how: Whisk the yolks with the sugar until pale.
Heat the milk with the vanilla until it steams, and pour it slowly onto the yolks while whisking.
Return it to the pan over low heat and stir without stopping, sweeping the whole bottom and the corners.
Take it off the heat the moment it coats the back of the spoon, and strain it at once into a cold bowl.

mistakes.fix: Take it off early and strain it straight into a bowl set in iced water. If it has only just started to grain, blending can rescue it.
mistakes.mistake: Letting it get too hot, so that the yolks scramble into grains.

mistakes.fix: Trust the line on the spoon, not the clock.
mistakes.mistake: Stopping too soon for fear of scrambling, which leaves a thin sauce.

comes_after.why: The mushrooms must be minced very fine before they are cooked down.

cues.text: The paste is dark and dry, and holds a line when a spoon is drawn through it.
A deep, roasted mushroom smell.

technique/make-a-duxelles.does: Cooks finely minced mushrooms and shallot in butter until all their water has gone, to a dark, dry paste that is spread or stuffed for its deep flavour.
how: Wipe the mushrooms clean with a cloth. Do not soak them.
Mince the mushrooms and the shallot very fine, with a knife.
Cook them in butter in a wide pan over a medium heat, stirring often, until the water has cooked off and the paste starts to brown.
Season with salt, then let the paste cool before it is used.

mistakes.fix: Keep cooking until the pan is dry.
mistakes.mistake: Stopping while the paste is still wet, so that it steams grey and makes a filling soggy.

mistakes.fix: Mince them very fine.
mistakes.mistake: Chopping the mushrooms coarse, so that the filling falls apart.

comes_after.why: The parsley is chopped small and even, and a cook has to be able to chop first.

cues.text: Bright lemon and green parsley, with a sharp edge of garlic.
The mix is fine and even and still bright green.

technique/make-a-gremolata.does: Chops parsley very fine with lemon zest and a little raw garlic, to be scattered over a rich, slow-cooked dish at the very end, where its sharp freshness cuts through the fat. Nothing is cooked.
how: Pick the parsley leaves from the stalks and dry them well.
Grate the zest of the lemon in fine strips, taking only the yellow.
Peel the garlic and chop it fine with the parsley, then chop in the zest, until everything is small and even.
Make it just before serving and scatter it over the dish at the table, and not into the pot.

mistakes.fix: Take only the yellow of the peel.
mistakes.mistake: Grating in the white pith, which tastes bitter.

mistakes.fix: Scatter it over the dish at the very end.
mistakes.mistake: Mixing it into the pot early, so that it loses its freshness and turns dull.

mistakes.fix: Dry the leaves first.
mistakes.mistake: Chopping wet parsley, which turns to a paste.

comes_after.why: The onion and garlic are softened in oil before the meat goes in.

cues.text: Warm cinnamon and allspice over sweet tomato, with no sharp smell of raw wine.
The sauce is thick, and a spoon drawn across the pan leaves a track that closes slowly.

technique/make-a-kima.does: Cooks minced meat with softened onion, tomato and a little red wine, scented with cinnamon, allspice and a bay leaf, until it is a thick, moist, mildly sweet sauce that sits under a white sauce in a baked dish or is spooned over pasta.
how: Soften the onion and garlic in olive oil first, and keep the pan wide so that the meat browns and does not stew.
Add the minced meat in small lots and break it up with a spoon. Let it take colour before more goes in.
Pour in the wine and let it bubble away almost completely.
Stir in the tomato paste, then the tomatoes, the cinnamon, the allspice and the bay leaf.
Simmer gently with the lid ajar, stirring now and then, until the meat is tender and the sauce is thick enough to hold a track.
Take out the bay leaf, season, and stir in the parsley. A kima for baking is cooked drier than one for pasta, so that it does not flood the dish.

mistakes.fix: Add them with the tomato, once the wine has gone.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the spices to a pan that is too hot, so that they scorch and taste bitter.

mistakes.fix: Cook it until a spoon leaves a track.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the sauce loose, so that it floods the dish it is baked in.

mistakes.fix: Add it in small lots and let each take colour.
mistakes.mistake: Tipping all the meat in at once, so that it steams grey.

variant_of.differs: A kima is spiced with cinnamon, allspice and a bay leaf, and is built on onion and tomato paste, where a ragu starts from a soffritto of onion, carrot and celery and is finished with milk. It is cooked drier, so that it can sit under a white sauce without flooding it.

comes_after.why: The cream is made with the sweet yolk foam, which must be whisked and cooled first.

cues.text: The cream is smooth and glossy, with no grains and no streaks.
It holds a soft peak on the spatula and does not run.

technique/make-a-mascarpone-cream.does: Loosens soft mascarpone with a cooled, sweet egg-yolk foam into a smooth, thick cream that holds its shape in a spoon. It is the cream of tiramisu and of other cold layered desserts.
how: Cool the egg-yolk foam completely. A warm foam melts the cheese into a loose soup.
Put the mascarpone into a wide bowl and stir it with a spatula only until it is smooth. Never beat it hard.
Stir in a spoonful of the foam to loosen the cheese, then fold in the rest in small lots.
Stop as soon as the cream is smooth and even, with no streaks. Use it at once or keep it cold.

mistakes.fix: Stir it gently with a spatula, only until smooth.
mistakes.mistake: Beating the mascarpone hard, so that it turns grainy and then oily.

mistakes.fix: Let the foam cool first.
mistakes.mistake: Mixing in a foam that is still warm, which thins the cheese.

variant_of.differs: Nothing is whipped to hold air. A dense, soft cheese is loosened with a foam and combined with a spatula until smooth, and beating it hard would spoil it.

comes_after.why: A pesto starts as a pounded paste, and a cook has to be able to grind food in a mortar without bruising it.

cues.text: The paste is bright green and thick, with the oil bound into it and not floating on top.
It smells of fresh basil, with no trace of bitterness.

technique/make-a-pesto.does: Crushes fresh basil leaves with a little coarse salt and garlic in a mortar, then pine nuts, then grated hard cheese, and works in olive oil last, into a thick, green, raw sauce. It is the sauce of Genoa and the coast of Liguria, and it is never cooked.
how: Pick the basil leaves and dry them. Wet leaves make a dull, watery sauce.
Pound the garlic with coarse salt in a stone mortar until it is a paste.
Add the pine nuts and pound them in, then the basil a handful at a time, grinding each lot against the wall in circles until it is a rough green paste.
Work in the grated cheese, then pour in the olive oil in a thin stream, stirring, until the sauce is thick and glossy.
Keep it raw. Stir it into hot pasta off the heat, loosened with a spoonful of the cooking water.

mistakes.fix: Pound it in a mortar, or pulse it briefly with chilled things.
mistakes.mistake: Chopping the basil in a fast blade, which warms it and turns it dark and bitter.

mistakes.fix: Stir it into the pasta off the heat.
mistakes.mistake: Heating the pesto in the pan, which dulls the basil and splits the oil.

mistakes.fix: Add it in a thin stream, stirring.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring in all the oil at once, so that the sauce does not bind.

variant_of.differs: The ingredients go in a fixed order, from the hardest to the softest, and the oil and cheese are worked in at the end. The sauce is never heated, and it is a finished sauce and not just a paste.

comes_after.why: A ragu is built on a soffritto that has been cooked until it is soft and golden.

cues.text: The fat gathers in a glossy red ring at the edge, and the sauce is thick enough to hold the trail of a spoon.
Rich and sweet, with the raw smell of tomato gone.

technique/make-a-ragu.does: Cooks minced meat very slowly with a soffritto, wine and tomato until it turns into a thick, rich sauce that clings to pasta or fills a rice ball. Every region has its own ragu, and this card holds the common method.
how: Make a soffritto in a wide, heavy pot and cook it until it is soft and golden.
Add the minced meat in small lots and break it up with a spoon. Let it brown before moving on, and stir so that it cooks in fine crumbs.
Pour in the wine and let it bubble away almost completely.
Add the tomato and a little stock or milk, then turn the heat low and leave it to simmer with the lid ajar, stirring now and then, until the meat is very tender and the fat shows at the edge.
Season at the end.

mistakes.fix: Add the meat in small lots and let each brown.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding the pan, so that the meat steams grey and does not brown.

mistakes.fix: Keep the heat low and give it time to cook down.
mistakes.mistake: Rushing it, so that the sauce is thin and tastes raw.

mistakes.fix: Break it up as it browns.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the meat in lumps, which makes a coarse sauce that does not cling.

variant_of.differs: The meat is minced and browned loose in crumbs and not left in pieces, and the pot is left with the lid ajar so that the sauce thickens and does not stay a thin liquid.

cues.text: The smell changes from raw flour to biscuit, then to toasted nuts as it darkens.
A smooth paste that froths like wet sand and pulls away from the pan.

technique/make-a-roux.does: Cooks flour in melted butter to a paste that thickens a liquid without lumps or a raw taste.
how: Melt the butter over medium-low heat until it foams.
Tip in an equal weight of flour, all at once, and stir until smooth.
Keep stirring as the paste bubbles, until the raw smell of flour is gone.
Go on to the colour the sauce needs: pale for a white sauce, sandy for a blond one, nut-brown for a brown one.
Add the liquid cold to a hot roux, or hot to a cold one, a little at a time, whisking each addition smooth.

mistakes.fix: Give the roux time, until it smells of biscuit.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the liquid before the flour has cooked, which leaves a pasty taste that no simmering removes.

mistakes.fix: Add it in stages and whisk each one smooth. A lumpy sauce can be rescued through a sieve.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring in all the liquid at once, which makes lumps.

en: cook the yolks to a ribbon

cues.text: Pale, thick and foamy. The whisk draws lines that hold for a moment, and the mixture falls from it in a ribbon.
The bowl is warm to the hand, never hot.

technique/make-a-sabayon.does: Whisks egg yolks with a little liquid over gentle heat until they are thick, pale and foamy, ready to take butter.
how: Put the yolks and a spoonful of water for each in a round-bottomed bowl.
Set it over a pan of barely simmering water, or over the lowest heat.
Whisk without stopping, and lift the bowl off the heat whenever it feels hot to the hand.
Stop when the whisk leaves a trail that shows the bottom of the bowl.

mistakes.fix: Lift the bowl off the heat and keep whisking. If grains have formed, start again.
mistakes.mistake: Too much heat, which scrambles the yolks at the edge of the bowl.

mistakes.fix: Whisk until the trail holds.
mistakes.mistake: Stopping early, so that the sauce stays thin however much butter goes in.

variant_of.differs: The whisking is done over gentle heat, which cooks the yolks as it fills them with air.

comes_after.why: A sauce is brought to its body at a simmer.

cues.text: It coats the back of a spoon, and a finger drawn through the coat leaves a clear line.
Round and clean, with neither a raw floury taste nor a raw sharpness of spice.

technique/make-a-sauce.does: Builds a sauce from a flavouring base cooked in fat, a liquid and a short simmer, until it coats a spoon. It is seasoned at the end, and strained or blended if it should be smooth.
how: Cook the flavouring base in the fat first: a roux, tomato, or a spice such as paprika stirred into oil off the heat.
Add the liquid a little at a time, whisking, until the sauce is smooth.
Simmer gently, stirring now and then, until the sauce coats the back of a spoon.
Blend or strain it if it should be smooth.
Taste and season last, because a sauce grows saltier as it thickens.

mistakes.fix: Season at the end.
mistakes.mistake: Salting early and then boiling the sauce down, so that it ends up too salty.

mistakes.fix: Add it a little at a time and whisk.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring all the liquid in at once, which makes lumps.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat first.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring a spice into hot oil, where it burns and turns the sauce bitter.

comes_after.why: A soffritto is only as good as its cut, and the pieces must be small and even to melt.

cues.text: Sweet and rounded, with the raw sharpness of the onion gone.
The pieces have melted into a soft golden mass, and the oil is lightly tinted.

technique/make-a-soffritto.does: Cooks very finely chopped onion, carrot and celery slowly in olive oil, until they melt together into a soft, sweet, golden base on which the rest of the dish is built.
how: Chop the onion, carrot and celery very fine and as even as you can, so that they melt into the dish and do not show as pieces.
Warm olive oil in a wide, heavy pan over low heat, then add the vegetables with a little salt.
Stir now and then and keep the heat gentle. The vegetables first give up their water, then slowly turn soft and pale gold.
Take it as far as the dish needs: pale and sweet for a delicate soup, deeper gold for a sauce or a ragu. Stop before it turns dark or bitter.

mistakes.fix: Lower the heat and add a spoonful of water to hold back the colour.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking it over high heat, so that it browns before it softens and tastes bitter.

mistakes.fix: Chop them small and even.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting the vegetables in different sizes, so that some burn while others stay hard.

mistakes.fix: Give it the time it needs.
mistakes.mistake: Going on to the next ingredient too soon, before the vegetables have melted, so that the base tastes raw.

variant_of.differs: It uses olive oil and not butter, the vegetables are chopped much finer, and it is cooked longer, until it turns gold, where a sweat stops before any colour. A French mirepoix is cut larger and is often strained out of the dish. A soffritto stays in.

comes_after.why: Small, even pieces melt into the paste together.

cues.text: The oil seeps out at the edges of the paste, which has darkened from bright red to deep brick.
Sweet and rich, like jam. The sharp smell of raw tomato and raw garlic has gone.
Sweet and deep, with no raw sourness.

technique/make-a-sofrito.does: Cooks onion, garlic and ripe tomato slowly in a generous amount of olive oil until their water has gone and what is left is a dark, sweet, jammy paste. It is the base of rice dishes, stews and sauces.
how: Chop the onion and the garlic fine, if they are used. Grate or chop the tomato and keep its juice.
Warm a generous amount of olive oil in a wide pan over a low to medium heat.
Cook the onion with a little salt, stirring now and then, until it is soft and pale gold. Add the garlic for the last moments.
Add the tomato and keep cooking, stirring now and then, as it gives up its water and the mixture thickens.
Go on until the oil seeps out at the edges and the paste is dark, sweet and jammy. Do not hurry it with a high heat.
If paprika is wanted, take the pan off the heat and stir it in, because it turns bitter in hot oil.

mistakes.fix: Keep the heat low, and add a splash of water if it starts to catch.
mistakes.mistake: Turning up the heat to hurry it, so that the garlic and the paste scorch and turn bitter.

mistakes.fix: Keep going until the oil seeps out at the edges.
mistakes.mistake: Stopping while the tomato is still wet and sharp, which leaves a thin, sour base.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat first.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring the paprika into hot oil, where it burns within moments.

variant_of.differs: Sweating stops while the vegetables are soft and pale. A sofrito goes on much longer, in much more oil and with tomato added, until the mixture is dark, sweet and jammy.

cues.text: The liquid is clear, with no grains at the bottom, and the bubbles grow large and slow.
A cooled drop pressed between finger and thumb is sticky and draws out a short thread.

technique/make-a-syrup.does: Dissolves sugar in water over heat and simmers it briefly to a clear, lightly thick liquid, which soaks into pastry, sweetens fruit and drinks, or glazes a cake.
how: Put the sugar and the water in a saucepan, with a strip of lemon peel or a stick of cinnamon if the syrup is to be flavoured.
Stir over a gentle heat until every grain has dissolved, then stop stirring.
Bring to a boil and wipe down any crystals on the side of the pan with a wet brush.
Simmer until the liquid is clear and just thick enough to coat a spoon lightly. It thickens more as it cools, so stop early.
Add a little lemon juice near the end if the syrup is to keep, which stops it turning to crystals.
Let it cool to the heat the dish needs. Syrup poured onto pastry at the same heat leaves the pastry soggy, so one of them is cold.

mistakes.fix: Stir only until the sugar has dissolved, and wipe the side down with a wet brush.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring after it boils, which throws sugar up the side of the pan and sets the whole pan to crystals.

mistakes.fix: Take it off the heat while it is still clear and pale.
mistakes.mistake: Boiling on until the syrup browns, which makes a caramel and not a syrup.

comes_after.why: The garlic is crushed with salt first, so that it fries evenly and gives its scent at once.

cues.text: A sweet, sharp scent of garlic and green coriander, with no bitter edge.
The garlic is pale gold and never brown, and the coriander has wilted to a dark green.
A lively sizzle as the mixture meets the hot liquid.

technique/make-a-taqliyeh.does: Fries crushed raw garlic and chopped fresh coriander in hot fat for a short moment, until the garlic smells sweet and the coriander wilts and darkens, then stirs the sizzling mixture into the pot, most often at the end. It gives a stew, a soup or a dish of pulses a sharp, fresh scent.
how: Crush the garlic with salt to a rough paste, and chop the coriander fine.
Heat the fat in a small pan until it shimmers.
Add the garlic and stir at once. Add the coriander when the garlic turns pale gold and smells sweet.
Take the pan off the heat the moment the coriander has wilted and darkened, and tip it, sizzling, into the pot.
Stir it in and serve soon, while the scent is still bright.

mistakes.fix: Add the coriander as soon as the garlic turns pale gold, and take the pan off the heat quickly.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the garlic brown, which turns the whole pot bitter.

mistakes.fix: Add it at the very end, off the heat.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring the mixture in early and cooking it on, so that the fresh scent is lost.

mistakes.fix: Chop the leaves and tender stems fine.
mistakes.mistake: Chopping the coriander coarse, so that stems stay tough.

variant_of.differs: The fat holds crushed fresh garlic and chopped fresh coriander and not dry spices. It is cooked for a moment only and is stirred into the pot, most often at the end, so it finishes a dish more than it starts one.

comes_after.why: The sauce thickens by a steady simmer, so a cook has to be able to hold one.

cues.text: A spoon drawn across the pan leaves a trail, with a sheen of oil at the edge and a deep red colour.
Bright and sweet, with no raw sharpness.

technique/make-a-tomato-sauce.does: Cooks tomatoes in olive oil, with garlic or chilli, until they break down into a thick, bright sauce, with no cream or flour. A quick sauce is done in the time the pasta takes to boil, and a slow one grows deeper and sweeter.
how: Warm olive oil gently with whole garlic, or with chilli, until the oil smells of it. Do not let the garlic brown.
Add the tomatoes, crushed or chopped, with a little salt, and bring to a bubble.
Keep it at a lively simmer, stirring now and then and crushing the tomatoes against the pan, until the sauce has thickened and the oil shines at the edges.
Tear in basil at the end, off the heat, and adjust the salt.

mistakes.fix: Warm the oil gently and add the tomatoes as soon as the garlic smells sweet.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the garlic brown, which turns the whole sauce bitter.

mistakes.fix: Keep it at a simmer until it thickens, and add only a splash of water at the end if it is too thick.
mistakes.mistake: Adding water to a sauce that is too thick before it has cooked down, which leaves it thin and dull.

mistakes.fix: Stir and lower the heat.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking it too hard, so that it catches on the pan and tastes burnt.

cues.text: Sharpness and sweetness arrive together, and neither wins.
The syrup coats a spoon in a thin, shining layer.

technique/make-agrodolce.does: Melts sugar into hot vinegar and cooks it down to a glossy sweet-sour syrup, which is poured over fried vegetables, fish or meat, or cooked into them. It is a balance and not a caramel: the sugar is never taken to colour. Sicilian kitchens use it for caponata.
how: Warm the vinegar in a small pan over medium heat with the sugar, and stir until the sugar has dissolved.
Let it bubble gently until it thickens a little and smells mellow and not sharp.
Pour it over the fried vegetables, or add them to the pan, and stir over low heat until they are glazed.
Taste. Add sugar if it bites and vinegar if it cloys, until sweet and sour are in balance, then let it cool in the pan so that the flavours settle.

mistakes.fix: Keep it at a gentle bubble and stop while the syrup is pale.
mistakes.mistake: Boiling it hard until the sugar browns, which turns it bitter and takes away the balance.

mistakes.fix: Dissolve and cook them together first.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring raw vinegar and sugar over the food without cooking them together, so that it tastes sharp and grainy.

variant_of.differs: The sugar is melted into vinegar and boiled down to a sweet-sour syrup. It is never taken to colour, and it is cooked to dress food and not to be a caramel.

comes_after.why: The sauce starts as garlic pounded smooth with salt in a mortar.

cues.text: The paste turns from translucent to pale and creamy and stands in soft peaks.
The pestle goes heavy and the sauce clings to the bowl of the mortar.
Sweet and sharp with garlic, with no bitter edge.

technique/make-alioli.does: Works garlic with salt in a mortar to a smooth paste, then works in olive oil drop by drop with the pestle, always in one direction, until the paste turns into a thick, pale, glossy sauce. No egg is used: the garlic holds the oil.
how: Peel the garlic and take out any green shoot, which is bitter. Pound it with a little salt in the mortar until it is a smooth paste with no lumps.
Start turning the pestle in one direction only, and add the oil a drop at a time. Wait until each drop has been taken up before adding more.
As the sauce thickens and turns pale, the oil can go in as a very thin thread. Keep turning the pestle in the same direction.
Stop when the sauce is thick enough to stand up on the pestle. Taste, and add salt or a drop of water if it is too strong.

mistakes.fix: Add it a drop at a time at first. To mend a split sauce, pound a fresh clove with a little water and work the split sauce into it slowly.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the oil too fast, so that the sauce splits into oil and a grainy paste.

mistakes.fix: Turn the pestle in one direction only.
mistakes.mistake: Changing the direction of the pestle, which can undo the sauce.

mistakes.fix: Cut each clove open and take the shoot out.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the green shoot in the garlic, which tastes bitter.

variant_of.differs: A paste of pounded garlic and no egg yolk holds the oil, and the sauce is made by hand in a mortar with a pestle turned one way, slowly. A mayonnaise is whisked in a bowl with egg yolk.

cues.text: The dough is soft as an earlobe, springs back slowly when pressed, and does not stick to the hands.
The surface is smooth and even, with no cracks, after the rest.

technique/make-atta-dough.does: Works whole wheat flour and water into a soft, smooth dough with no yeast, then lets it rest. A rested dough is easy to roll thin and cooks into a soft, flexible flat bread.
how: Put the flour in a wide bowl with a little salt, and make a well.
Add warm water a little at a time, and bring the flour together with the fingers of one hand.
Press and fold the dough with the heel of the hand until it is smooth and soft, and no longer sticks to the bowl. It should be softer than a bread dough.
Rub the surface with a drop of oil, cover the bowl with a damp cloth, and leave the dough to rest.
Knead it briefly once more, then tear off equal balls and roll each one between the palms until it is smooth.

mistakes.fix: Add water until the dough is soft and just short of sticky.
mistakes.mistake: Making the dough stiff, so that the breads turn hard and do not puff.

mistakes.fix: Cover it and leave it until it is relaxed.
mistakes.mistake: Skipping the rest, so that the dough springs back as it is rolled.

mistakes.fix: Cover it with a damp cloth or a plate.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the covered dough dry, so that a crust forms and shows as cracks and specks in the bread.

variant_of.differs: The dough has no yeast and is worked only until it is smooth and soft, then left to rest. It is never worked until it turns elastic, and the softness comes from a high share of water.

comes_after.why: The eggs are beaten frothy before any hot liquid reaches them.

cues.text: The sauce turns pale yellow and creamy, and coats the back of a spoon.
A clean sharpness of lemon, rounded by the egg, with no trace of grain on the tongue.

technique/make-avgolemono.does: Beats eggs with lemon juice until frothy, warms them with ladles of hot broth, and stirs them back into the pot off the boil, where they turn the broth into a pale, creamy, sharp sauce.
how: Take the pot off the heat and let the liquid stop bubbling, because a boiling pot sets the eggs into threads.
Beat the eggs in a bowl until pale and frothy, then beat in the lemon juice a little at a time.
Beat in a ladle of the hot liquid, then another, and go on until the egg mixture is warm to the finger.
Pour the warm mixture back into the pot in a thin stream, stirring, or swirl the pot to mix it in.
If the sauce needs more body, set the pot on the lowest heat and stir until it thickens a little. It must never bubble.
Taste, and add salt or more lemon juice. Serve soon, and warm it only gently if it must wait.

mistakes.fix: Take the pot off the heat and warm the eggs with a few ladles of the liquid first.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring the eggs straight into a boiling pot, which sets them into strings.

mistakes.fix: Keep the heat below a bubble. A sauce that has started to grain can sometimes be rescued with a whisk, off the heat.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the sauce bubble after the eggs have gone in, so that it splits and grains.

mistakes.fix: Beat the lemon juice into the eggs first.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the lemon juice to the hot pot and not to the eggs, which can make the sauce curdle.

variant_of.differs: The lemon juice is beaten into the eggs, whole or yolks only, and there is no cream. The hot liquid is the broth of the dish itself, and the sauce is stirred back in off the boil and never boiled again, where the French liaison is made with cream.
The eggs are tempered with hot broth and then beaten with lemon juice into the soup, off the boil, so that they thicken it as a sauce and do not set in strands.

comes_after.why: The aubergine is charred whole over a flame first, which gives the cream its smoke.
The cream is built on a roux.

cues.text: A thick, pale cream flecked with the dark of the smoke, that holds a soft peak on the spoon.
A smoky, sweet smell of charred aubergine with a note of melted cheese.
Smooth and smoky, with no raw flour.

technique/make-begendi.does: Beats the soft flesh of charred aubergine into a cooked white sauce of flour, butter and milk with melted cheese, to a thick, pale, smoky cream that is spooned out under braised meat.
how: Pull the charred flesh off the skin, drain off the bitter juice and mash the flesh with a fork to a pulp.
Cook the flour in the butter to a roux, without letting it colour.
Whisk in warm milk a little at a time and stir until the sauce is thick and smooth.
Stir in the aubergine and the cheese and keep stirring until the cheese has melted.
Season, and loosen with a splash of milk if it is stiff. It should hold its shape on a spoon.
Spoon it out warm, so that it can carry a ladle of stew.

mistakes.fix: Drain the flesh first.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the aubergine with its bitter juice, which thins the cream and sours it.

mistakes.fix: Whisk it in a little at a time.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the milk all at once, so that the roux lumps.

mistakes.fix: Keep the heat low and stir.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the cream on a hot flame once the cheese is in, so that it turns stringy and catches.

variant_of.differs: Charred aubergine flesh and a melting cheese are stirred into the white sauce, and there is no nutmeg. It is cooked thick, to serve as a bed under meat and not as a sauce poured over it.

cues.text: Toasted hazelnuts.
The sputter dies away just before it browns. Silence means the water has gone.
Golden-brown specks on the bottom and a clear amber fat.

technique/make-brown-butter.does: Cooks butter until its milk solids turn nut-brown and it smells of hazelnuts.
how: Melt the butter in a pale pan, so that you can see its colour.
Let it foam. The foam is its water boiling off.
Swirl the pan as the foam falls and the solids on the bottom turn golden.
Take it off the heat the moment it smells of hazelnuts, and stop it with a squeeze of lemon or by pouring it out.

mistakes.fix: Pour it straight over the food, or into a cold dish.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving it in the hot pan, where it goes from brown to black and bitter in moments.

comes_after.why: Choux paste starts like a roux, as flour cooked in hot fat and liquid, so a cook who can cook flour without lumps can make it.

cues.text: The finished paste is smooth and glossy, and falls from the spoon in a thick ribbon.
The dried paste is heavy and stiff to beat. It loosens and turns silky as the eggs go in.

technique/make-choux-pastry.does: Cooks flour into boiling water and butter to a thick, smooth paste, then beats in eggs until it turns glossy and soft enough to spoon or pipe. Baked, the paste puffs into hollow shells. Poached, it makes light dumplings.
how: Bring the water, the butter and a little salt to a boil, so that the butter has melted by the time the water bubbles.
Take the pan off the heat, tip in all the flour at once and beat hard with a wooden spoon.
Put the pan back on a low heat and keep beating until the paste pulls into one ball, leaves a thin film on the pan and no longer sticks to the spoon.
Move the paste to a bowl and let it cool a little, or the eggs will cook in it.
Beat in the eggs a little at a time. Each addition must be taken up before the next goes in.
Stop when the paste is glossy and falls from the spoon in a slow, thick ribbon. Keep back any egg that is not needed.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat, tip all the flour in at once and beat.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the flour a little at a time, so that it lumps.

mistakes.fix: Let the paste cool a little first.
mistakes.mistake: Beating in the eggs while the paste is still hot, so that they cook into strings.

mistakes.fix: Add it a little at a time and stop when the paste falls from the spoon in a thick ribbon.
mistakes.mistake: Adding all the egg at once, which leaves a paste too loose to hold its shape.

comes_after.why: The batter is a whisked liquid, so a cook has to be able to whisk it smooth first.

cues.text: The batter runs off a spoon like thin cream and leaves only a light coat.
The edges turn golden and lift from the pan, and the underside has a lacy pattern.

technique/make-crepes.does: Cooks a thin batter of flour, egg and milk in a hot buttered pan, a ladle at a time, into thin pancakes that are folded or rolled round a filling.
how: Whisk the flour, the eggs and a little salt, then add the milk slowly, whisking, until the batter is smooth and as thin as pouring cream.
Leave the batter to rest, so that the flour swells and the bubbles settle.
Heat a wide pan and brush it lightly with butter.
Pour in a small ladle of batter and tilt and swirl the pan at once, so that the batter spreads thin to the edge.
Cook until the edges lift and the underside is golden, then turn it with a spatula and cook the other side briefly.
Stack the crepes as they are done, so that they stay soft.

mistakes.fix: Whisk in more milk a spoonful at a time until the batter pours like thin cream.
mistakes.mistake: Making the batter too thick, so that the crepes turn out heavy and doughy.

mistakes.fix: Wait until the pan is hot, and treat the first crepe as a test.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring into a pan that is not hot enough, so that the crepe is pale and tough.

mistakes.fix: Add it slowly, whisking all the time.
mistakes.mistake: Adding all the milk at once, which leaves lumps.

cues.text: The paste leaves the sides and the bottom of the pan and gathers into one mass round the spoon.
It is heavy to stir and holds the trail of the spoon.
After chilling it holds the cut of a spoon and does not stick to floured hands.

technique/make-croqueta-paste.does: Cooks flour in butter with a little onion, stirs in chopped ham, then beats in warm milk a little at a time over the heat until the mixture is so thick that it pulls away from the pan in one mass. Spread in a tray and chilled, it sets firm enough to shape by hand.
how: Melt the butter in a wide pan over a gentle heat and soften the finely chopped onion in it without colour.
Stir in the flour and cook it, stirring, until it smells of biscuit.
Add the finely chopped ham. Pour in warm milk a little at a time, beating hard with a wooden spoon after each addition until smooth before the next goes in.

Keep stirring over a low heat until the mixture is very thick and pulls away from the sides and the bottom of the pan as one mass. Season with nutmeg. The ham is already salty, so taste before adding salt.
Spread the paste in a shallow dish, press a sheet of film onto the surface so that no skin forms, and chill it until it is firm all the way through.

mistakes.fix: Warm the milk and add it a little at a time, beating smooth after each addition.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the milk cold and all at once, which makes lumps.

mistakes.fix: Keep stirring until the paste pulls away from the pan, and chill it until firm.
mistakes.mistake: Stopping while the paste is still loose, so that the croquetas slump and burst in the oil.

mistakes.fix: Chill it overnight if there is time; a cold paste is easy to roll.
mistakes.mistake: Shaping the paste while it is still soft.

variant_of.differs: Far more flour is used for the same milk, the ham and onion go in with it, and it is cooked until it leaves the pan in one mass and is then chilled to a firm block. A béchamel is kept loose enough to pour or coat.

comes_after.why: Dashi is kept below a boil, so a cook has to be able to hold a liquid at a steady gentle heat first.

cues.text: The stock smells of the sea and of smoke, with nothing harsh in it.
The stock is pale gold and clear.

technique/make-dashi.does: Steeps dried kelp and dried bonito in hot water for a short time, to draw out a clear, savoury stock. Nothing is boiled long: a long boil turns the stock bitter and cloudy.
how: Wipe the kelp with a damp cloth and leave the white bloom on, as it carries taste. Put it in cold water and bring the water up slowly.
Take the kelp out just before the water boils.
Turn off the heat, scatter in the bonito flakes and let them sink by themselves.
Leave them to steep until they have all sunk, then pour the stock through a fine sieve. Do not press the flakes, or the stock turns cloudy and fishy.
For a plant-only stock, leave out the bonito and steep the kelp alone for longer.

mistakes.fix: Lift the kelp out as the first small bubbles rise.
mistakes.mistake: Boiling the kelp, which turns the stock slimy and bitter.

mistakes.fix: Let it drip by itself.
mistakes.mistake: Squeezing the bonito in the sieve, which clouds the stock.

mistakes.fix: Steep it off the heat only.
mistakes.mistake: Simmering the bonito, which makes the stock fishy.

cues.text: The sauce is salty and sweet together, with no sharp edge of raw alcohol or vinegar.
The sauce is clear and no grains of sugar show on the bottom of the pan.

technique/make-dipping-sauce.does: Warms a few thin seasoning liquids together, such as stock, soy sauce, mirin or vinegar, with sugar if it is wanted, until the sugar has dissolved and the alcohol has cooked off. It then cools into one smooth, salty-sweet sauce.
how: Put the mirin or the sake in a small pan and bring it up to a boil for a moment, so that its alcohol goes off.
Add the other liquids and any sugar, and stir over a low heat only until the sugar has dissolved.
Do not let it boil hard, or it reduces and turns too salty.
Take it off the heat and let it cool. Taste it, and add stock if it is too strong.

mistakes.fix: Warm it only until the sugar has gone.
mistakes.mistake: Boiling the sauce hard, which concentrates the salt.

mistakes.fix: For cold noodles, cool it first. For fried food that should drink it in, pour it on while the food is hot.
mistakes.mistake: Using it hot on food that should stay crisp.

comes_after.why: The garlic has to be crushed to a smooth paste with salt before it goes into the yogurt.

cues.text: The yogurt is smooth and even, with no streaks or flecks of garlic.
The garlic is clear and round, and the yogurt is lightly salted and cool.

technique/make-garlic-yogurt.does: Stirs crushed, salted garlic into cold, thick yogurt until it is smooth and evenly scented, so that it can be spooned under or over hot and cold food. The yogurt is never heated.
how: Crush the garlic with the salt to a smooth paste, so that no raw lump is left to bite.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl and beat it with a spoon until it is smooth. Loosen very thick yogurt with a splash of cold water if it will not spread.
Stir in the garlic until it is evenly mixed, then taste and add more salt if it needs it.
Keep it cold until it is needed, so that the garlic mellows into the yogurt.

mistakes.fix: Crush it to a paste with the salt first.
mistakes.mistake: Dropping the garlic in raw and in lumps, so that some bites are harsh.

mistakes.fix: Keep it cold and spoon it under or over the hot food at the table.
mistakes.mistake: Putting the yogurt on the heat, or on food that is boiling, so that it splits and turns grainy.

mistakes.fix: Add water a splash at a time and stop as soon as it spreads.
mistakes.mistake: Thinning it with too much water, so that it runs off the food.

cues.text: The dough is soft and smooth, a little tacky, and holds a ball with no cracks.
The surface of each ball is smooth and unbroken.

technique/make-khoya-dough.does: Crumbles khoya and works it with a little flour, milk and a trace of raising agent into a soft, smooth dough with no cracks, and rolls it into small balls that will not split in the fat.
how: Crumble the khoya fine, with no lumps, in a wide bowl.
Add a little flour and the raising agent, and mix lightly with the fingertips.
Add milk a spoonful at a time and press the mixture together. Work it gently, only until it is soft and smooth.
Rub a little ghee on the palms. Roll the dough into small balls with no cracks on the surface.
Keep the balls covered until they are fried.

mistakes.fix: Mix lightly and stop as soon as the dough is smooth.
mistakes.mistake: Working the dough hard, which makes the cooked balls tough and chewy.

mistakes.fix: Use only as much flour as is needed to bring the khoya together.
mistakes.mistake: Adding too much flour, so that the balls turn dense and floury.

mistakes.fix: Add a drop of milk and roll again until the surface is smooth.
mistakes.mistake: Rolling balls with cracks, which open and split in the hot fat.

variant_of.differs: The dough is made of crumbled khoya, with only a little flour, and is worked gently and briefly. There is no gluten to build. Kneading it hard would make the balls tough.

comes_after.why: The peppers and tomato are softened in fat first, without browning.

cues.text: The eggs are streaked, with bright yolk and white still showing, lying in a juicy red base.
The spoon meets soft, loose eggs and no firm curds.

technique/make-menemen.does: Sets whole eggs gently in a pan of softened tomato and pepper, breaking them in and stirring only lightly, so that the dish ends loose and juicy, streaked with white and yolk, instead of in fine curds.
how: Soften the peppers in butter or oil, then add the tomato and cook until it has collapsed into a thick, juicy base. Salt it.
Lower the heat. Break the eggs straight on to the base and leave them until the edges begin to set.
Stir lightly a few times with a wooden spoon, so that the white and the yolk only half mix.
Take the pan off the heat while the eggs are still soft and moist, because they go on setting in the heat of the pan.
Serve at once in the pan, with bread to scoop it up.

mistakes.fix: Break them in whole and stir only a few times.
mistakes.mistake: Beating the eggs and stirring without pause, which gives a dry scramble.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat while it is still wet and soft.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking the dish until the eggs are firm and the base has dried out.

mistakes.fix: Cook the tomato down until it is thick before the eggs go in.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the eggs to a watery base, so that the dish turns to soup.

variant_of.differs: The whole eggs go straight on to a base of cooked tomato and pepper and are barely stirred, so that the dish is left juicy and streaked. Scrambling beats the eggs first, stirs without pause and aims at small creamy curds.

cues.text: The dough is soft as a lobe of the ear, elastic and a little sticky, and springs back slowly when pressed.
A small piece pulled out between the fingers goes thin and clear before it breaks.

technique/make-msemen-dough.does: Works flour and fine semolina with warm salted water, by hand and for a good while, on an oiled surface, until the dough is smooth, soft and stretchy, then divides it into balls and rests them under oil so that they can later be stretched paper thin.
how: Mix the flour, the semolina and the salt, and add warm water a little at a time until a soft, wet dough forms.
Oil the hands and the work surface and work the dough with the heels of the hands for a good while, until it is smooth, soft and stretchy.
Divide it into balls of an even size and roll each one in oil.
Cover the balls and leave them to rest until they relax and can be stretched without tearing.

mistakes.fix: Keep it wetter than seems right and work it with oiled hands.
mistakes.mistake: Making the dough stiff with too little water, so that it tears when stretched.

mistakes.fix: Rest the oiled balls until they relax.
mistakes.mistake: Skipping the rest, so that the dough springs back and will not stretch.

variant_of.differs: Kneading works a firm dough on a floured board. This dough is wet, worked on an oiled surface with oiled hands, and divided into balls that are rested under oil so that they can be stretched thin.

cues.text: The dough has swelled well past its first size and the surface is smooth and domed.
It is soft and a little tacky, and springs back slowly when pressed with a finger.

technique/make-naan-dough.does: Works flour, yeast, yogurt, milk and a little oil into a soft, slightly sticky dough, then leaves it covered to rise until it is puffy and light. The yogurt and the yeast together make a dough that stays soft and chewy once it is cooked on a hot plate.
how: Stir the yeast and the sugar into the warm milk and leave them until the top turns foamy.
Mix the flour and the salt in a large bowl, make a well, and pour in the yeast milk, the yogurt and the oil.
Work it together into a rough dough, then knead on a floured board until it is smooth, soft and only a little sticky.
Put the dough in an oiled bowl, turn it once to coat it, and cover it.
Leave it in a warm place until it has swelled and feels light and springy.

mistakes.fix: Keep the dough soft and use only a dusting of flour on the board.
mistakes.mistake: Adding much more flour to stop the stickiness, which gives a dry, tough bread.

mistakes.fix: Use milk that is only comfortably warm to a finger.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring hot milk onto the yeast, which kills it so the dough never rises.

mistakes.fix: Cover the bowl with a damp cloth or a plate.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the dough uncovered, so that a dry skin forms.

variant_of.differs: The dough is leavened with yeast and enriched with yogurt, milk and oil, so it is softer and stickier, kneaded briefly and left to rise before it is cooked.

comes_after.why: A watery vegetable has to be salted and squeezed dry first, or it thins the yogurt.

cues.text: The raita is thick and creamy, with the vegetable spread evenly through it and no pool of water.
It tastes cool, lightly salted and gently tangy, with a roasted note of cumin.

technique/make-raita.does: Whisks cold yogurt smooth and stirs in a cool, drained raw or cooked vegetable, with salt and a roasted ground spice, to make a cooling side that tempers the heat of a spiced meal.
how: Whisk cold yogurt in a bowl until it is smooth and creamy. Thin it with a splash of cold water only if it is very thick.
Wring the vegetable dry, or drain it well, so that it does not thin the yogurt.
Stir the vegetable into the yogurt with salt and a roasted, ground spice such as cumin.
Taste and adjust the salt. Chill the raita before it is served and stir it again just before.

mistakes.fix: Salt and squeeze the vegetable first.
mistakes.mistake: Adding a watery vegetable without drying it, so that the raita turns thin and sour.

mistakes.fix: Keep it cold from start to end.
mistakes.mistake: Heating the yogurt, so that it splits.

mistakes.fix: Mix it shortly before serving, or squeeze the vegetable very dry.
mistakes.mistake: Mixing it long before the meal, so that it turns watery as it sits.

cues.text: The meat comes apart at the touch of a fork, with no resistance.
The shredded meat is in ragged threads, glistening with fat, and not a smooth paste.

technique/make-rillettes.does: Cooks cut meat very slowly in its own fat and a little wine until it can be pulled apart with a fork, shreds it, mixes it back with some of the melted fat and packs it in a pot under a layer of fat, to be spread cold on bread.
how: Cut the meat and the fatty belly into pieces of about the same size, and season them generously.
Put the meat in a heavy pot with a little white wine, garlic and herbs, cover it and cook at the gentlest heat in the oven until it falls apart and sits in a pool of clear fat.
Take out the herbs and lift the meat from the fat with a slotted spoon. Keep the fat.
Pull the meat apart with a pair of forks while it is still warm until it is in soft, ragged threads. Do not mash it.
Mix in enough of the warm fat to make the meat spreadable, and taste it. It should be seasoned boldly, as cold food tastes milder.
Pack the meat firmly into jars, press out any air pockets and seal the top with a layer of fat. Keep it cold and let it rest for a few days before eating.

mistakes.fix: Keep the heat low, with the pot covered, until the meat falls apart.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking at too high a heat, so that the meat fries and goes dry instead of turning soft.

mistakes.fix: Pull it into threads with a pair of forks.
mistakes.mistake: Pounding or blending the meat, which makes a heavy paste.

mistakes.fix: Taste the mixture and season it boldly while it is still warm.
mistakes.mistake: Seasoning lightly, so that the cold rillettes taste flat.

variant_of.differs: A confit keeps whole pieces and lifts them out of the fat to be stored. Rillettes cooks cut meat with its own fat and some wine, pulls it into threads, mixes it with fat and packs it in jars to be spread cold.

cues.text: A smooth sauce the colour of brick that coats the back of a spoon in a thin, glossy layer.
Smoky and warm with a bite from the hot paprika, and no raw taste of flour.
Toasty and sweet, with no burnt edge.

technique/make-salsa-brava.does: Toasts a little flour in olive oil, takes the pan off the heat to stir in sweet and hot paprika, then whisks in water and tomato paste and simmers it to a thin, glossy, brick-red sauce with a sharp bite, to spoon over fried potatoes.
how: Warm the olive oil in a small pan over a low heat. Stir in the flour and cook it, stirring, until it smells nutty and has only just darkened.
Take the pan off the heat and stir in the sweet paprika and the hot paprika. Paprika scorches in hot oil and turns the sauce bitter.
Whisk in the tomato paste, then pour in the water a little at a time, whisking smooth after each addition. Add a crushed clove of garlic if it is liked.
Put the pan back on a low heat and simmer, whisking now and then, until the sauce is thick enough to coat a spoon lightly. Season it with salt at the end.
Keep it warm and spoon it over the potatoes at the last moment, so that they stay crisp.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat first and stir it in at once.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring the paprika into hot oil, so that it scorches and the sauce turns bitter.

mistakes.fix: Pour it in a little at a time, whisking smooth after each addition.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring in all the water at once, which leaves lumps of flour.

mistakes.fix: Loosen it with a little water until it flows off the spoon.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the sauce get too thick, so that it clings to the potatoes as a paste.

variant_of.differs: The fat is olive oil and not butter, the flour is only lightly toasted, the paprika goes in off the heat, and the sauce stays thin and sharp. A roux is cooked to a set colour and is the thickener of a smooth white or brown sauce.

comes_after.why: The dried peppers are soaked until soft before their pulp is scraped out.

cues.text: The onion is pale, soft and translucent before the pepper goes in, and the sauce is brick-red and smooth after sieving.
Sweet and deep, with the mild warmth of dried pepper and no raw onion.
It coats the back of a spoon thickly and falls from it slowly.

technique/make-salsa-vizcaina.does: Cooks a large quantity of onion very slowly in olive oil until it is sweet and soft, joins it with the pulp of dried choricero peppers that have been soaked until soft, simmers them together and rubs the sauce through a sieve into a thick, smooth, sweet, brick-red sauce for salt cod.
how: Cover the dried peppers with hot water and leave them until they are soft and wrinkled. Split them, scrape the pulp from the skins and keep the soaking water.
Cook plenty of sliced onion with the garlic in olive oil, with the lid ajar, over a very low heat until it is soft, sweet and pale. Do not let it brown.
Stir in the pepper pulp and a ladle of the soaking water, and simmer gently until the onion falls apart. For more body, simmer a piece of stale bread in the sauce.
Rub the sauce through a sieve with the back of a ladle, or blend it and then sieve it, so that no skin is left. Loosen it with soaking water if it is too thick.
Season with salt at the end, once the sauce has reduced.

mistakes.fix: Cook it over a very low heat with the lid ajar, and add a splash of water if it begins to colour.
mistakes.mistake: Browning the onion, which turns the sauce bitter and dark.

mistakes.fix: Rub the sauce through a sieve until only skin is left.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving out the sieve, so that bits of pepper skin stay in the sauce.

mistakes.fix: Season at the end.
mistakes.mistake: Salting early, before the sauce has reduced, which leaves it too salty.

variant_of.differs: The onion is cooked down for much longer until it is a sauce, joined by the pulp of dried peppers, and then rubbed through a sieve. Sweating only softens cut vegetables at the start of a dish.

cues.text: The crumbs are cool and dry, and the dough holds when it is pinched but does not stick to the fingers.
Small flecks of butter show in the finished dough, and it is not smooth.

technique/make-shortcrust-pastry.does: Rubs cold butter into flour with the fingertips until the mixture looks like fine crumbs, then binds it with a little cold water into a dough. Baked, the dough is short, which means crumbly and tender, and not chewy. It is rested in a cool place before it is rolled.
how: Cut the cold butter into small pieces and put it in a bowl with the flour and a little salt.
Rub the butter into the flour with the tips of the fingers, lifting the mixture as you go to let in air, until it looks like fine crumbs with no big lumps of butter left.
Sprinkle on cold water a little at a time and cut it in with a knife until the crumbs begin to cling.
Press the crumbs together into a flat round. Do not knead it.
Wrap the dough and rest it in a cool place until it is firm, so that the flour relaxes and the butter sets again.

mistakes.fix: Work fast with the fingertips, and chill the bowl and the butter first if the kitchen is warm.
mistakes.mistake: Working the butter with warm hands for too long, so that it melts into the flour and the pastry turns greasy and tough.

mistakes.fix: Add the water a spoonful at a time and stop as soon as the dough holds.
mistakes.mistake: Adding too much water, which makes the pastry tough and makes it shrink in the oven.

mistakes.fix: Press it together once, and leave it alone.
mistakes.mistake: Kneading the dough until it is smooth, which makes it elastic and chewy.

comes_after.why: A paste starts with aromatics pounded and broken down with salt.

cues.text: The paste is an even deep colour with no dry streaks of powder.
It clings to the spoon and does not run off.

technique/make-spice-paste.does: Works ground spices, with fresh garlic, ginger or chilli, salt and a little liquid, into a thick paste by pounding or blending. The paste clings to fish, meat or vegetables, and seasons them all over.
how: Pound or blend the garlic, ginger and fresh chilli with the salt to a rough mash. The salt helps break them down.
Add the ground spices.
Add a little liquid, such as water, lemon juice or yogurt, a spoonful at a time, and work it in.
Stop when the paste is thick and smooth, and holds on the spoon without running.
Use it at once, or let it stand briefly so the flavours join.

mistakes.fix: Add it a spoonful at a time and stop when the paste clings.
mistakes.mistake: Adding all the liquid at once, so that the paste runs off the food.

mistakes.fix: Cook it gently, with a splash of liquid, or use it as a coating.
mistakes.mistake: Frying the raw paste on a high heat, so that the powders scorch.

comes_after.why: The pieces are folded into the mayonnaise, not beaten in.

cues.text: The sauce is thick and flecked with small pieces, and does not run.
The sauce is creamy first and then sharp.

technique/make-tartar-sauce.does: Folds finely chopped pickles, boiled egg and onion into mayonnaise, to make a thick, creamy sauce with a sharp bite for fried food.
how: Chop the pickles, the boiled egg and a little onion small. Squeeze the onion dry in a cloth if it is strong.
Put the mayonnaise in a bowl and fold in the chopped pieces.
Add a few drops of lemon juice, taste, and season with pepper.
Chill it briefly so that the flavours join.

mistakes.fix: Chop them small.
mistakes.mistake: Chopping the pickles too coarsely, so that the sauce is lumpy.

mistakes.fix: Pat them dry before they go in.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the pickles wet, which thins the sauce.

comes_after.why: The rice must be nearly done and still loose before the finish.

cues.text: The risotto turns glossy and creamy and spreads out slowly like a wave when it is spooned onto a plate.
The spoon moves easily through the rice, which flows and does not stand in a lump.

technique/mantecare.does: Takes the pan off the heat and beats cold butter and grated hard cheese hard into the rice, so that fat and starch blend into a creamy, glossy, flowing finish. The Italian name is mantecatura.
how: When the rice is a few moments from ready, take the pan off the heat. The risotto should still be loose, because it tightens as it rests.
Add cold butter in cubes and a generous handful of finely grated cheese.
Beat hard with a wooden spoon and shake the pan with a quick circular motion, until the fat has vanished and the rice turns glossy and flows.
Cover for a short rest, then serve in warm bowls at once.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat first, and loosen it with a splash of hot stock if it is too tight.
mistakes.mistake: Beating it in over strong heat, so that the cheese turns stringy and the butter runs to oil.

mistakes.fix: Use butter cold from the fridge, cut small.
mistakes.mistake: Using soft or melted butter, which goes straight to oil.

mistakes.fix: Keep the pan loose and wet before the finish.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the risotto stiff before the butter goes in, so that it ends as a stiff lump.

variant_of.differs: French mounting whisks butter into a reduced liquid, to thicken a sauce. Here butter and grated cheese are beaten into rice, and it is the starch of the rice, not a reduced liquid, that holds the fat in a creamy sauce.

cues.text: Meat from a wine marinade is stained on the outside. The colour does not reach far inside.
The meat smells of the wine and the herbs.

technique/marinate.does: Steeps food in a seasoned liquid before it is cooked, so that its surface takes on the flavour.
how: Mix the wine or the acid with the aromatics and a little oil.
Turn the food in it until it is coated, in a bowl that acid does not attack.
Cover it and keep it in the fridge, turning it once or twice.
Lift the food out and dry it well before browning it. Keep the marinade for the pot.

mistakes.fix: Drain it and pat it dry first.
mistakes.mistake: Browning meat straight from the marinade, wet, so that it steams and will not colour.

mistakes.fix: It flavours the surface. Only long, gentle cooking makes a tough cut tender.
mistakes.mistake: Expecting a marinade to make a tough cut tender.

cues.text: Bright lemon and dried oregano, with garlic underneath.
Every piece is coated in a glossy film of oil and none sits in a pool.

technique/marinate-in-oil-and-lemon.does: Turns small pieces of meat in olive oil, lemon juice, oregano and garlic for a short while before they are grilled, so that the surface takes up the flavour and the oil keeps the meat from drying on the fire.
how: Cut the meat into even pieces so that they take the marinade and cook at the same pace.
Mix the oil, the lemon juice, the oregano, the crushed garlic and a little salt in a bowl.
Turn the meat in it until every piece shines, then cover the bowl and keep it in the cold.
Keep the time short. Lemon juice dries meat the longer it sits, and the surface turns chalky.
Lift the meat out and let the extra drip off before it goes on the skewers or the grill. Do not spoon used marinade over food that has been cooked.

mistakes.fix: Keep the time short.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the meat in lemon juice for a long time, so that it turns dry and chalky.

mistakes.fix: Let the extra marinade drip away first.
mistakes.mistake: Putting the meat on the fire dripping wet, so that it flares and scorches.

mistakes.fix: Use a little salt and season again at the end.
mistakes.mistake: Salting heavily in the marinade, which draws out juice.

variant_of.differs: The liquid is olive oil and lemon juice with oregano and garlic, with no wine, and the time is short, because lemon juice dries meat. The oil carries the flavour and protects the meat on the fire, where a wine marinade is made for a long braise.

cues.text: The pieces are stained an even brown and glisten, with only a little liquid left in the bowl.
The bowl smells strongly of ginger and garlic.

technique/marinate-in-soy-sauce.does: Steeps pieces of poultry for a short while in soy sauce and sake with ginger and garlic, so that the flavour sinks in and the surface is seasoned. The salty liquid is let drip off before frying and is not kept for the pot.
how: Cut the meat into even, bite-sized pieces, so that each takes up the same amount of flavour.
In a bowl, mix the soy sauce and the sake with finely grated ginger and garlic.
Add the meat and work the liquid in with your hands until every piece is wet.
Leave it for a short while, turning the pieces once. Soy is salty, and a long steep turns the meat firm and dry.
Lift the pieces out and let the extra liquid drip off before they are coated.

mistakes.fix: Steep it for a short while only.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the meat in the soy for too long, so that it turns salty and firm.

mistakes.fix: Let the extra liquid drip off first.
mistakes.mistake: Coating the pieces while they are still dripping, which turns a dry coat to paste.

variant_of.differs: The liquid is salty soy sauce and sake with ginger, not wine or acid, and the steeping is brief, since soy firms the meat if it sits long. The meat is let drip and not dried, because a little soy stays on for the coat to cling to.

comes_after.why: The marinade is built on a paste of garlic, ginger, chilli and ground spices, so the paste has to be made first.

cues.text: The marinade sits on the food as an even, thick coat that does not slide off.
Thick pieces of meat feel a little softer under the finger after the wait.

technique/marinate-in-yogurt.does: Steeps meat or firm cheese in yogurt that has been mixed with a spice paste and salt, so that the mild acid of the yogurt softens the surface and the spices are carried right into it. The coat browns and chars in strong heat.
how: Make the spice paste first, with garlic, ginger, fresh chilli, ground spices, salt and a little lemon juice.
Whisk the paste into thick yogurt. Hang the yogurt in a cloth first if it is thin, so that the marinade clings and does not run off.
Cut a few slashes into thick pieces of meat so that the marinade can get in.
Turn the food in the marinade until every surface is coated, cover the bowl and keep it in the fridge. Tough cuts want a long wait. Tender pieces and paneer want a short one.
Lift the food out and let the extra drip away before it meets the heat. Thick yogurt left on it will steam and not char.

mistakes.fix: Give them a short wait only, and give the long wait to tough cuts.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving paneer or tender pieces in the yogurt for too long, so that they turn mushy and sour.

mistakes.fix: Hang the yogurt in a cloth to drain, or strain it, before the paste goes in.
mistakes.mistake: Using thin, watery yogurt, so that the marinade runs off and the food steams in the pan.

mistakes.fix: Use a glass, china or steel bowl that does not take on a metallic taste.
mistakes.mistake: Using a metal bowl that reacts with the acid.

variant_of.differs: The liquid is thick yogurt and not wine or vinegar, and it carries a spice paste into the food. Its lactic acid is gentle, so it tenderises without turning the surface chalky, and the coat is meant to stay on and char in hot, dry heat.

comes_after.why: The potatoes are boiled first.

cues.text: A smooth, glossy purée that falls slowly from the spoon and holds a soft peak.
No lumps under the spoon, and nothing gluey or stretchy.

technique/mash.does: Crushes boiled potatoes while they are hot and dry, then beats in butter and hot milk to make a smooth purée.
how: Boil floury potatoes in their skins or in large pieces, starting in cold salted water.
Drain them and let them steam dry for a moment.
Push them through a ricer or a food mill while they are still hot.
Beat in cold butter first, then hot milk little by little, until the purée is smooth and soft.

mistakes.fix: Use a ricer, a food mill or a masher, and stop when it is smooth.
mistakes.mistake: Using a blender or a food processor, which turns potato to glue.

mistakes.fix: Mash them hot, straight after they have steamed dry.
mistakes.mistake: Mashing potatoes that are cold or waterlogged.
