comes_after.why: The flesh is soft and smoky from the flame before it is mashed.

cues.text: Rough strands and small soft lumps, not a smooth paste.
No firm bits left under the fork.

technique/mash-with-a-fork.does: Breaks soft, cooked flesh into a rough, stringy mash with a fork, so that some texture is left and the smoky taste of the food is not lost to a machine.
how: Make sure the flesh is completely soft, and let any bitter juice drain off.
Put the flesh in a bowl and press and drag a fork through it until it falls into strands and small soft lumps.
Stir in the dressing a little at a time as you go, so that the flesh takes up the seasoning.
Stop while some texture is left.

mistakes.fix: Use a fork, and stop while strands are still showing.
mistakes.mistake: Blending it to a smooth paste, so that the texture is lost.

mistakes.fix: Keep it on the heat until it has collapsed completely.
mistakes.mistake: Mashing flesh that is not soft all the way, which leaves hard bits.

variant_of.differs: The flesh is broken into a rough, stringy mass by hand and not beaten smooth, and no butter or milk goes in.

cues.text: Smooth and glossy, with no lumps and no grainy streaks.
Barely warm to the touch, never hot.

technique/melt.does: Turns chocolate or a solid fat liquid over gentle heat, without letting it colour, scorch or seize.
how: Chop chocolate into small, even pieces, and cut butter into cubes.
Set a bowl over a pan of barely simmering water, with the bottom of the bowl clear of the water.
Stir now and then, and take the bowl off while a few small lumps are left. They melt as you stir.
Butter on its own can be melted in a small pan over low heat.

mistakes.fix: Keep the bowl and the spoon dry, and the water at a bare simmer.
mistakes.mistake: Letting steam or a drop of water into chocolate, which makes it seize into a stiff, grainy paste.

mistakes.fix: Melt it over water, and off the heat for the last lumps.
mistakes.mistake: Heating chocolate straight on the flame or too fast, so that it scorches and turns thick and bitter.

cues.text: A fine, moist pile with no piece larger than a grain.
Garlic smells sharp and strong the moment it is cut this fine.

technique/mince.does: Cuts food so fine that it melts into a dish and leaves no piece to bite on.
how: Slice the food thinly, then cut across the slices.
Rock the knife over the pile, scraping it together now and then, until no piece stands out.
For garlic, crush the clove under the flat of the blade first, so that the skin slips off and the flesh breaks open.

mistakes.fix: Mince it last, just before it goes into the pan.
mistakes.mistake: Mincing garlic long before it is needed, so that it turns harsh.

variant_of.differs: It goes on much longer, until the pieces are almost a paste and vanish into the dish.

comes_after.why: Butter can only be mounted into a liquid that has been boiled down first.

cues.text: The sauce turns opaque, glossy and creamy, with no beads of clear fat at the edge.
It coats a spoon lightly, like thin cream.

technique/mount-with-butter.does: Whisks cold butter into a hot liquid off the boil, so that it melts into a smooth, glossy, lightly thickened sauce and not into a layer of fat.
how: Boil the liquid down first, until only a few syrupy, strong spoonfuls are left in the pan.
Take the pan off the heat, or turn the heat to its lowest.
Add cold butter in small cubes, a few at a time, and whisk or swirl the pan until each lot has vanished before the next goes in.
Stop when the sauce is glossy and coats a spoon. Season it and serve it at once: it can be neither boiled nor kept.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat. If the sauce splits, whisk in a spoonful of cold water or cream off the heat.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the butter over high heat, or letting the sauce boil afterwards, which melts the butter to oil and leaves the sauce greasy.

mistakes.fix: Use butter cold from the fridge, cut small.
mistakes.mistake: Using soft or melted butter, which goes straight to oil.

mistakes.fix: Reduce further before the butter goes in.
mistakes.mistake: Too much liquid left in the pan, so that the butter cannot thicken it.

variant_of.differs: The fat is cold butter, the liquid is hot, and nothing but the butter's own milk solids holds the sauce together.

cues.text: The pan shines lightly, with no pool of oil.
Egg poured in gives a soft hiss.

technique/oil-the-pan.does: Wipes a thin film of oil over the pan with a folded paper towel, to keep thin layers of batter or egg from sticking, with no pool of oil left to fry them.
how: Warm the pan over a medium heat.
Fold a paper towel, dip the corner in oil and wipe it over the whole surface of the pan, including the sides.
Wipe the pan again between layers, so that every layer meets a fresh, thin film.
Keep the towel to hand on a small dish.

mistakes.fix: Wipe on a thin film only.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring oil straight in, so that the layers fry and turn pitted.

mistakes.fix: Oil again each time.
mistakes.mistake: Skipping the oil between layers, so that later layers stick.

cues.text: An even, golden underside.
A steady, gentle sizzle. Spitting means the heat is too high or the food is wet.

technique/pan-fry.does: Cooks a flat piece of food in a thin layer of hot fat, turning it once.
how: Heat a film of fat in the pan over medium heat.
Lay the food in, away from you, and leave it alone.
Turn it once, when the underside is golden and it lifts without sticking.
For an egg, keep the heat gentle and spoon hot fat over the white until it is set.

mistakes.fix: Turn it once. If it sticks, it is not ready to turn.
mistakes.mistake: Turning the food again and again, so that it never browns.

variant_of.differs: Larger, flat pieces that lie still and are turned once, over gentler heat.

comes_after.why: Rice for layering must lose its loose starch first or it clumps, so rinsing comes before boiling.

cues.text: A grain bends but then snaps, and the core is firm and chalky white.
The grains have grown long and are still separate, with no mush in the water.

technique/parboil-rice.does: Boils rinsed and soaked rice in a large pot of well-salted water, with whole spices if the dish asks for them, only until each grain is nearly tender with a firm core, then drains it at once. The grains finish later, in steam, in a layered dish.
how: Rinse the rice in several changes of cold water until the water is nearly clear, then leave it to soak in cold water for a good while and drain it.
Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil with plenty of salt, and the whole spices if there are any. The water should taste of the sea.
Slide in the rice, bring the water back to the boil and stir once, gently, to stop the grains sticking.
Test a grain often. It is ready when it snaps cleanly and shows a white, firm core when pressed between the fingers.
Drain it at once into a colander and spread it out. Do not rinse it. It must not be left to sit and go on cooking.

mistakes.fix: Drain it while the core is still firm. It has a long steam still to come.
mistakes.mistake: Boiling the rice until it is soft, so that it turns to paste during the final steaming.

mistakes.fix: Rinse until the water is nearly clear, then soak before boiling.
mistakes.mistake: Skipping the rinse and the soak, so that the grains clump and break.

mistakes.fix: Salt the water boldly. Most of it goes down the drain.
mistakes.mistake: Salting the water too lightly, so that the finished dish tastes flat.

variant_of.differs: The rice is boiled in a great deal of water, as pasta is, and drained while a firm core remains. It is not cooked in a measured amount of water until all the water is gone. The last of the cooking is done later in steam.
The food is rice, boiled in a large pot of well-salted water only until nearly tender, to be finished later by steaming.

cues.text: Smooth flesh, with no skin left and no deep gouges.

technique/peel.does: Takes off the skin or the shell, and as little as possible of what lies under it.
how: Wash the vegetable first, so that dirt does not travel from the skin to the flesh.
Draw a peeler along its length in long strokes, turning it as you go.
Use a knife for a thick or knobbly skin: cut a flat base, then follow the curve from top to bottom.
For a boiled egg, crack the shell all over and peel from the wide end under a thin stream of water.
For a cooked lobster or crab, crack the shell and ease the flesh out in whole pieces.

mistakes.fix: Peel just before use, or hold the pieces under water with a little lemon juice.
mistakes.mistake: Peeling long before cooking, so that potato and celeriac turn brown.

cues.text: A clean rim, and each part easy to tell from the others.
A plate for hot food is warm to the hand.

technique/plate.does: Arranges the finished parts on a plate, so that each reaches the table at its best.
how: Warm the plates for hot food and chill them for cold.
Have every part ready before the first one is plated.
Set the main part down first, then build around it without crowding the rim.
Sauce last, beside or under anything crisp, and wipe the rim clean.

mistakes.fix: Warm the plates in a low oven or under hot water.
mistakes.mistake: Plating hot food on cold plates, so that a sauce sets and eggs cool before they reach the table.

mistakes.fix: Put the sauce beside it or under it.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring sauce over crisp skin or crust, which softens it at once.

comes_after.why: Poaching sits just under a simmer, so a cook has to be able to find a simmer first.

cues.text: The surface shivers and steams, and nothing rolls.
A poached egg feels like a soft cushion when pressed: the white is set and the yolk is loose inside.

technique/poach.does: Cooks delicate food gently in liquid that is hot but never boils.
how: Heat the liquid until it trembles, with small bubbles on the bottom of the pan and almost none rising.
Slide the food in gently.
Hold the heat there. Turn it down the moment bubbles start to break the surface.
Lift the food out with a slotted spoon and drain it well.
For an egg, add a little vinegar to the water, crack the egg into a small bowl first, and tip it in at the surface.
For dumplings of choux paste, drop spoonfuls into salted water at a tremble, and lift them out with a slotted spoon once they float and feel firm.

mistakes.fix: Turn the heat down, or add a splash of cold liquid.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the liquid boil, which tears an egg apart and toughens fish and chicken.

mistakes.fix: Use the freshest eggs you have, and drain off the watery part of the white through a sieve.
mistakes.mistake: Using an old egg, whose thin white spreads into rags.

cues.text: A thick, glossy paste with no whole pieces of leaf.
The scent of garlic and basil rises sharply as they break down.

technique/pound.does: Crushes food in a mortar until it becomes a paste.
how: Start with the hardest thing: garlic, with a little coarse salt to grip it.
Pound straight down to break it, then grind in circles against the wall of the mortar.
Add soft leaves a few at a time, and grind each lot to a paste before the next.
Work in oil or cheese last, a little at a time.

mistakes.fix: Add a few leaves at a time.
mistakes.mistake: Filling the mortar with leaves, which slide about and bruise without breaking down.

cues.text: The surface oil, which floated as a sheen, has run off with the water.
The smell of oil or of the making is gone.

technique/pour-boiling-water-over.does: Pours boiling water over a ready-made food, to wash off the surface oil or the smell from the making before it goes into a pot or a dish. The food is not cooked, only scalded.
how: Put the food in a colander or a heatproof bowl.
Pour boiling water over it, slowly and evenly, so that every surface is touched.
Drain it, and press it gently with a clean cloth or paper if it will be fried or stuffed.
Cut or use it right away.

mistakes.fix: Only scald it by pouring.
mistakes.mistake: Boiling the food in the pot, which makes it soft and waterlogged.

mistakes.fix: Scald it first, every time.
mistakes.mistake: Skipping the scald before simmering, so that the broth turns greasy.

comes_after.why: The food is laid out in the dish first, and the liquid goes over it last.

cues.text: The liquid stands at one level all round, and the tops of the pieces show above it.

technique/pour-over.does: Pours a liquid or a loose sauce onto food laid in a dish, slowly and from the side, so that it settles into the gaps without washing off the top.
how: Lay the food out in the dish first, in the way it is to be served.
Pour from low down near the rim, in a thin steady stream, and not straight onto the middle.
Stop when the liquid has reached the level the dish asks for. Leave the top of the food showing if it is to brown.
Tap the dish gently so that the liquid settles into every gap.

mistakes.fix: Pour low, from the side, in a thin stream.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring from high up, which splashes and washes off the seasoning or the topping.

mistakes.fix: Leave a gap below the rim.
mistakes.mistake: Filling the dish to the brim, so that it spills in the oven.

cues.text: The cloth is wet and the block has become a little thinner.
The tofu is firm and springs back.

technique/press-tofu.does: Presses water out of a block of firm tofu under a light weight, so that it is firmer, absorbs a sauce and browns instead of steaming.
how: Wrap the block in a clean cloth or paper towels.
Set it on a tray or a board, put a plate and a light weight on top and tilt the tray so the water runs off.
Leave it until the water has stopped running out.
Unwrap, pat dry and cut.

mistakes.fix: Use a plate or a light bowl only.
mistakes.mistake: Pressing with a heavy weight, which cracks the block.

mistakes.fix: Pat it dry.
mistakes.mistake: Skipping the drying, so that the tofu spits in the pan.

comes_after.why: Rinsing washes off dust and loose skins that would foam up and clog the valve.
Large hard pulses are soaked first so that they cook evenly in the pot.

cues.text: A steady hiss or a regular whistle from the valve. Wild spitting means the heat is too high.
A cooked pulse crushes easily between the fingers, with no hard core.
Split pulses have fallen apart into a thick, creamy mass when stirred.

technique/pressure-cook.does: Cooks pulses in a sealed pot that holds steam in, so that the liquid gets hotter than in an open pot and hard dried seeds soften and fall apart in a fraction of the usual time.
how: Rinse the pulses. Soak the large hard kinds such as kidney beans, if the recipe asks.
Put them in the pot with plenty of water and a little turmeric. Fill the pot no more than half, as pulses swell and foam.
Close the lid, seat the valve or weight and heat on high until the steam starts to hiss or whistle steadily.
Turn the heat down so that the hiss stays steady, and cook for the time the pulse needs.
Take the pot off the heat and let the pressure fall on its own before opening it. Open the lid away from you.
Stir. Mash the soft pulses against the side of the pot if the dish should be smooth.

mistakes.fix: Fill the pot no more than half and add a spoonful of oil or ghee to calm the foam.
mistakes.mistake: Filling the pot too full, so that foam rises and clogs the valve.

mistakes.fix: Let the pressure fall by itself first.
mistakes.mistake: Opening the lid before the pressure has dropped, which sprays hot steam and liquid.

mistakes.fix: Cover them with plenty of water. Add more if the dish is too thick.
mistakes.mistake: Using too little water, so that the pulses scorch at the bottom.

variant_of.differs: The pot is sealed, so the liquid gets hotter than a simmer and the pulses cook in a fraction of the time. The cook cannot lift the lid to check, and the pressure must fall before the pot is opened.

cues.text: A neat spread of small holes all over, none of them a tear.

technique/prick.does: Makes small holes in a skin or a crust with the tip of a knife or a fork, so that steam can leave and the skin does not split or the crust puff.
how: Dry the surface, so that the tip does not slip.
Prick evenly all over with the point, a little way in, about as far apart as the width of a fork.
On a sausage, turn it and prick on every side. On pastry, prick the base and the sides.
Cook it soon after, before the holes close.

mistakes.fix: Prick only just through the skin.
mistakes.mistake: Stabbing deep into a sausage, which lets the juices run out and dries it.

mistakes.fix: Prick evenly, all over.
mistakes.mistake: Pricking unevenly, which leaves a patch that still splits or puffs.

variant_of.differs: Scoring cuts shallow lines. Pricking makes only small holes and takes nothing away, so that steam leaves without the skin or the crust splitting or puffing.

comes_after.why: A dough rises evenly only once it has been worked smooth.

cues.text: The dough has swelled and looks puffy and domed, with small bubbles under the skin.
A fingertip leaves a dent that fills back slowly.
A mild, yeasty, slightly sweet smell, and not a sharp sour one.

technique/proof.does: Leaves shaped yeast dough in a warm, still place to rise, so that the yeast fills it with gas and it swells and turns light, airy and ready to bake or fry.
how: Shape the dough and set it in a lightly oiled bowl, or on a tray, with room to swell.
Cover it with a damp cloth or oiled film, so that its skin does not dry out.
Leave it somewhere warm and free of draughts until it has roughly doubled, or puffed as the shape asks.
Press a fingertip lightly into it: it is ready when the dent fills back slowly.
Bake or fry it at once, and handle it gently so that the air stays in.

mistakes.fix: Choose a gently warm place and give it more time.
mistakes.mistake: Proofing in a spot that is too hot, so that the dough turns sour and loose.

mistakes.fix: Wait until the dent fills back slowly.
mistakes.mistake: Baking too soon, so that the bread is dense and tight.

mistakes.fix: Check it often and bake it as soon as it is ready.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving it too long, so that it collapses when it is touched or baked.

comes_after.why: Food is simmered soft before it is pureed.

cues.text: It falls from the spoon in a smooth ribbon, with no grains or strings.
Nothing gritty between finger and thumb.

technique/puree.does: Breaks cooked food down until it is smooth, in a blender or through a sieve.
how: Cook the food until it is completely soft. Nothing firm will blend smooth.
Blend with only part of the cooking liquid at first.
Add more liquid little by little until the texture is right.
Pass it through a fine sieve for a truly smooth finish.

mistakes.fix: Fill it less than half way, hold the lid down with a cloth and start slowly.
mistakes.mistake: Filling a blender to the top with hot soup, so that the steam blows the lid off.

mistakes.fix: Hold liquid back. It is easy to thin a puree and hard to thicken one.
mistakes.mistake: Adding all the liquid at once and ending with a thin soup.

mistakes.fix: Blend a potato soup only briefly, or push it through a sieve.
mistakes.mistake: Blending potatoes hard, which turns them to glue.

cues.text: Sand and grit gather on the bottom of the bowl, and the clams show their siphons a little.

technique/purge-clams.does: Leaves live clams in cold, well-salted water, like the sea, so that they open a little, breathe and spit out the sand they hold, before they are cooked.
how: Look over the clams. Throw away any that are broken, or that stay open when they are tapped on the counter.
Stir plenty of salt into cold water until it tastes like the sea, in a bowl wide enough to hold the clams in a single layer.
Lay in the clams without crowding and leave them in a cool, dim place, so that they spit out their sand.
Lift them out of the water with your hands or a slotted spoon, leaving the grit on the bottom of the bowl. Do not tip them into a colander, which pours the sand back over them.

mistakes.fix: Make the water as salty as the sea.
mistakes.mistake: Using fresh water, which makes the clams shut or kills them.

mistakes.fix: Lift them out by hand and leave the grit behind.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring the clams into a colander, so that the sand falls back over them.

mistakes.fix: Lay them in a single layer somewhere cool.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding them in a warm place, so that they do not open.

variant_of.differs: The water is cold and as salty as the sea, not fresh. The aim is not to soften the food but to make live shellfish spit out their sand, and they are lifted out and not drained.

comes_after.why: A pan sauce is deglazed first and reduced second.
A cook who can hold a simmer can judge a boil that must not scorch.

cues.text: The bubbles grow larger and slower, and a finger drawn across the back of a coated spoon leaves a clear path.
The boil deepens from a rattle to a slow, thick plop.

technique/reduce.does: Boils a liquid down, so that its water leaves as steam and what remains is thicker and stronger.
how: Use a wide pan. The wider the surface, the faster the water leaves.
Boil steadily, uncovered.
Watch the level against the side of the pan, and the size of the bubbles.
Stop when it coats the back of a spoon, and season only then.

mistakes.fix: Season at the end.
mistakes.mistake: Salting before reducing, so that the salt is concentrated with everything else.

mistakes.fix: Stay with it once it starts to thicken, and pull it off the heat early.
mistakes.mistake: Walking away near the end, when a sauce goes from syrup to scorched in moments.

comes_after.why: Refreshing is how boiling or blanching ends.

cues.text: A piece is cold to the middle when it is squeezed.
The colour stays as bright as it was in the pot.

technique/refresh.does: Stops the cooking at once by plunging hot food into iced water, which keeps green vegetables bright and firm.
how: Have a large bowl of water and ice ready before the food is cooked.
Lift the food straight from the pot into the iced water.
Leave it only until it is cold to the middle.
Drain it well, so that it does not soak.

mistakes.fix: Take it out as soon as it is cold and drain it on a cloth.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving food to soak in the water, which washes out its taste.

comes_after.why: Food is warmed again at a gentle simmer, so a cook has to be able to hold one.

cues.text: Small, steady bubbles break at the surface in the middle of the pan as well as at the edge.
The spoon moves freely along the bottom, with nothing stuck.

technique/reheat.does: Brings food that was cooked earlier back to a hot, bubbling state, gently enough that it neither dries out nor catches on the pan. Beans and soups often taste better for the rest, and the Tuscan ribollita is made for exactly that: a soup that is boiled again.
how: Take the food from the fridge a little ahead of time if it is thick and dense.
Put it in a heavy pan with a splash of stock or water, to loosen it and stop it catching.
Warm it over low heat, stirring up from the bottom now and then, until it bubbles gently at the centre as well as at the edge.
Taste and adjust the salt, which can flatten as the food rests.

mistakes.fix: Use low heat and stir up from the bottom.
mistakes.mistake: Reheating over high heat, so that the bottom catches while the top is still cold.

mistakes.fix: Add a splash of stock or water first.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving a thick soup or stew with no extra liquid, so that it dries and sticks.

mistakes.fix: Keep it at a gentle bubble.
mistakes.mistake: Boiling hard, so that beans break and fall apart.

cues.text: No liquid pools at the bottom of the bowl, and the grains have swollen to about double their size.
The grains are tender with at most a little bite, and fall apart when they are pressed lightly between the fingers.

technique/rehydrate-couscous.does: Swells precooked, dried couscous grains in hot liquid poured over them off the heat, and lets them stand covered until the liquid is taken up, so that no steaming is needed.
how: Put the grains in a wide bowl with a little salt and a spoonful of oil or butter, and rub until every grain is coated, so that they do not clump when the liquid arrives.
Bring the liquid, plain water or a well-flavoured stock, to a boil. Measure it by volume against the grains: about the same amount, a little more for a softer grain.
Pour the boiling liquid over the grains all at once, stir once, and cover the bowl tightly with a plate or a lid.
Leave it off the heat until the liquid has gone and the grains have swollen. Then uncover and fluff.

mistakes.fix: Measure the liquid against the grains. If it is already wet, spread the grains on a tray and let the steam go.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring on too much liquid, which leaves a wet, gluey mass.

mistakes.fix: Bring the liquid to a boil first.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring on liquid that is not hot, so that the centres of the grains stay hard.

mistakes.fix: Cover it tightly while the grains drink.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the bowl uncovered, so that the steam escapes and the top layer stays dry.

mistakes.fix: Coat the dry grains with oil or butter before the liquid goes on.
mistakes.mistake: Skipping the oil, so that the grains stick in clumps.

variant_of.differs: The grains are precooked and dried, so they only need to drink hot liquid. There is no couscoussier, no steam over a stew, and no rounds of sprinkling and raking: the grain is ready in the time it takes to stand covered. The result is a little denser and less airy than grain steamed by hand, and it tastes of its liquid alone and not of the stew's steam.

cues.text: The seaweed has opened out and turned a glossy dark green.
It is soft and slippery, with no hard, dry centre.

technique/rehydrate-seaweed.does: Soaks dried seaweed in cold water until it swells and turns soft, silky and bright green, then squeezes out the water and cuts away any hard rib.
how: Put a small handful of dried seaweed in a large bowl, as it swells to many times its size.
Cover it with cold water and leave it until it is soft and glossy.
Lift it out, drain it and squeeze it lightly.
Cut away any hard rib and cut the rest into bite-sized pieces.

mistakes.fix: Start with a small handful.
mistakes.mistake: Using too much, so that the bowl overflows with swollen seaweed.

mistakes.fix: Lift it out as soon as it is soft.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving it in the water for too long, so that it turns slimy and loses its bite.

variant_of.differs: Dried seaweed swells very fast and to many times its size in cold water, so it is soaked for a short while only, then squeezed, and any hard rib is cut away.

cues.text: A slow sizzle that grows as the fat pools.
Clear fat in the pan, and pieces that have shrunk and turned golden at the edges.

technique/render.does: Melts the fat out of bacon or skin over gentle heat, leaving the meat crisp and the fat clear for cooking.
how: Start with a cold pan and no added fat.
Lay the pieces in a single layer and set the pan over medium-low heat.
Let the fat run slowly, stirring now and then.
Turn the heat up at the end to crisp the pieces, then lift them out and keep the fat.

mistakes.fix: Start cold and take your time.
mistakes.mistake: Starting in a hot pan, which browns the outside before the fat has melted, so that the pieces stay chewy.

comes_after.why: Resting is how a sear ends.

cues.text: Little juice runs out when it is sliced, and the cut face is evenly coloured.
The meat has relaxed and gives a little under a finger.

technique/rest.does: Leaves cooked meat alone off the heat for a while, so that its juices settle and stay in when it is cut.
how: Lift the meat out of the pan onto a rack or a warm plate.
Leave it uncovered, or loosely tented, somewhere warm.
Wait about as long as it took to sear a steak, and much longer for a large roast.
Pour the juices it gives up back into the sauce.

mistakes.fix: Wait. The meat stays hot inside for longer than you think.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting it straight away, so that the juice floods the board and the meat eats dry.

mistakes.fix: Leave it open, or tent the foil loosely.
mistakes.mistake: Wrapping it tightly in foil, which steams the crust soft.

comes_after.why: Rice rests only after it has been cooked.

cues.text: The surface of the rice is dry and shiny, with no wet patches.
The grains are plump, separate and slightly sticky.

technique/rest-and-fluff.does: Leaves cooked rice covered off the heat for a while, so that the steam spreads evenly through the grains, then cuts through it with a paddle to let the steam out and loosen the grains.
how: As soon as the rice is cooked, take it off the heat and keep the lid on.
Leave it to rest, undisturbed, so that the grains finish steaming.
Wet a rice paddle, and cut through the rice in a slicing motion, turning it over from the bottom.
Cover it again until it is served.

mistakes.fix: Keep it shut until the rest is over.
mistakes.mistake: Lifting the lid during the rest, so that the steam escapes.

mistakes.fix: Cut and fold with a wet paddle.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring the rice, which crushes the grains and makes it pasty.

variant_of.differs: The rice rests in its own steam under a lid and is then cut through with a wet paddle to loosen it.

comes_after.why: The batter must be mixed before it can rest.

cues.text: A few bubbles have risen to the surface and the batter has thickened slightly.
The batter is smoother when stirred than just after mixing.

technique/rest-batter.does: Leaves a mixed batter to stand, so that the flour takes up its liquid and the batter turns smooth and thickens a little. Cooked after resting, it spreads evenly and comes out tender.
how: Cover the bowl of batter.
Leave it to stand in a cool place, or in the fridge if it will wait for long.
Stir it gently once before it is used.
If it has thickened too much, loosen it with a splash of liquid.

mistakes.fix: Let it stand first.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking the batter right away, so that the pancakes are tough and uneven.

mistakes.fix: Give it only one gentle stir.
mistakes.mistake: Beating it again after it has rested, which knocks out the bubbles.

variant_of.differs: The food that rests is a batter, left covered so that its flour swells, and not a piece of cooked meat.

cues.text: The last water stays as clear as it went in.
Brined food tastes pleasantly salty and no longer harsh.

technique/rinse.does: Washes food in cold water, to carry off grit, loose starch, or the salt and brine it was kept in.
how: Put the food in a colander, or in a large bowl of cold water.
Run cold water over it, or move it about in the bowl with your hands.
Change the water until it stays clear. Lift leaves out of the water, so that the grit stays behind.
Drain it well, and dry whatever will be fried or dressed.

mistakes.fix: Lift the leaves out and leave the grit at the bottom.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring washed leaves and their water out together, so that the grit lands back on them.

mistakes.fix: Taste as you go, and stop while they still have bite.
mistakes.mistake: Rinsing sauerkraut or capers until none of their sharpness is left.

comes_after.why: Roasting is searing done by an oven: the same dry surface and the same patience, on a larger piece.

cues.text: A deep golden-brown surface, and browned juices stuck to the tin.
A rich roasting smell fills the kitchen well before the food is done.
A steady sizzle from the tin.

technique/roast.does: Cooks food uncovered in the dry heat of a hot oven, so that the outside browns while the inside cooks in its own juices.
how: Dry the surface of the food well.
Season it, and rub it with a little fat.
Set it in a tin that fits it without crowding, in an oven that is fully hot.
Turn it or baste it now and then, so that it browns evenly.
Rest it before carving, and make a jus from what is left in the tin.

mistakes.fix: Leave space around every piece, or use a second tin.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding the tin, so that the food steams and stays pale.

mistakes.fix: Rest it first, loosely covered.
mistakes.mistake: Carving a roast straight from the oven.

cues.text: A deep, warm scent fills the kitchen. A sharp, bitter smell means they are scorched.
The spices turn a shade darker and the seeds begin to smoke very lightly.

technique/roast-spices.does: Roasts whole spices in a dry, heavy pan over a low heat until they darken a shade and smell strong, then cools them, so that they can be ground into a blend or a powder that keeps its scent.
how: Set a heavy dry pan over a low heat and let it warm.
Add the spices that take the longest first, such as coriander seed and cumin, and the softer ones a little later. Roast each at its own pace if they differ.
Stir or shake all the while so that nothing sits and scorches.
Tip the spices out onto a cold plate the moment they smell strong and have darkened a shade.
Let them cool completely before grinding, so that the powder does not turn damp or gummy.

mistakes.fix: Keep the heat low and take your time.
mistakes.mistake: Roasting on a high heat, so that the outsides scorch while the insides stay raw.

mistakes.fix: Roast the hard ones first, or roast each kind in turn.
mistakes.mistake: Roasting all the spices together when they take different times.

mistakes.fix: Cool them completely first.
mistakes.mistake: Grinding the spices while they are still hot, so that the powder clumps.

variant_of.differs: Toasting browns one food for a short while. Here a mix of whole spices is roasted slowly, each at its own pace, as the first step of making a blend, and then cooled and ground, and nothing is left whole to garnish.

comes_after.why: Rolling is wrapping with a flat wrapper, so a cook who can close a wrapper snugly rolls neater.

cues.text: The roll is even in width, with the ends tucked in and the seam underneath.
A finished roll is firm and gives slightly when pressed.

technique/roll.does: Rolls a flat wrapper, such as a leaf, a sheet of dough or a thin pancake, up around a line of filling into a neat cylinder, with the ends folded in so that nothing can fall out.
how: Soften the wrapper if it is stiff, by blanching a leaf or covering a sheet of dough with a damp cloth.
Lay it flat with the side that should show on the outside facing down, and set a line of filling near the edge closest to you.
Fold that edge over the filling and fold the sides in towards the middle.
Roll away from you, firm but not tight, and set the roll down with its seam underneath.

mistakes.fix: Use a thin line of filling and leave room at the ends.
mistakes.mistake: Overfilling, so that the roll splits when the filling swells.

mistakes.fix: Roll firmly, keep the seam underneath and pack the rolls snugly in the pot.
mistakes.mistake: Rolling loosely, so that the roll unwinds as it cooks.

mistakes.fix: Soften it first with a quick blanch or a damp cloth.
mistakes.mistake: Rolling a brittle leaf or sheet that cracks.

variant_of.differs: The wrapper is a flat sheet that is rolled up round the filling into a cylinder with its ends folded in, and not folded into a parcel.

comes_after.why: The first half of an omelette is a fast scramble. A cook who can stop a scramble in time can stop an omelette in time.

cues.text: A pale yellow, smooth skin with no brown. The top still glistens when you start to roll.
The omelette slides freely when the pan is shaken.

technique/roll-an-omelette.does: Sets beaten eggs into a thin, tender sheet with a creamy middle, and rolls it into a smooth, pale cylinder.
how: Heat butter in a pan over medium heat until it foams and the foam starts to fall.
Pour in the beaten eggs and stir fast in small circles while shaking the pan.
Stop stirring when the eggs are mostly set but still wet on top, and let the bottom firm for a moment.
Scatter any filling down the middle.
Tilt the pan, fold the near edge over, and roll the omelette to the far lip.
Turn it out onto the plate, seam side down.

mistakes.fix: Lift the pan off the heat while you stir, and turn the heat down.
mistakes.mistake: The pan is too hot, so the skin browns and turns leathery.

mistakes.fix: Roll while the top is still wet. The heat inside finishes it.
mistakes.mistake: Waiting for the top to dry before rolling, which leaves the middle firm and dull.

cues.text: Each layer is thin, and the finished block shows many thin spirals.
The block is springy and tender, and holds together when lifted.

technique/roll-in-layers.does: Cooks a thin layer of egg in a pan, rolls it up while it is still soft, then pours more egg into the room left behind, cooks it and rolls again, so that the block grows layer upon layer.
how: Oil the pan and heat it. Pour in a thin layer of beaten egg and tilt it to cover the pan.
When the egg is almost set but still wet on top, roll it up toward the far side with chopsticks or a spatula.
Push the roll to the far side, oil the empty part and pour in more egg, lifting the roll so that the egg runs under it.
When it is nearly set, roll the block back toward you around the first one.
Repeat until the egg is used up, and turn out the finished block.

mistakes.fix: Pour in just enough to coat the pan thinly.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring in too much egg, so that the layers are thick and hard to roll.

mistakes.fix: Roll while the top is still wet.
mistakes.mistake: Waiting until the egg is fully set before rolling, so that the layers will not join.

variant_of.differs: The egg is cooked and rolled in several thin layers, each one added while the roll is still moist, so the result is a firm, layered block and not one creamy cylinder.

comes_after.why: A dough has to be smooth and rested before it rolls out evenly without tearing.

cues.text: The sheet is even, with no thick middle or thin rim and no tears.
The dough slides freely on the surface when it is nudged.

technique/roll-out.does: Flattens a dough with a rolling pin into an even sheet of the thickness the dish asks for, whether thin enough to see through, for a filled pastry, or thick enough to stay soft, for a flat bread.
how: Rest the dough first, or it will spring back. Shape it into a flat round or square before the pin touches it.
Dust the surface and the pin lightly with flour, so that the dough slides and does not stick.
Roll from the middle outwards in one steady push, lift and give the dough a quarter turn, and roll again.
Turn the dough over now and then and dust again only where it sticks.
Stop when the sheet is even from edge to edge. Let it rest and spring back before it is cut or filled.

mistakes.fix: Cover it and let it rest, then roll again.
mistakes.mistake: Rolling a tense dough that keeps shrinking back.

mistakes.fix: Use only as much as it takes to stop it sticking, and brush off the extra.
mistakes.mistake: Dusting with too much flour, which dries the dough and leaves white streaks.

mistakes.fix: Roll from the middle outwards and stop short of the edge.
mistakes.mistake: Rolling over the edges, which leaves them thin and the middle thick.

comes_after.why: The rounds are rolled from a rested atta dough, so the dough comes first.

cues.text: The round is even in thickness and has a smooth edge with no cracks.
It peels from the board without sticking and does not tear.

technique/roll-out-a-chapati.does: Rolls a ball of atta dough into a thin, even round, a little at a time, turning it often, so that it is the same thickness all over and puffs evenly when it is cooked.
how: Flatten a ball of dough in a dish of dry flour, coating both faces lightly.
Roll from the centre outwards with short, firm strokes. Give the dough a small turn after each stroke, so that it grows into a round.
Use just enough flour to stop it sticking. Shake off the extra, because burnt flour makes a bitter smell on the hot plate.
Stop when the round is thin and even from the middle to the edge, with no thick patches or tears.
Cook it at once. A rolled round that waits dries at the edge and tears when lifted.

mistakes.fix: Roll from the centre outwards and turn the dough after every stroke.
mistakes.mistake: Rolling thick in the middle and thin at the edge, so that it cooks unevenly and does not puff.

mistakes.fix: Dust lightly and shake off what is not needed.
mistakes.mistake: Using too much dry flour, which burns on the hot plate.

mistakes.fix: Cook each one as it is rolled.
mistakes.mistake: Stacking rolled rounds without flour, so that they stick.

variant_of.differs: Each round is rolled alone, from a small ball, and cooked at once. The dough is soft and unrested between rolls. The aim is a thin, even disc that will puff, and not a sheet that holds its shape and is cut.

cues.text: Liquid has collected under the colander, and the pieces have gone limp and glossy.
A piece bends without snapping.

technique/salt-and-drain.does: Draws water out of a watery vegetable with salt before it is cooked or dressed, so that it keeps its bite and does not flood the dish.
how: Slice or dice the vegetable and toss it with fine salt.
Leave it in a colander over a bowl until it has given up its water.
Rinse off the salt if the dish will be salted again, and press or pat the pieces dry.

mistakes.fix: Press it gently in a cloth before you use it.
mistakes.mistake: Skipping the drying, so that the vegetable goes into the pan or the dressing still wet.

mistakes.fix: Taste before you add any more salt.
mistakes.mistake: Salting the dish as usual afterwards, so that it ends up far too salty.

cues.text: The slices have gone limp and flexible.
The bitterness is softer.

technique/salt-and-squeeze.does: Rubs thin slices of a watery or bitter vegetable with salt, leaves them to wilt a little, and squeezes them by hand to wring out the bitter liquid. They keep a firm bite and a milder taste.
how: Slice the vegetable thin and put it in a bowl.
Sprinkle on salt and rub it in lightly with your hands.
Leave it for a short while until it has softened and given up water.
Squeeze the slices in a handful and pour off the liquid. Rinse and squeeze again if they are still harsh.

mistakes.fix: Sprinkle evenly and rub lightly.
mistakes.mistake: Adding salt in a heap, which makes the slices too salty.

mistakes.fix: Squeeze firmly but not to a pulp.
mistakes.mistake: Squeezing too hard, which bruises them.

variant_of.differs: The slices are rubbed with salt and squeezed by hand to wring out the liquid, instead of being left to drain in a colander.

cues.text: Beads of water form on the skin, and the flesh looks firmer.
The fishy smell is less sharp.

technique/salt-fish.does: Sprinkles fresh fish with a little salt and leaves it for a short while before grilling or frying, to season it, firm the flesh and draw out the surface water and smell. It is not the long curing of salt cod.
how: Pat the fish dry.
Sprinkle salt evenly over both sides, and a little more on the tail and fins if the fish is whole.
Leave it at room temperature for a short while, until beads of water show on the skin.
Wipe the water off with paper and cook the fish at once.

mistakes.fix: Salt lightly and evenly.
mistakes.mistake: Using too much salt, which makes the fish too salty.

mistakes.fix: Wipe it dry as soon as water shows and cook it.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving it too long, so that it turns dry and hard.

cues.text: The palms are damp and a little gritty with salt, and the rice no longer clings.
The outside of the shaped rice is lightly salty.

technique/salt-hands.does: Wets the hands and rubs salt over the palms before shaping warm rice, so that the rice does not stick and is lightly seasoned from the outside.
how: Keep a bowl of cold water and a small dish of salt beside the board.
Dip your fingers in the water and shake off the excess.
Rub a little salt over the palms and fingers.
Wet and salt your hands again for each portion.

mistakes.fix: Rub on only a light dusting.
mistakes.mistake: Using too much salt, so that the rice is too salty.

mistakes.fix: Use cold water.
mistakes.mistake: Using hot water, which burns the hands and makes the rice stick.

cues.text: The filling shows evenly at the edge and does not squeeze out.
The pieces stick lightly to the filling.

technique/sandwich.does: Places a filling between flat pieces of soft bread or pancake, so that it holds together and is eaten in one hand.
how: Lay out the bottom pieces in a row.
Spoon or spread the filling on each, leaving a narrow edge clear.
Cover with the top pieces and press gently so that the filling spreads without spilling.
Pat the edges together, then serve.

mistakes.fix: Spread a thin even layer and leave an edge.
mistakes.mistake: Overfilling, so that the filling is squeezed out.

mistakes.fix: Let them cool a little first.
mistakes.mistake: Using pieces that are too hot, which melts the filling.

comes_after.why: Sweating teaches how a pan sounds and looks on low heat. Sautéing asks for the same watchfulness at speed.

cues.text: A lively sizzle from the moment the food goes in. If it falls silent, the pan is too full or too cool.
Golden-brown edges, and a dry pan with no liquid pooling in it.

technique/saute.does: Cooks small pieces fast in a hot pan with a little fat, moving them so that they brown on all sides.
how: Heat the pan first, then the fat, until the fat shimmers.
Add the food in a single layer, with room between the pieces.
Leave it a moment to take colour, then toss or stir.
Keep the heat high and the food moving until it is browned outside and just tender inside.

mistakes.fix: Cook in batches, and let the pan heat up again between them.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding the pan, so the food steams and turns grey.

mistakes.fix: Salt mushrooms, courgette and aubergine near the end.
mistakes.mistake: Salting watery vegetables at the start, which draws their water into the pan.

cues.text: The skin is smooth under a finger run from tail to head, with no rough edge.
A dry rasping sound as the scales lift. It goes quiet once the skin is bare.

technique/scale-a-fish.does: Scrapes the scales off the skin of a whole fish, so that none are left to catch in the mouth or to make the skin gritty.
how: Hold the fish firmly by the tail on a board that cannot slip. A deep sink or a large tray catches the flying scales.
With the back of a knife, scrape from the tail towards the head in short firm strokes, against the way the scales lie.
Turn the fish over and do the other side. Go carefully round the fins, the belly and the base of the head, where scales hide.
Rinse the fish under cold water and run a finger from tail to head to find any scale that is left.

mistakes.fix: Scrape from the tail towards the head, against the scales.
mistakes.mistake: Scraping from the head towards the tail, which only presses the scales flat.

mistakes.fix: Use the back of the blade, in short firm strokes.
mistakes.mistake: Using the sharp edge of the knife, which cuts the skin.

cues.text: A neat pattern of diamonds, with white fat in every cut and no red flesh showing.

technique/score.does: Cuts shallow lines through skin or fat, so that the fat can melt out and the skin crisps without curling.
how: Chill the piece so that the fat is firm.
Draw a sharp knife across the fat in parallel lines a finger apart, cutting through the fat but not into the flesh.
Turn the piece and cut across the first lines to make diamonds.

mistakes.fix: Use the tip of the knife with a light hand, and stop when the colour changes.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting into the flesh, so that the meat loses juice and dries where it was cut.

comes_after.why: The eggs are whisked before they are scrambled.

cues.text: Small, glossy curds held in a thick, creamy sauce, with no dry or browned bits.
The spoon leaves a trail that closes slowly.

technique/scramble.does: Stirs beaten eggs over gentle heat until they set into small, soft, creamy curds.
how: Whisk the eggs with salt until no streaks of white are left.
Melt butter in a pan over low heat until it foams.
Pour in the eggs and stir without stopping, scraping the bottom and the corners.
Lift the pan off the heat whenever the curds form too fast, and keep stirring.
Stop while the eggs still look wet, and stir in a little cold butter or cream to halt the cooking.

mistakes.fix: Keep the heat low and take the pan off it often.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking over high heat, which gives large, dry, rubbery curds that weep water.

mistakes.fix: Take them off while they still look too wet. They go on setting on the way to the plate.
mistakes.mistake: Waiting until the eggs look done in the pan.

comes_after.why: The pot is filled in layers first, and sealed only when everything is in.

cues.text: An unbroken ring of paste all round the join, with no gap for steam to find.
The paste is pliable and does not crack when it is rolled.

technique/seal-with-dough.does: Closes the gap between a pot and its lid with a rope of plain flour paste, so that no steam leaves during a long, slow bake. The seal is broken open at the table.
how: Mix flour with just enough water to make a stiff paste that rolls between the hands and does not stick.
Fill the pot, then put the lid on.
Roll the paste into a rope long enough to go round the rim.
Press the rope into the join where the lid meets the pot, and smooth it into both sides with a wet finger. Leave no gap.
Bake without lifting the lid. Break the seal open when the pot is brought to the table.

mistakes.fix: Work in more flour until it is stiff.
mistakes.mistake: Making the paste too wet, so that it runs and does not hold.

mistakes.fix: Run a wet finger round the whole join before the pot goes in the oven.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving a gap in the ring, so that steam escapes and the liquid cooks away.

comes_after.why: Sautéing teaches a hot pan and room between the pieces. Searing adds the hardest part: leaving the food alone.

cues.text: A loud, steady sizzle that does not fade. A weak hiss means the pan was not hot enough.
A deep brown crust, and a brown line climbing the side of the piece.
The piece lets go of the pan when it is ready to turn. If it sticks, it is not ready.

technique/sear.does: Browns the surface of meat or fish fast in a very hot pan, building a crust full of flavour while the inside stays underdone.
how: Dry the surface well. Wet food steams before it browns.
Salt it just before it goes in.
Heat a heavy pan until a thin film of oil shimmers and gives off its first wisp of smoke.
Lay the food in away from you and press it flat. Then leave it alone.
Turn it when it lifts off the pan by itself and the underside is deep brown.
Take it out to rest. The crust left on the pan is the fond for a sauce.

mistakes.fix: Leave it until it releases by itself.
mistakes.mistake: Moving the food before it has browned, which tears the crust and leaves it on the pan.

mistakes.fix: Sear in batches with space between the pieces, and let the pan heat up again.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding the pan, so that the pieces stew in their own juice and turn grey.

mistakes.fix: Pat it dry with paper on every side first.
mistakes.mistake: Putting food in the pan while its surface is wet.

cues.text: The dish tastes more of itself and not of salt. It is bright, and nothing sticks out.

technique/season.does: Brings out the taste of a dish with salt, and balances it with pepper, acid or fat.
how: Salt in small steps as the dish cooks, not only at the end.
Taste before serving, from a clean spoon.
Add a little salt if the dish tastes flat, and a few drops of acid if it tastes dull or heavy.
Stir, wait a moment and taste again.

mistakes.fix: Salt lightly anything that will reduce, and correct it at the end.
mistakes.mistake: Salting a liquid fully before it has boiled down, so that it ends up too salty.

mistakes.fix: Taste every time. No amount on paper replaces it.
mistakes.mistake: Seasoning without tasting.

cues.text: The white is clear, with no streak of yellow in it, and the yolk is whole and round.

technique/separate-eggs.does: Parts the yolk of an egg from its white, so that each can be used alone: the yolks to enrich or thicken, the whites to whip.
how: Set out a small bowl to separate over, and a larger bowl for the whites that are clean.
Crack the egg on a flat surface, not on a rim, and open it over the small bowl with the yolk in one half of the shell.
Pass the yolk gently from one half of the shell to the other until the white has run into the bowl.
Tip the yolk into its own bowl, and move the white to the larger bowl only when it is clean.

mistakes.fix: Separate each egg over a small bowl first, and lift out any speck with a piece of shell.
mistakes.mistake: Letting a speck of yolk fall into the whites, which then will not whip.

mistakes.fix: Crack it on a flat surface.
mistakes.mistake: Cracking the egg on the rim of a bowl, which pushes in shell and breaks the yolk.

cues.text: The surface loses its wet shine and the edge pulls cleanly from the tin.
A light press on the middle springs back, and a cut leaves a clean face.

technique/set.does: Leaves a hot, cooked mixture to cool undisturbed in its mould or tin until it firms enough to hold its shape and be cut.
how: Pour or spoon the mixture into the mould or tin while it is still hot. Press it into the corners and smooth the top.
Leave it somewhere cool and still. Do not stir it, shake it or cut it while it sets.
Let it cool right through before it is cut or turned out. Chill it only if the dish asks for it.
Cut with a thin knife dipped in hot water, or run the knife round the edge and turn it out onto a plate.

mistakes.fix: Wait until it has cooled right through.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting or turning it out while it is still warm, so that it slumps.

mistakes.fix: Leave it still in a cool place.
mistakes.mistake: Moving the tin while it sets, which cracks the surface.

mistakes.fix: Cook it longer next time, until it comes away from the sides of the pan before it is poured.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring in a mixture that was cooked too little, so that it never firms.

comes_after.why: Setting is chilling a liquid until it holds, so a cook has to be able to chill evenly first.

cues.text: The cooled jelly runs slowly off a spoon and leaves a thin coat.
A finished set trembles when the dish is shaken, and holds its shape when it is cut.

technique/set-in-aspic.does: Holds cooked food in a clear, savoury jelly, which sets as it cools and turns a loose mixture into a firm block that can be turned out and cut in slices.
how: Make the jelly from a clear, well-flavoured stock with enough gelatin to hold it. Soak the gelatin in cold water first, then melt it into the warm stock.
Let the jelly cool until it is syrupy and just starting to thicken, before it meets the food.
Pack the cooked food loosely into a deep dish, with herbs between the layers.
Pour the jelly over the food until it is covered, and press gently so that it runs into every gap.
Chill until it is firm throughout. To turn it out, dip the dish briefly in hot water and tip it over a plate.

mistakes.fix: Use less, and aim for a gentle tremble.
mistakes.mistake: Using too much gelatin, so that the jelly turns stiff and rubbery.

mistakes.fix: Let it cool until it starts to thicken.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring the jelly on while it is still hot, so that the herbs turn dull and the pieces rise to the top.

mistakes.fix: Leave it to chill until it is firm all the way through.
mistakes.mistake: Turning the set out too early, while the centre is still loose.

cues.text: The sauce goes from clear and oily to pale and creamy.
The pan grows heavier to move as the sauce thickens.

technique/shake-the-pan.does: Moves fish that gives up its own gelatine in a pan by holding the handle and shaking the pan in small circles, with no spoon or whisk, so that delicate pieces stay whole while the oil and the juices slowly bind into a creamy sauce.
how: Use a wide pan, with the fish in a single layer in a little oil and a splash of liquid, over a low, steady heat.
Hold the handle and shake the pan back and forth in small circles, so that the sauce swirls round the pieces.
Keep it up as the juices and the oil turn pale and creamy. Lift the pan off the heat for a moment if it starts to catch.
Add a splash of water if the sauce gets too thick, and stop when it coats the fish like a thin cream.

mistakes.fix: Shake the pan and leave the pieces alone.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring with a spoon, which breaks the fish into flakes.

mistakes.fix: Keep the heat low, and lift the pan off it for a moment when the sauce gets hot.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking over too high a heat, so that the sauce splits into oil and water.

variant_of.differs: Nothing is whisked. The pan is shaken in circles so that the oil and the juices of the fish bind into a sauce while the pieces stay whole.

cues.text: Pieces of one size with smooth surfaces and no cracks.
The piece holds when it is lifted, and gives a little under a finger.

technique/shape.does: Forms a soft mixture into even pieces that hold together when they are cooked.
how: Chill the mixture first. A cold mixture holds its shape and does not stick.
For quenelles, dip a pair of spoons in hot water, scoop the mixture with the first, and pass it back and forth between them until its sides are smooth.
For patties and balls, wet your hands and press lightly, only until the piece holds.
Make every piece the same size, so that they cook in the same time.

mistakes.fix: Handle it as little as you can.
mistakes.mistake: Working the mixture for too long or pressing it hard, which makes it dense and tough.

mistakes.fix: Chill it until it is firm before you start.
mistakes.mistake: Shaping a warm, loose mixture, which sticks to everything and falls apart in the pot.

comes_after.why: The mixture is kneaded until it holds before it is shaped.

cues.text: Each piece is an even oval with the print of the fingers along it.
The piece holds together when lifted and does not crumble.

technique/shape-a-finger-kofte.does: Squeezes a small lump of a soft, cool mixture in the closed fist, so that it takes the print of the fingers and comes out as a small ridged oval, with nothing cooked afterwards.
how: Keep a bowl of water beside the work and wet the hands lightly.
Take a small lump of the mixture and close the fist around it.
Squeeze, so that it presses into an oval along the fingers and takes their marks.
Set it on a platter and go on until the mixture is used.
Keep it cool and serve it cold.

mistakes.fix: Wet the hands lightly and often.
mistakes.mistake: Working with dry hands, so that the mixture sticks and tears.

mistakes.fix: Leave it to swell longer, or knead in a little more fine bulgur.
mistakes.mistake: Shaping a mixture that is still loose, so that the pieces slump.

mistakes.fix: Take about the same amount each time.
mistakes.mistake: Making the pieces different sizes, which looks untidy on the plate.

variant_of.differs: There is no meat and nothing is cooked afterwards. The piece is squeezed in the fist into a ridged oval and not rolled round between the palms, and it is served cold.

comes_after.why: The mixture is worked until it is sticky and holds together before it is shaped.

cues.text: Each piece is an even, smooth oval with a shallow dent and no cracks at the edge.
The piece holds together when it is lifted and springs back a little when it is pressed.

technique/shape-a-flat-kofte.does: Presses a portion of rested kofte mixture between wet palms into a short, flat oval with a shallow dent from the thumb, so that it holds together over the fire and cooks fast and evenly, and is cooked afterwards on a grill or in a pan.
how: Keep a bowl of water beside the work and wet the hands lightly, so the mixture does not stick.
Take a portion about the size of a walnut and roll it once between the palms to bring it together.
Press it into a short oval, a little longer than it is wide, and flatten it so that it is the same thickness from end to end.
Press the thumb along the middle for a shallow dent, which keeps the middle from puffing up as it cooks.
Set the pieces on a tray, close in size, and keep them cool until they go on the heat.

mistakes.fix: Knead it until sticky and let it rest in the cold before shaping.
mistakes.mistake: Shaping a mixture that was not worked or rested, so that the pieces crack and fall apart on the grill.

mistakes.fix: Flatten them to an even, modest thickness.
mistakes.mistake: Making the pieces thick and round, so that the outside burns before the middle is done.

mistakes.fix: Wet the hands lightly and often.
mistakes.mistake: Working with dry hands, so that the meat clings and tears.

variant_of.differs: The piece is pressed into a flat oval with a thumb dent and not rolled into a ball, and the mixture takes soaked bread as its binder. It is made to be cooked fast over fierce heat.

en: shape rice balls round a filling

comes_after.why: There is no risotto to shape until it has been cooked, then cooled and chilled.
The beaten-in butter and cheese make the rice cling together when it is cold.

cues.text: Cold rice holds together when pressed and does not cling to wet hands.
Each ball is closed all round, with no filling showing and an even coat of crumbs.

technique/shape-a-stuffed-rice-ball.does: Presses cold, firm risotto round a small piece of filling into a ball, a cone or an oval, and coats it in flour, beaten egg and crumbs in turn, so that it fries with a crisp shell around a soft, savoury middle.
how: Cook the risotto a little firmer and thicker than for eating. Spread it out thin on a tray and let it cool right down, then chill it until it is stiff and holds together when pressed.
Have the filling cold and in small pieces. Set out shallow dishes in a row: flour, beaten egg and crumbs.
Wet the hands. Press a handful of rice into a hollow in the palm, set the filling in the middle, close the rice over it and turn it into the shape wanted, pressing out any crack or gap.
Roll it in the flour and shake off the extra, turn it through the egg, then roll it in the crumbs, pressing so that they cover it all round.
Lay them on a tray without touching and chill them for a short while before frying, so that the shell holds.

mistakes.fix: Cook the risotto a little firmer, then cool it right down and chill it until it is stiff.
mistakes.mistake: Shaping risotto that is warm or loose, which sticks to the hands and bursts in the oil.

mistakes.fix: Close the rice all the way over the filling and press out any crack before the coat goes on.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving a gap over the filling, through which it leaks out in the hot oil.

mistakes.fix: Use a small piece of filling and enough rice to wrap it with a firm wall all round.
mistakes.mistake: Packing in too much filling, so that the rice wall is thin and splits.

names.en: Shape and crumb stuffed rice balls

variant_of.differs: The mixture is whole grains of cold risotto and not a smooth paste, and it is pressed round a piece of filling, which a croqueta does not have. The shell is the same flour, egg and crumbs.

The rice is risotto cooked in stock and chilled until stiff, and not plain warm rice, and it is wrapped round a filling and then coated in flour, egg and crumbs to be fried. Onigiri are plain rice pressed warm with salted hands and eaten as they are.

comes_after.why: There is nothing to shape until the paste has been made and chilled.

cues.text: The paste rolls clean between floured hands and does not stick.
Each croqueta is covered all round with an even coat of crumbs and no bare patch.

technique/shape-and-crumb-croquetas.does: Rolls cold, firm croqueta paste into small logs or balls and coats each one in flour, beaten egg and breadcrumbs in turn, so that it fries with a crisp shell and a soft, creamy middle.
how: Set out shallow dishes in a row: flour, beaten egg and breadcrumbs, in that order. Have a tray ready.
Scoop a spoonful of the chilled paste and roll it between floured hands into a short log or a ball. Keep them all one size.
Roll each one in the flour and shake off the extra, turn it through the egg, then roll it in the crumbs, pressing so that they cover it all round.
Lay them on the tray without touching. For a thicker shell, dip them in the egg and the crumbs a second time.
Chill them again for a short while before frying, so that the shell sets.

mistakes.fix: Turn each one through the egg and the crumbs until it is covered all round.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving a bare patch, through which the paste bursts out in the hot oil.

mistakes.fix: Chill the paste until it is firm, and flour your hands.
mistakes.mistake: Shaping warm paste, which squashes and sticks to the hands.

mistakes.fix: Keep one hand for the flour and the crumbs and the other for the egg.
mistakes.mistake: Using the same hand for the dry coats and for the egg, which builds up gluey lumps on the fingers.

variant_of.differs: The food is a soft paste that has to be rolled to shape first, and it takes flour, then egg, then crumbs, so that the shell holds the paste in when it is fried. The coat of a cutlet goes straight onto firm meat with egg or mustard and crumbs.

comes_after.why: Wet, salted hands come first.

cues.text: The rice holds together when lifted, and still feels light.
The shape has clean edges and a surface with no cracks.

technique/shape-by-hand.does: Presses a portion of warm cooked rice between wet, salted hands into a firm triangle, ball or barrel that holds together but is not packed hard.
how: Wet your hands in cold water, rub a little salt over the palms and shake off the excess.
Scoop up a portion of warm rice and press it lightly into a ball.
Turn it in the hollow of one hand while pressing the other hand into a corner or an edge, to form the shape. Add a filling in the middle first if it is wanted.
Squeeze only enough to hold it together, so that air stays between the grains.

mistakes.fix: Press just until it holds.
mistakes.mistake: Packing the rice hard, which turns it dense and heavy.

mistakes.fix: Wet and salt your hands each time.
mistakes.mistake: Shaping with dry hands, so that the rice sticks to them.

variant_of.differs: Warm cooked rice is shaped with wet, salted hands and kept light, so that the grains stay whole, not packed like a meat mixture.

comes_after.why: The mat shapes an egg block that has already been cooked in layers.

cues.text: The block has an even shape with square edges.
The block is firm and holds together when it is cut.

technique/shape-in-a-mat.does: Rolls a warm, soft food up in a bamboo mat and presses it, so that it sets into a firm, even block with square edges.
how: Lay the mat on the board with the bamboo sticks running side to side.
Place the warm food at the near edge and roll the mat over it tightly.
Press and squeeze along the whole length so that the sides are straight.
Leave it rolled in the mat for a short while to set, then unroll and cut.

mistakes.fix: Shape it while it is still warm.
mistakes.mistake: Rolling when the food is cold and stiff, so that it cracks.

mistakes.fix: Squeeze the whole length of the mat with both hands.
mistakes.mistake: Pressing unevenly, so that one end is thinner.

variant_of.differs: The food is rolled and pressed in a bamboo mat, which gives straight, square edges that hand shaping cannot.

comes_after.why: Minced meat is kneaded with its seasoning so that it holds together before it is rolled.

cues.text: The balls are the same size, smooth and round, with no cracks.
Each ball holds together when it is lifted, and springs back a little under a finger.

technique/shape-meatballs.does: Rolls seasoned minced meat between wet palms into round balls of an even size, so that they hold together and cook at the same pace.
how: Knead the minced meat with its seasoning until it holds together, and chill it briefly so that it handles well.
Wet the hands, or rub them with a little oil, so that the meat does not stick.
Take up equal portions with a spoon, to keep the balls the same size.
Roll each portion between the palms with light pressure until it is round and smooth, with no cracks.
Set the balls on a tray, not touching, until they are cooked.

mistakes.fix: Roll with light pressure, only until they hold.
mistakes.mistake: Packing the balls hard, which makes them dense and dry.

mistakes.fix: Portion the meat with a spoon before rolling.
mistakes.mistake: Making balls of different sizes, so that some are done before others.

mistakes.fix: Wet or oil the hands often.
mistakes.mistake: Working with dry hands, so that the meat sticks and tears.

variant_of.differs: Shape forms a soft mixture into even pieces between spoons. Here the meat is firm enough to be rolled by hand into round balls, and the mixture must first be kneaded to bind.

cues.text: The slivers are thin, slightly curled and about the same length.
The water in the bowl turns brown, and clears when changed.

technique/shave.does: Whittles a long root into thin, curled slivers, turning it against the knife as a pencil is sharpened. The slivers cook fast and keep a crunch.
how: Scrub the root and scrape off the skin, but not too hard, as most of the taste lies just under it.
Hold the root at a slant and turn it against the knife, taking thin slivers as it turns.
Let the slivers fall straight into a bowl of cold water.
Change the water when it turns brown.

mistakes.fix: Let them fall into water as they are cut.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the slivers in the air, where they brown at once.

mistakes.fix: Shave them thin.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting thick slivers, which stay hard.

variant_of.differs: The root is turned against the blade and whittled to slivers, instead of being cut straight across.

cues.text: The threads are very fine and loose, and spring up when they are lifted.
The threads crunch when they are bitten.

technique/shred-cabbage.does: Cuts cabbage into very fine, long threads, which stay crisp and fresh. They are then often soaked briefly in cold water, so that they fluff and stiffen.
how: Cut the cabbage into wedges and cut out the hard core.
Stack a few leaves, roll them up tightly and slice them across as thin as paper.
Put the threads in cold water for a short while, so that they curl and crisp.
Drain them very well and dry them in a cloth, so that they do not water down the dish.

mistakes.fix: Roll the leaves tightly and slice as thin as possible.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting thick shreds, which are tough.

mistakes.fix: Drain and dry them well.
mistakes.mistake: Serving them wet, so that the plate floods.

variant_of.differs: The cut is as thin as thread and the shreds are crisped in cold water, to be eaten raw beside a rich fried dish.

comes_after.why: A simmer is found by coming down from a boil, so a cook has to know a boil first.

cues.text: A bubble or a small cluster of them rising every moment or so, and a surface that shivers.
Near silence. A pot that rolls and rattles is boiling.

technique/simmer.does: Cooks food in liquid that is kept just below a boil, so that it turns tender without being knocked about.
how: Bring the liquid up to a boil, then turn the heat down at once.
Find the setting where a few bubbles break the surface now and then.
Leave the lid off or ajar, so that the heat does not build back up to a boil.
Look in from time to time, and top the pot up if food shows above the liquid.

mistakes.fix: Turn the heat down, or move the pot half off the burner.
mistakes.mistake: Letting it boil, which toughens meat and turns a stock cloudy.

mistakes.fix: Leave the lid ajar.
mistakes.mistake: Covering the pot tightly, so that it climbs to a boil unseen.

comes_after.why: The leaves are filled and rolled first, and a loose roll will not survive the pot.

cues.text: The rolls are plump and have kept their shape, and the liquid is mostly taken up and glossy with oil.
A leaf is tender and the rice inside is soft when a roll is pressed.

technique/simmer-rolled-leaves.does: Cooks filled, rolled leaves packed snugly seam down in a lined pot, weighed down with a plate, in a little oil, lemon juice and water. The leaves turn soft and tart and the rice inside swells and softens.
how: Line the base of a wide pot with slices of tomato or a few spare leaves, so that the rolls do not catch.
Pack the rolls tightly, seam down, in circles, layer on layer, so that none can unroll.
Pour in the olive oil and the lemon juice, add water to come part of the way up the rolls, and salt the liquid.
Set a plate that fits inside the pot upside down on the rolls, so that they stay put.
Cover, bring to a gentle simmer and cook on a low heat until the leaves are tender and the filling has swelled. Leave the rolls to cool in the pot.

mistakes.fix: Pack them tight and weigh them with a plate.
mistakes.mistake: Packing the rolls loosely, so that they float and unroll.

mistakes.fix: Add liquid only part of the way up.
mistakes.mistake: Covering the rolls completely with liquid, so that the filling washes out and the dish turns watery.

mistakes.fix: Keep the pot at a gentle simmer.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking on a high heat, which splits the leaves and breaks the rolls.

variant_of.differs: The food is rolled leaves packed seam down and held under a plate, in liquid that comes only part of the way up, and it is left to cool in the pot.

comes_after.why: The butter is melted gently first, without letting it colour.

cues.text: The butter is a clear, bright red and the flakes are sizzling gently, not black.
A warm, sweet smell of dried pepper, with no scorched edge.

technique/sizzle-chilli-butter.does: Melts butter, takes it off the heat and stirs in dried chilli flakes or paprika, which sizzle for a moment and turn the butter bright red and fragrant. It is spooned over yogurt, eggs, dumplings or soup at the last moment.
how: Melt the butter in a small pan over a gentle heat until it foams, and stop before it browns.
Take the pan off the heat and stir in the chilli flakes or the paprika.
Stir for a few moments while the flakes sizzle gently and the butter turns a deep red.
Spoon it over the food at once, while it is still bubbling.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat before the chilli goes in.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the pan on the heat after the chilli goes in, so that it scorches and turns the butter bitter.

mistakes.fix: Melt the butter only until it foams.
mistakes.mistake: Browning the butter first, which gives a nutty taste and a dull colour in place of the clean red.

mistakes.fix: Make it as the dish is ready and spoon it over while it is hot.
mistakes.mistake: Making it long before it is needed, so that it turns thick and dull.

variant_of.differs: The fat is butter and not ghee or oil, the spice is ground or flaked red pepper and not whole seeds, and the pan is off the heat when the pepper goes in, so that the red does not scorch. The butter is spooned over finished food as a sauce.

cues.text: The pieces sit straight and snug, and are all about the same size.
The pieces do not spin on the skewer when it is turned.

technique/skewer.does: Threads pieces of food, or presses a mince round a flat skewer, so that they can be turned as one and cook evenly over fierce heat, with their juices held in.
how: Soak wooden skewers in water first, so that they do not scorch. Metal skewers need no soaking.
Cut the food into pieces of an even size, so that they cook at the same pace.
Thread the pieces on snugly, with a little room between them so that the heat reaches every face.
For mince, wet the hands and press it firmly round a flat skewer into a long shape, with no gaps.
Leave the ends of the skewer bare, to hold by.

mistakes.fix: Leave a little room between pieces.
mistakes.mistake: Packing the pieces tight, so that the insides stay raw while the outsides burn.

mistakes.fix: Thread each kind on its own skewer.
mistakes.mistake: Mixing pieces that cook at different speeds on one skewer.

mistakes.fix: Chill the mince and press it firmly with wet hands.
mistakes.mistake: Pressing mince too loosely, so that it falls off in the heat.

comes_after.why: Skimming only works on a pot held at a simmer.

cues.text: A clear surface with a few bright beads of fat and no grey foam.

technique/skim.does: Lifts off the foam and fat that rise to the top of a simmering liquid, so that it stays clear and tastes clean.
how: Bring the pot up slowly. The grey foam rises as it nears a simmer.
Hold a ladle flat, just under the surface, and let the foam flow into it.
Move the pot half off the heat, so that the foam gathers on the cooler side.
Skim often at the start, then now and then as fat collects.

mistakes.fix: Keep it at a bare simmer and skim as soon as foam appears.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the pot boil before skimming, which churns the foam and fat back in and clouds the liquid for good.

mistakes.fix: Leave it still. Stirring spreads through the liquid what was rising to be skimmed.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring a stock.

cues.text: Slices of the same thickness from the first to the last.
A quiet stroke. A knock on the board at every cut means you are chopping down, not slicing forward.

technique/slice.does: Cuts food into flat pieces of one thickness.
how: Give the food a flat side to rest on.
Hold it with your fingertips tucked back and your knuckles against the side of the blade.
Push the knife forward and down in one stroke, and let its length do the cutting.
Move the guiding hand back by the thickness of a slice after each cut.

mistakes.fix: Slide the blade forward as it goes down. Sharpen it if it still crushes.
mistakes.mistake: Pressing straight down, which crushes soft food such as a tomato.

mistakes.fix: Slow down. Even matters more than fast.
mistakes.mistake: Slices that grow thicker as the hand tires.

en: cook slowly in a sealed pot

comes_after.why: Slow cooking is a braise with less liquid and far more time, so a cook has to know how a braise behaves first.

cues.text: A fork slides in and the meat falls apart under light pressure.
The juices are glossy, with a layer of clear fat on top.
A deep, sweet smell rises when the pot is opened, and nothing smells scorched.

technique/slow-cook.does: Cooks a tough cut for a very long time at the lowest heat in a closed pot with only a little liquid, so that it softens in its own juices and fat until it falls apart, with its taste deep and little left to reduce.
how: Season the meat early, and rub it with the spices and the fat.
Pack it snugly into the pot with the aromatics, and add only a little liquid, well below the top of the meat.
Close the pot tightly: with its lid, with parchment tied over the mouth, or with a rope of dough around the lid.
Cook in a low oven, or on the lowest heat, and keep the pot shut for most of the time.
Open it near the end, and check that the meat falls apart under a fork and that the juices have turned into a small amount of rich sauce.

mistakes.fix: Keep the pot shut and trust the low heat.
mistakes.mistake: Lifting the lid often, which lets the steam out and stretches the time.

mistakes.fix: Add only a little, well below the top of the meat.
mistakes.mistake: Adding too much liquid, so that the meat boils and the sauce is thin.

mistakes.fix: Use the lowest heat and a heavy pot.
mistakes.mistake: Setting the heat too high, so that the bottom of the pot catches.

variant_of.differs: A braise browns the meat first, cooks it half covered in liquid and turns it now and then. Slow cooking skips the browning, uses only a little liquid, stays shut, and takes far longer at a lower heat, so the meat cooks in its own juices as much as in the liquid.

en: cook potatoes slowly in olive oil

comes_after.why: Slices of one thickness soften at one pace, so a cook has to be able to cut them even first.

cues.text: A slice breaks when it is pressed with the edge of a spoon, and bends without cracking.
