The oil only shimmers and barely bubbles, and the slices stay pale, at most a light gold.
A sweet, mild smell of potato and onion, with nothing toasty about it.

technique/slow-fry-in-olive-oil.does: Cooks thin slices of potato and onion in a deep pool of olive oil that is kept well below frying heat, turning them now and then, until they are soft and silky and have taken almost no colour. The oil is poured off afterwards and kept.
how: Slice the potato thin and even, and the onion thinner. Salt them lightly and turn them over by hand, so that the salt goes through evenly.
Pour olive oil into a wide, deep pan until it comes about halfway up the food, and warm it over a medium heat until a slice dropped in bubbles gently.
Add the potato and onion, then turn the heat down at once, so that the oil only shimmers and nothing fries hard.
Turn the slices over now and then with a spoon, breaking up any that cling together, until they give way under the edge of the spoon and have hardly taken any colour.
Tip everything into a colander set over a bowl. Keep the oil, which now tastes of potato and onion, for the next frying.

mistakes.fix: Turn the heat down until the oil only shimmers.
mistakes.mistake: Frying too hot, so that the slices crisp and brown outside and stay hard inside.

mistakes.fix: Use enough to come about halfway up the food, and turn it often.
mistakes.mistake: Using too little oil, so that the slices stick together and fry in patches.

mistakes.fix: Strain it and keep it for frying or for the next batch.
mistakes.mistake: Throwing the oil away, which wastes a flavoured oil.

variant_of.differs: The food is a shallow heap of thin slices turned in a pan and not lying under the fat. The oil is a little warmer, the cooking far shorter, and the oil is poured off and reused after it, not left round the food.

cues.text: Dried food is plump and smooth, with no wrinkles left.
A slice of bread is soft to the centre and still lifts in one piece.

technique/soak.does: Leaves food in a liquid until it has taken the liquid up, softened, or given up its salt.
how: Cover the food with plenty of liquid, as it will swell.
For dried pulses and dried fruit, use cold water and leave them until they are plump.
For salt cod, change the water several times and keep it cold.
For stale bread, turn the slices in the liquid until they are heavy with it and still hold together.

mistakes.fix: Use bread that is a day old or more, and lift it out as soon as the centre is soft.
mistakes.mistake: Soaking bread until it falls apart.

mistakes.fix: Soak them in the fridge.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving pulses or salt cod to soak in a warm kitchen.

cues.text: A grain bitten through is tender and slightly chewy, with no hard, dry core.
The grains have swelled to fill the bowl and the liquid is gone.

technique/soak-bulgur.does: Leaves fine bulgur in just enough cool liquid for the grains to swell and turn tender, with no cooking at all. The liquid can be water, lemon juice or the juice of tomatoes, and it flavours the grain as it goes in.
how: Rinse the bulgur in a sieve and let the water run off. Tip it into a bowl.
Pour over cool water, or lemon juice or tomato juice, to just cover the grains. They take up the liquid as they swell.
Leave it, and stir once or twice, until the grains are tender with a slight chew in the centre.
Tip it into a sieve, press out any liquid that is left, and fluff the grains with a fork before they meet other foods.

mistakes.fix: Use just enough to cover it, and press out the rest.
mistakes.mistake: Drowning the bulgur in a great deal of water, so that it turns soggy and the dish goes watery.

mistakes.fix: Coarse grades are simmered. Only the fine grades are soaked.
mistakes.mistake: Soaking coarse bulgur the same way, which leaves it hard.

variant_of.differs: The grain is given only as much liquid as it can take up, or is drained and pressed afterwards, and it is never simmered. Beans, bread and dried fruit are covered in plenty of liquid.

cues.text: The mushrooms are soft and pliable, with no hard dry centre.
A deep, earthy scent rises from the bowl.
The water turns dark brown.

technique/soak-dried-mushrooms.does: Steeps dried mushrooms in warm water until they are plump and soft, and keeps the dark, fragrant soaking water, strained of grit, to flavour the dish.
how: Rinse the dried mushrooms quickly under cold water to take off loose dust.
Cover them with warm water, not hot, in a bowl, and press them down so that they stay under.
Leave them until they are plump and pliable. The time depends on the mushroom and the size of the pieces.
Lift the mushrooms out with your hands, squeezing them gently over the bowl, and rinse off any grit.
Pour the soaking water slowly through a fine sieve and leave the last spoonfuls behind in the bowl, where the grit has settled. Keep it to use as stock.
Slice or chop the mushrooms for the dish.

mistakes.fix: Strain it and use it in the dish.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring the soaking water away, when most of the flavour is in it.

mistakes.fix: Pour it slowly through a fine sieve and leave the dregs behind.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring it in unstrained, so that grit ends up in the dish.

mistakes.fix: Use warm water.
mistakes.mistake: Using hot water, which can leave the mushrooms tasting flat.

variant_of.differs: The water is warm, and the soaking water is the prize: it is strained of grit and kept to flavour the dish, while the mushrooms are squeezed and rinsed.

cues.text: The sharp, sweet scent of the sauce rises as the hot food goes in.
The crust has softened slightly and the food is juicy.

technique/soak-in-sauce.does: Steeps just-fried food in a sharp, sweet sauce while it is still hot, so that it drinks up the sauce and turns juicy and flavoured through.
how: Make the sauce ahead and have it in a shallow dish.
Fry the food and lift it out of the oil, shaking off the excess.
Put the hot food straight into the sauce and turn it once.
Leave it to steep for a while, turning it now and then, then lift out and serve.

mistakes.fix: Put it in hot, as it comes from the oil.
mistakes.mistake: Putting the food into the sauce after it has cooled, so that it will not take it up.

mistakes.fix: Lift it out after a short while.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving it in the sauce for too long, so that it turns mushy.

variant_of.differs: Hot, fried food is steeped in a seasoned sauce, not left in water, and the soak lasts only as long as the food needs to drink the sauce.

comes_after.why: The syrup goes on while the baked pastry is still hot.
The syrup is made ahead and cooled.

cues.text: A sharp hiss as the cool syrup meets the hot pastry.
The syrup sinks away from the surface and the top stays pale and crisp.

technique/soak-in-syrup.does: Pours a cool syrup over a pastry as it comes hot from the oven, so that the syrup runs into every layer and the pastry drinks it up while the top stays crisp.
how: Make the syrup ahead and let it cool fully. Hot pastry takes cool syrup. Hot syrup on hot pastry turns it soggy.
Cut the pastry into portions before it is baked, so that the syrup can run down the cuts.
Pour the syrup slowly and evenly over the pastry as it comes out of the oven, and listen for the hiss.
Stop when the syrup stands in the cuts and a little pools at the edge. It goes on sinking in as the pastry cools.
Leave the pastry uncovered until it is cold. A lid traps steam and softens the top.

mistakes.fix: Let the syrup or the pastry be cold.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring hot syrup on hot pastry, so that the layers go limp.

mistakes.fix: Leave it uncovered until it is cold.
mistakes.mistake: Covering the pastry while it is still warm, so that steam softens the top.

mistakes.fix: Stop boiling the syrup while it is still thin enough to run off a spoon.
mistakes.mistake: Using a syrup boiled too thick, which sits on top and does not soak in.

variant_of.differs: The pastry is not left in a bath. The syrup is poured over the baked, hot pastry in one go, and either the syrup or the pastry must be cold, so that the layers drink it and stay crisp.

cues.text: The water turns brown or cloudy, and the pieces stay pale.
A piece tastes cleaner and less bitter than before.

technique/soak-in-water.does: Puts cut vegetables in cold water for a short time, to keep them from browning, to rinse off loose starch and to take out the harsh bitterness.
how: Fill a bowl with cold water before cutting.
Drop the pieces in as they are cut.
Leave them for a short while, and change the water when it turns cloudy or brown.
Drain and pat dry before they are cooked.

mistakes.fix: Soak only briefly.
mistakes.mistake: Soaking for too long, so that the pieces lose taste.

mistakes.fix: Drain and pat dry.
mistakes.mistake: Skipping the drain, so that water drips into the hot pan.

variant_of.differs: The soak is brief, in cold water, and aims to keep a cut vegetable pale and mild, not to swell or soften dried food.

comes_after.why: The rice is soaked after it has been washed.

cues.text: The grains turn from glassy to an even, chalky white.
A grain crushes easily between the fingers, with no hard core.

technique/soak-rice.does: Leaves washed rice in cold water until the grains have turned white and plump all through, so that they cook evenly and come out tender in the middle.
how: Put the washed, drained rice in the pot or in a bowl and cover it with cold water.
Leave it until the grains turn from clear to chalky white.
Drain it well and let it sit in the sieve for a short while.
Cook it in fresh measured water.

mistakes.fix: Soak it in cold water and shorter.
mistakes.mistake: Soaking for too long in warm weather, so that the rice sours.

mistakes.fix: Drain it and add the measured water.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking it in the soaking water, so that the amount of water is wrong.

variant_of.differs: It is a short soak of washed rice in cold water until the grains turn white, and not a long soak of dried pulses, and the water is poured off.

cues.text: An even layer, with the surface showing through at the thin places and a clear rim.
The spoon glides. If it drags, the paste is too stiff and wants more oil.

technique/spread.does: Smooths a soft paste, mash or butter over a surface in an even layer with the back of a spoon or a knife, so that every bite carries some and the edges stay clear.
how: Have the paste soft enough to move. Loosen it with a little oil or water if it is stiff.
Put a spoonful in the middle of the surface.
Push it outwards with the back of a spoon in slow circles, working towards the edge.
Stop a little short of the edge, so that the paste does not run off or burn on the pan.

mistakes.fix: Loosen it with a little oil first.
mistakes.mistake: Spreading a paste that is too stiff, so that it tears the dough.

mistakes.fix: Push it out in circles until the layer is even, to just short of the rim.
mistakes.mistake: Piling the paste in the middle and leaving the edge bare.

cues.text: The flour vanishes into a thin paste that coats every piece.
The raw, dusty smell gives way to a faint smell of biscuit.

technique/sprinkle-with-flour.does: Scatters flour over food that is already cooking in fat and cooks it for a moment, so that the liquid added next thickens as it simmers.
how: Scatter the flour evenly over the hot, fat-coated food, not in a heap.
Stir until no white shows.
Cook it for a moment, stirring, to take away the raw taste.
Add the liquid little by little at first, stirring it smooth.

mistakes.fix: Scatter it from high up, or through a sieve.
mistakes.mistake: Tipping the flour in as a heap, which makes lumps that never dissolve.

mistakes.fix: Give it a moment on the heat first.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the liquid at once, before the flour has cooked.

variant_of.differs: The flour goes onto food already cooking in fat, so that the roux forms around the pieces and is not made on its own.

comes_after.why: Leaves are squeezed once they have wilted or boiled and let go of their water. Raw leaves hold it in.

cues.text: The ball of leaves is dense and damp but gives out no more water when squeezed.
The water that comes out is a dark green, and the leaves loosen into a dry, fluffy heap.

technique/squeeze.does: Presses the water out of cooked leaves by the handful, or in a sieve, so that they can be seasoned and mixed without turning the dish watery.
how: Let the cooked leaves cool enough to handle.
Take up a handful and close the fist, or press the leaves against the side of a sieve with a spoon.
Squeeze hard and long, turning the ball in the hand, until only a few drops come out.
Shake the leaves loose, as they will be a tight lump, and chop or season them.

mistakes.fix: Let them cool, then squeeze hard.
mistakes.mistake: Squeezing the leaves while they are hot, which burns the hands and tempts a cook to squeeze too lightly.

mistakes.fix: Squeeze again until only a few drops come out.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the leaves wet, so that the oil and the dressing slide off them.

cues.text: The yogurt stays smooth and creamy, with no grains and no pool of thin liquid at the sides.
The spoon meets a gentle, even drag, like a thick cream.

technique/stabilise.does: Prepares yogurt so that it can be heated and simmered without splitting into curds and thin liquid. A starch or a beaten egg white is mixed into the cold yogurt, and the yogurt is stirred one way as it heats.
how: Whisk the yogurt smooth in a pan, off the heat.
Mix a little cornstarch with cold water until smooth, or beat an egg white loose, and whisk it into the yogurt.
Set the pan over a low heat and stir all the time, always in the same direction.
Bring it slowly up to a bare simmer without letting it boil hard, and keep stirring until it is thick and smooth.
Keep it at a gentle simmer from then on.

mistakes.fix: Stabilise it first and stir in one direction only.
mistakes.mistake: Heating plain yogurt fast, or stirring it first one way and then the other, so that it breaks into curds.

mistakes.fix: Hold it at a gentle simmer.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the stabilised yogurt boil hard, which can still break it.

variant_of.differs: The aim is not body but steadiness: a starch or egg white goes into the cold yogurt first, and the yogurt is stirred one way so that its milk proteins do not clump when it is heated. Thicken stirs a starch into a hot liquid.

cues.text: Vegetables are bright and just tender. Mussel shells gape wide open.
The lid rattles steadily.

technique/steam.does: Cooks food in the steam of a little boiling liquid under a tight lid, so that nothing of it is washed away.
how: Bring a shallow layer of water or wine to a boil in a wide pot.
Set the food in a basket above the liquid, or straight into the pot for shellfish, and cover it at once with a tight lid.
Keep the heat high and the lid on.
Sort mussels before they go in: throw away any with a broken shell, and any that stays open when it is tapped.
For mussels, shake the pot now and then, and take it off the heat as soon as the shells have opened. Throw away any mussel that stays shut.

mistakes.fix: Leave it shut until the time is nearly up.
mistakes.mistake: Lifting the lid again and again, which lets the steam out and slows everything down.

mistakes.fix: Take the pot off the heat the moment most of the shells are open.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving mussels on the heat after they have opened, so that they shrink and turn rubbery.

cues.text: Steam shows through the whole pile of grains before the steaming is counted.
The finished grains are tender, swollen and separate, and none sticks to the fingers.

technique/steam-couscous.does: Swells dry couscous grains in the steam of a simmering stew, in rounds, so that each grain turns light and separate. The grains are rubbed with water and oil, steamed, tipped out, sprinkled again and raked apart, then steamed once more until they are tender.
how: Tip the dry grains into a wide dish, sprinkle them with salted water and rub them between the palms until every grain is damp and nothing is clumped. Work in a little oil.

Bring the stew, or plain water, to a simmer in the base of the couscoussier. Seal the seam between the base and the top with a strip of damp cloth or a paste of flour and water, so that no steam escapes there.
Pile the damp grains loosely in the perforated top. Do not press them down, and do not cover them until steam rises through the whole pile.
Steam until the steam shows through the top, then tip the grains back into the dish.
Sprinkle them with a little cold salted water, rake them with the fingertips to break every lump, let them swell for a while, and steam them again in the same way.
Tip them out for the last time and rake in butter or smen until the grains shine. Heap them on a dish and serve with the stew.

mistakes.fix: Pile them loosely and let the steam find its way.
mistakes.mistake: Pressing the grains down in the top, which blocks the steam and leaves a hard core.

mistakes.fix: Seal the seam with damp cloth or a paste of flour and water.
mistakes.mistake: Letting steam leak at the seam, so that the grains stay dry and the stew goes thin.

mistakes.fix: Add water a little at a time and rake after each sprinkling.
mistakes.mistake: Sprinkling on too much water at once, which turns the grains gluey.

mistakes.fix: Keep them above the liquid, where only the steam reaches them.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking the grains in the stew liquid itself, which makes a paste.

names.fr: Cuire le couscous à la vapeur

variant_of.differs: Steam cooks fresh food in the steam of a little boiling water. Here the food is dry grain, wetted by hand between rounds, steamed over a stew in several rounds and raked apart each time, so that it never sets into a block.

comes_after.why: The stew is held at a gentle simmer, so a cook who can hold a simmer steady has the main skill.

cues.text: The broth turns dark green, glossy and a little thick, with the leaves hanging in it and not clumped.
The spoon moves through it easily. It is thick and silky and not stringy.
A deep, green scent, a little like cooked spinach.

technique/stew-jute-leaf.does: Simmers finely chopped jute leaf in hot broth, uncovered, until the leaves give up their slippery thickness and the broth turns dark green and silky. It is kept just below a boil, stirred little, and finished with a taqliyeh of garlic and coriander.
how: Strip fresh leaves from their stems, wash and dry them well, and chop them very fine. Frozen leaves go in as they are. Dried leaves are soaked briefly first.
Bring the broth to a gentle simmer and keep it hot.
Stir in the leaves, and keep the pot just below a boil, uncovered.
Cook until the leaves have sunk into the broth and thickened it to a silky stew, stirring only now and then.
Take the pot off the heat before the garlic and coriander taqliyeh and the lemon juice go in.

mistakes.fix: Keep it just below a boil, uncovered.
mistakes.mistake: Boiling it hard or putting a lid on, so that the stew turns dull and stringy.

mistakes.fix: Chop them very fine, or use leaves that are already chopped.
mistakes.mistake: Chopping the leaves coarse, so that they stay in long strings.

mistakes.fix: Add it at the end.
mistakes.mistake: Adding lemon juice early, which dulls the green.

variant_of.differs: The leaf is chopped very fine and cooked uncovered, just below a boil, until it thickens the broth itself, and it is stirred little.

cues.text: The spoon drags more heavily across the base as the mixture thickens.
The surface stays smooth, with no brown bits at the edges.
A caught, scorched smell means it was left still for too long.

technique/stir.does: Moves a spoon through food as it heats, scraping the base of the pan, so that it cooks evenly, does not catch and scorch, and stays smooth.
how: Use a spoon with a flat edge, or a wooden spoon, and a pan with a heavy base.
Keep the heat gentle and reach the whole base and the corners with each pass.
Stir in slow loops or long sweeps, and not so hard that the food breaks.
Keep going for as long as the dish thickens, since the base catches first.

mistakes.fix: Stay with it and stir throughout.
mistakes.mistake: Walking away, so that the base catches and the whole pan tastes burnt.

mistakes.fix: Stir slowly and only as much as needed to stop it catching.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring a rice pudding hard, so that the grains break and turn to paste.

mistakes.fix: Turn the heat down.
mistakes.mistake: Using high heat, which scorches the base faster than the spoon can reach.

en: stir fry in a hot pan

comes_after.why: Stir-frying is sautéing at higher heat and greater speed, so a cook has to read a hot pan first.

cues.text: A steady, loud sizzle, which fades if the pan has been crowded.
The pieces are glossy and coloured at the edges, and none sits in a pool of liquid.
A toasty, sweet smell, and not a burnt one.

technique/stir-fry.does: Cooks small, even pieces very fast in a little hot oil in a wide pan, keeping them moving all the time with a spoon or a spatula, so that they take colour at the edges and stay crisp or just tender inside.
how: Cut everything small and even, and have it all at hand before the pan goes on, because the cooking is quick.
Heat a wok or wide pan until very hot, then add a little oil and swirl it.
Add the food that takes longest first, then the rest in order, and keep it moving the whole time.
Add sauces and seasoning at the end, so that they coat the food and do not stew it.
Take it out as soon as it is done, since it carries on cooking in the pan.

mistakes.fix: Cook in smaller batches and keep the heat high.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding the pan, so that the food stews in its own water.

mistakes.fix: Add the pieces in order of how long they take.
mistakes.mistake: Adding everything together, so that some pieces are raw and others limp.

mistakes.fix: Keep it moving.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the food still for long, so that it scorches.

variant_of.differs: The pan is hotter and wider, the pieces are cut smaller, and they are kept moving with a spoon or spatula and added in order of how long they take, where a sauté lets them sit to colour between tosses.

cues.text: A clear stock shows the bottom of the ladle through it.

technique/strain.does: Pours a liquid through a sieve, so that the solids stay behind and the liquid comes out clear.
how: Set a fine sieve over a pot or a bowl large enough for all the liquid.
Ladle the liquid in, a little at a time at first.
Let it drain by its own weight. For a clear stock, do not press on the solids.
For a soup or a sauce that should be thick, press the solids through with the back of a ladle.

mistakes.fix: Ladle from the top and leave the last cloudy part in the pot.
mistakes.mistake: Tipping a full stockpot over the sieve in one go, which stirs up the sediment and clouds the stock.

cues.text: A plump, even shape with no filling showing at the seams.
It gives a little when it is pressed. It is not drum-tight.

technique/stuff.does: Fills a hollow, a pocket or a rolled slice with a seasoned mixture, which flavours the food from inside and keeps it moist.
how: Season the filling well and let it cool before it goes in.
Fill loosely. A filling swells as it cooks, and one that is packed tight bursts its wrapper.
Close the opening by folding, tying or pinning, so that the filling stays inside.
For a rolled slice, flatten the slice, spread the filling short of the edges, roll it up and tie it.
Check the centre of the filling against a trusted guide to doneness. It is the last part to heat.

mistakes.fix: Leave room for it to swell.
mistakes.mistake: Packing the filling in tightly, so that the wrapper splits as it cooks.

mistakes.fix: Cool the filling first, and stuff just before the food goes on the heat.
mistakes.mistake: Stuffing with a warm filling long before cooking.

cues.text: The filling lies flat and even, with none showing at the edge.
The closed bread is firm and flat under the hand, and does not slide apart.

technique/stuff-a-pita.does: Opens a round of pita and spreads a thin layer of raw, spiced meat mixture inside, then presses the bread shut, so that the filling cooks and the bread crisps and soaks up its juices on the heat.
how: Cut round the edge of the pita with a knife, or split it along one side, and open it into layers.
Spread the filling thinly and evenly over the inner face of one layer, right to the edge.
Close the pita over the filling and press it down firmly with the hand, so that the layers hold together.
Cut it in half, or leave it whole, and cook it at once.

mistakes.fix: Spread it thin, as thin as a finger, and even.
mistakes.mistake: Piling the filling thick in the middle, so that the bread crisps and burns before the filling is done.

mistakes.fix: Warm the bread first, so that it bends.
mistakes.mistake: Using a dry, cracked pita that splits as it is opened.

variant_of.differs: The pocket is a round of bread, and the filling is raw meat spread flat as a thin layer and pressed shut so that it cooks with the bread. It is not packed into a hollow of a bird or a vegetable.

cues.text: The skin lifts easily from the flesh on a fingertip and does not tear.
The flavouring shows through the skin as an even pattern, with no bare patches.

technique/stuff-under-the-skin.does: Slides a flavouring, such as slices of truffle or a soft herb butter, between the skin and the flesh of a bird, so that it seasons the meat directly and keeps the breast moist as it cooks.
how: Dry the bird well. Start at the neck end and work a finger gently between the skin and the breast, then loosen the skin over the whole breast and a little way down the legs, without tearing it.
Season the flesh under the skin.
Slide the flavouring in flat and spread it in an even layer, then smooth the skin back down over it.
Tuck the neck skin under the bird, so that nothing slips out.
Truss the bird if it is to be poached or roasted whole, and cook it soon after.

mistakes.fix: Work slowly with a finger and not a nail, and lay the skin back over any small tear.
mistakes.mistake: Tearing the skin, so that the flavouring leaks out and the flesh dries.

mistakes.fix: Use thin flat slices, or a soft smooth butter spread evenly.
mistakes.mistake: Pushing in a lumpy filling that leaves gaps and slides about.

variant_of.differs: The filling goes between the skin and the flesh and not into the hollow of the bird, so it flavours and bastes the meat directly and is never packed in.

comes_after.why: Even pieces soften together. Uneven ones leave some raw and some brown.

cues.text: A quiet, steady hiss. A loud sizzle means the heat is too high.
The onion turns glassy and limp, with no brown at the edges.
Sweet, with the raw sharpness gone.

technique/sweat.does: Softens cut vegetables in a little fat over low heat, so that they give up their water and turn sweet without browning.
how: Warm the fat in a wide pan over low heat.
Add the vegetables with a little salt and stir to coat them.
Keep the heat low and stir now and then, so that nothing sits long enough to colour.
Cover the pan to go faster: the trapped steam softens them.
Stop when the pieces are soft and glassy.

mistakes.fix: Turn the heat down and add a spoonful of water to stop the colour.
mistakes.mistake: The heat is too high, so the edges brown before the middle softens.

mistakes.fix: Use a wider pan, or let the water cook off before going on.
mistakes.mistake: Too many vegetables in a small pan, so they stew in their own water.

cues.text: The sweetness is clear but does not drown the taste of the food.
No grains of sugar remain.

technique/sweeten.does: Adds sugar to a food a little at a time and tastes after each addition, to bring it to the right level of sweetness without hiding its own taste.
how: Cook the food until it is soft enough to take up the sugar.
Add the sugar in portions, stirring each in until it has dissolved.
Taste after each portion and stop when the sweetness is balanced.
Add a small amount of salt at the end to round the taste.

mistakes.fix: Add it a little at a time.
mistakes.mistake: Adding all the sugar at once, so that it is too sweet and cannot be corrected.

mistakes.fix: Cook them soft first.
mistakes.mistake: Adding sugar to dried beans before they are soft, so that they stay hard.

comes_after.why: The lentils are simmered until soft before the bulgur is stirred in.

cues.text: The liquid has gone and the mixture is thick and damp, with no dry grains left.
The grains are tender all through, with no hard core when pressed.

technique/swell-bulgur-in-hot-liquid.does: Stirs fine bulgur into a pan of hot, freshly cooked lentils or other hot liquid, covers it and leaves it off the heat until the grains have swollen and softened in the liquid and taken its flavour.
how: Cook the lentils until they are very soft, with enough water left in the pan to wet the bulgur.
Take the pan off the heat and stir in the bulgur.
Cover at once and leave it to stand until the grains are swollen and the mixture is thick.
Stir it once and let it cool until it can be handled.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat before the bulgur goes in.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the pan on the heat, so that the bulgur cooks to a paste.

mistakes.fix: Leave more liquid in the pan, or sprinkle on hot water and cover again.
mistakes.mistake: Using too little liquid, which leaves hard grains.

mistakes.fix: Leave it covered until the stand is over.
mistakes.mistake: Lifting the lid to look, which lets the heat out.

variant_of.differs: The liquid is hot, and the bulgur swells in the heat of a covered pan taken off the stove, instead of soaking in cool liquid with no heat at all. It takes the flavour of what was cooked in the liquid.

comes_after.why: The eggs are whisked first, and the hot liquid is whisked in.

cues.text: The bowl is warm and not hot, and the mixture is smooth with no threads of cooked egg.
The mixture is glossy and thinner than it was.

technique/temper.does: Warms eggs or yolks gently by whisking a little hot liquid into them, so that they can then join the hot liquid in the pan without turning to specks. The word here is for eggs, not for chocolate.
how: Whisk the eggs or yolks, usually with the sugar, in a bowl big enough to take the liquid.
Heat the milk or cream until it steams. It must not be boiling.
Pour a little of the hot liquid onto the eggs in a thin stream while whisking all the time.
Add a little more in the same way, until the bowl feels warm to the touch.
Tip the warmed mixture back into the pan and finish over gentle heat, stirring.

mistakes.fix: Pour a thin stream while whisking hard.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring the hot liquid in all at once, which cooks the egg into specks.

mistakes.fix: Take the liquid off the heat first, and warm the eggs with a little of it.
mistakes.mistake: Tipping the eggs into liquid that is boiling.

en: fry whole spices in hot fat

cues.text: Mustard seeds crackle and pop, then go quiet. A loud, steady sizzle means the fat is hot enough.
Cumin seeds turn a shade darker, the dried chilli puffs and darkens, and the curry leaves go glassy and crisp.
A warm, nutty scent rises. A sharp, acrid smell means the spices have gone too far.

technique/temper-spices-in-hot-fat.does: Fries whole seeds, dried chillies and leaves in a little very hot fat until they crackle, darken a shade and give up their scent, then pours the scented fat and the spices over the food. Done at the start it is the base that onions and vegetables cook in. Done at the end it is a last layer of flavour poured over a finished dish.
how: Heat a small amount of ghee or oil in a small pan until it shimmers and a single seed dropped in sizzles at once.
Add the slowest seeds first: mustard seed, which will crackle and jump, and any split lentils that should turn golden. Cover the pan with a lid if they leap out.
When the popping slows, add cumin, fenugreek seed, cardamom and the dried chilli, and stir for a moment.
Add the curry leaves, dry, and the asafoetida last. They burn the quickest, and wet leaves spit.
Stop the moment the seeds darken a shade and the scent rises, and take the pan off the heat.
Pour the fat and the spices straight into the food, or over a finished dish, and stir it in or leave it on top.

mistakes.fix: Test with a single seed first. It must sizzle at once.
mistakes.mistake: Putting the spices into fat that is not hot enough, so that they soak it up and taste raw.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat the moment the scent rises and pour out at once.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the pan on the heat after the seeds have darkened, so that they scorch and turn bitter.

mistakes.fix: Add them last, with the pan off the heat or nearly so.
mistakes.mistake: Adding asafoetida or chilli powder first, so that it burns before the seeds are ready.

mistakes.fix: Pat the leaves dry first and stand back as they go in.
mistakes.mistake: Dropping wet curry leaves into the fat, which makes it spit.

variant_of.differs: The spices are whole, few and cooked for a moment, in a small amount of hot fat on their own, and the scented fat is the point. A French sauce starts with spices or aromatics that cook slowly along with the vegetables, and it never pours the fat over a finished dish.
Toasting browns spices in a dry pan to be ground later. Here the spices go whole into hot fat, which carries their scent into the food, and the cooking is over in moments.

comes_after.why: Starch thickens at a simmer, so a cook has to be able to hold a liquid there.

cues.text: The liquid turns glossy and clear, or silky if it holds milk, and coats the back of a spoon.
The spoon drags a little more as it moves through.

technique/thicken.does: Gives a thin hot liquid more body by stirring in a starch, mixed smooth in a little cold liquid first, and bringing it to a simmer so that the starch swells and the liquid turns glossy and coats a spoon.
how: Mix the starch with a little cold liquid until it is smooth, with no lumps.
Bring the liquid to a gentle simmer and stir it round.
Pour the mixture in a thin stream while stirring, and keep stirring.
Let it bubble gently for a short while so that the raw taste of the starch cooks out and the body is full.
Stop when it coats the back of a spoon. It will thicken a little more as it cools, so take it off the heat while it still pours.

mistakes.fix: Mix it smooth in cold liquid first.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the dry starch straight to hot liquid, which lumps.

mistakes.fix: Let it bubble gently only until it has thickened.
mistakes.mistake: Boiling hard for long, which breaks the starch down so that the liquid thins again.

mistakes.fix: Add a little at a time and stop while it still pours.
mistakes.mistake: Thickening too much at the start, since it keeps thickening as it cools.

comes_after.why: It asks for the same judgment as a custard: yolks thickening a liquid just short of scrambling.

cues.text: The sauce turns ivory and velvety, and coats the spoon more thickly than before.

technique/thicken-with-egg-yolk.does: Enriches and lightly thickens a hot sauce with egg yolks beaten with cream, without letting the yolks scramble.
how: Beat the yolks with the cream in a bowl.
Take the sauce off the boil.
Whisk a ladle of the hot sauce into the yolks to warm them, then another.
Pour the mixture back into the pan, stirring all the time.
Heat gently, stirring, just until the sauce thickens a little. It must not boil again.

mistakes.fix: Warm the yolks with a little hot sauce first.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring the yolks straight into a boiling sauce, which sets them into threads.

mistakes.fix: Keep it below a simmer. A sauce that has started to grain can sometimes be rescued through a fine sieve.
mistakes.mistake: Boiling the sauce after the yolks have gone in.

en: thicken a soup with flour paste

comes_after.why: The paste goes into a soup that is already simmering, so a cook has to hold a steady simmer first.

cues.text: The soup turns from thin and clear to glossy and slightly cloudy, and coats the back of a spoon.
The raw taste of flour is gone and the soup tastes round.

technique/thicken-with-tadouira.does: Stirs a loose paste of flour and cold water into a hot soup in a slow stream, then keeps the soup at a simmer until the flour has lost its raw taste, so that the soup turns silky and gains body. Beaten egg is sometimes stirred in at the end.
how: Whisk the flour into plenty of cold water until it is as smooth and loose as cream, with no lump left.
Bring the soup to a steady simmer and keep stirring as you pour the paste in, in a thin stream.
Keep stirring until the soup comes back to the simmer, then let it bubble gently for a good while, so that the flour cooks out.
Stir in the beaten egg last, if the soup is to have it, off the boil.

mistakes.fix: Pour it in a thin stream while stirring.
mistakes.mistake: Tipping the paste into the soup all at once, which leaves lumps.

mistakes.fix: Always whisk the flour with cold water first.
mistakes.mistake: Mixing the flour with hot liquid, which clots it.

mistakes.fix: Let it simmer on until the taste is gone.
mistakes.mistake: Stopping as soon as the soup thickens, which leaves a taste of raw flour.

variant_of.differs: Thickening stirs a starch mixed smooth in a little cold liquid into a sauce. Tadouira uses plain wheat flour whisked into a loose paste with a good deal of cold water, poured into the soup in a thin stream, and the soup is then simmered on for a good while so that the flour cooks out. No roux is made.

cues.text: Bread is dry and pale gold. Nuts are a shade darker than they were.
A warm, nutty scent rises. An acrid smell means it has gone too far.

technique/toast.does: Dries and browns bread, nuts or spices in dry heat, which makes them crisp and wakes their scent.
how: Spread the food in a single layer on a tray or in a dry pan.
Use a moderate heat: an oven, a grill or a pan with no fat.
Turn bread once. Shake nuts and spices often.
Tip nuts and spices out of the hot pan as soon as they are done, as they go on browning in it.

mistakes.fix: Stay with them and shake the pan.
mistakes.mistake: Walking away, as nuts go from golden to burnt within moments.

mistakes.fix: Tip them onto a cold plate at once.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving toasted nuts or spices in the hot pan, where they keep browning.

cues.text: The pieces puff and show golden patches.
A piece gives way softly when pressed.

technique/toast-mochi.does: Browns pieces of hard rice cake under a grill, in a dry pan or in an oven until they puff, blister and turn soft and stretchy inside, with a lightly crisp skin.
how: Cut the mochi into pieces and set them apart on a tray or in a dry pan.
Cook over a gentle heat and watch them, as they puff quickly.
Turn them once they swell and brown in places.
Lift them off as soon as they are puffed and soft, and eat or add them to a hot dish at once.

mistakes.fix: Leave a gap between them.
mistakes.mistake: Setting the pieces close together, so that they fuse.

mistakes.fix: Use a moderate heat and watch.
mistakes.mistake: Using strong heat, which scorches the outside before the inside softens.

variant_of.differs: The food is a rice cake that swells and turns stretchy inside as it browns, and it is toasted gently so that the inside softens before the outside burns.

comes_after.why: The rice goes into onion that has been softened without colour.

cues.text: A dry, gentle rustle of grains in the pan, and a faint crackle when they are properly hot.
The edges of the grains turn translucent while the centre stays white.
A faint nutty scent rises from the pan.

technique/toast-rice.does: Stirs raw rice in hot fat until the outside of each grain turns translucent and the grains are hot and dry, so that they keep their shape and take up stock slowly. The Italian name for this first step of a risotto is tostatura.
how: Make the base of the dish first in the same wide pan, such as onion softened in butter, and leave it soft.
Tip in the dry, unwashed rice and stir over medium heat, so that every grain is coated in fat.
Keep stirring until the edges of the grains turn translucent, with a pearly dot left at the centre, and the rice is too hot to hold comfortably.
If wine is used, pour it in now and stir until it has been taken up and the sharp smell has gone.

mistakes.fix: Use the rice dry, straight from the packet.
mistakes.mistake: Rinsing the rice first, which washes off the starch that makes the sauce creamy.

mistakes.fix: Stop when the edges are translucent and no more.
mistakes.mistake: Taking it too far, so that the grains brown and taste scorched.

mistakes.fix: Coat them in hot fat first.
mistakes.mistake: Skipping the step, so that the grains go soft outside before the centre is tender.

variant_of.differs: The grains are stirred in hot fat, in the pan they will cook in, and not dried alone in dry heat. They are taken only to translucent edges and never to colour.

cues.text: Every piece glistens, and nothing pools in the bottom of the bowl.

technique/toss.does: Coats every piece evenly with a dressing or a sauce by lifting and turning.
how: Put the food in a bowl far larger than it needs.
Add the dressing a little at a time, around the edge and not on top.
Lift from the bottom and let the pieces fall, with clean hands or a pair of spoons.
Taste a piece and adjust before serving.

mistakes.fix: Toss at the last moment.
mistakes.mistake: Dressing leaves long before serving, so that the acid and salt make them limp.

mistakes.fix: Add it in stages and stop when everything is lightly coated.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring on all the dressing at once, which drowns the food.

comes_after.why: The pasta is taken from the pot a little early, with some of its water kept back, to finish in the sauce.

cues.text: The sauce is glossy and clings to the pasta, with no loose liquid and no dry patches in the pan.
The pieces slide freely against each other and do not clump.

technique/toss-pasta-with-sauce.does: Moves just-drained pasta into the sauce and tosses it over the heat with a splash of the starchy cooking water, so that sauce and water bind into a glossy coat that clings to every piece. The pasta is dressed in the pan and not on the plate.
how: Have the sauce ready in a wide pan before the pasta is drained, with a mug of the cooking water set aside.
Lift the pasta straight from the pot into the pan, still wet and hot, a little before it is ready.
Toss and stir over the heat, adding the cooking water a splash at a time, until the sauce turns glossy and clings in a thin coat.
For a sauce that holds egg or cheese, take the pan off the heat first, so that the egg warms into a cream and does not scramble.
Serve at once, while the sauce still flows.

mistakes.fix: Finish the pasta in the pan with a splash of the cooking water.
mistakes.mistake: Spooning sauce on top of dry, drained pasta at the table, so that it slides off.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat and loosen with the cooking water.
mistakes.mistake: Tossing an egg sauce over strong heat, so that the egg scrambles.

mistakes.fix: Add it a splash at a time and watch the sauce.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring in all the water at once, so that the sauce turns thin.

variant_of.differs: The pasta is tossed over heat and not in a cold bowl, and the starchy cooking water is added so that the sauce and the starch bind together.

cues.text: Clean, even surfaces with no silvery skin, no ragged flaps and no dark outer leaves.

technique/trim.does: Cuts away what will not be eaten or will not cook well: sinew, surplus fat, tough leaves, stalks and ragged edges.
how: Slide the tip of the knife under a strip of sinew, angle the blade up against it and draw the knife along, so that the sinew comes away with almost no meat.
Leave a thin, even layer of fat on a joint that will be roasted.
Snap or cut the ends off beans, and pull away any string.
For an artichoke, break off the stalk, pull away the dark outer leaves, cut off the top, pare the base smooth and scoop out the hairy choke. Rub every cut with lemon at once.
Keep meat trimmings for a stock or for rendering.

mistakes.fix: Keep the blade angled up against what you are taking off.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting deep and wasting good flesh along with the sinew.

mistakes.fix: Rub each cut with lemon, or drop the trimmed artichoke into water sharpened with lemon.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving a cut artichoke in the air, where it turns brown within moments.

cues.text: A neat, plump shape with nothing sticking out, and string that is snug without cutting in.

technique/truss.does: Ties a bird or a joint into a compact shape, so that it cooks evenly and keeps its form.
how: Tuck the wing tips under the back of the bird.
Pass a length of string under the tail, cross it over the ends of the drumsticks and pull them together.
Run the string along the sides, between the legs and the breast, and tie it at the neck.
For a joint, tie loops of string along it at even spaces, snug but not tight.

mistakes.fix: Pull it snug and no more.
mistakes.mistake: Tying so tightly that the string cuts into the flesh and squeezes the juice out.

mistakes.fix: Draw the legs in against the breast.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the legs splayed, so that the breast dries before the thighs are done.

comes_after.why: A vegetable is peeled before it is turned.

cues.text: Small barrels of one size, with smooth curved faces and blunt ends.

technique/turn.does: Pares a vegetable into a neat barrel with curved sides, so that every piece cooks in the same time and rolls in the pan.
how: Cut the vegetable into pieces of one length, and split large ones into halves or quarters.
Hold a piece between thumb and finger and draw a small knife from end to end in one curved stroke.
Turn the piece a little and cut again, until it has even faces and tapers at both ends.
Drop potatoes into cold water as they are done, and keep the parings for a soup or a mash.

mistakes.fix: Take each face in one long stroke, turning the wrist.
mistakes.mistake: Short, choppy cuts, which leave flat steps instead of a curve.

mistakes.fix: Cut all the pieces to one length before you start.
mistakes.mistake: Pieces of different sizes, which cook unevenly.

comes_after.why: The dish starts with crepes that are already cooked, so a cook has to be able to make them thin and supple first.

cues.text: The sauce is thick enough to coat a spoon and clings to the crepes in a glossy layer.
A warm smell of orange and caramel.

technique/warm-crepes-in-orange-sauce.does: Folds cooked crepes into a hot sauce of caramel, orange and butter, warms them in it and sets a spirit alight over them at the end. The crepes soak up the sauce, and the flame burns off the harshness of the spirit.
how: Make the sauce first in a wide pan: stir the orange juice, some zest and the butter into a pale caramel and simmer until it is syrupy.
Fold each crepe in half and in half again, to make a fan.
Lay the crepes in the sauce, spoon the sauce over them and turn them once so that both sides are coated and warm.
Warm the spirit in a small pan. Take the pan with the crepes off the heat and pour the spirit around the edge, never straight from the bottle.
Stand back and light it with a long match, or tilt the pan to the flame, and spoon the burning sauce over the crepes until the flame dies.
Serve at once on warm plates, with the sauce spooned over.

mistakes.fix: Measure the spirit into a small pan first, and pour it around the edge, off the heat.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring the spirit from the bottle into the hot pan, where the flame can run back into the bottle.

mistakes.fix: Add the juice as soon as the sugar is a pale amber.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the caramel go dark and bitter before the juice goes in.

mistakes.fix: Warm them just long enough to coat them, and serve at once.
mistakes.mistake: Soaking the crepes for too long, so that they turn limp and tear.

names.fr: Réchauffer les crêpes au beurre d'orange

variant_of.differs: The flame is not used to start a pan sauce. The crepes are warmed in a finished sauce of caramel, orange and butter, and the spirit is lit at the end, over the whole dish.

en: rinse rice until the water runs nearly clear

cues.text: The washing water turns from milky to almost clear.
The grains feel smooth and separate.

technique/wash-rice.does: Rubs rice gently in cold water and pours the cloudy water away, again and again, to take off the loose starch, so that the cooked grains are separate and clean-tasting.
how: Put the rice in a large bowl and cover it with cold water. Stir quickly with your hand and pour the cloudy water away at once.
Rub the rice lightly with the heel of the hand in a circular motion.
Add fresh water, swirl, and drain again.
Repeat until the water runs nearly clear. It does not need to be perfectly clear.
Drain the rice in a sieve.

mistakes.fix: Pour off the first water at once.
mistakes.mistake: Washing slowly in the first water, which lets the rice soak up the starch.

mistakes.fix: Rub lightly.
mistakes.mistake: Rubbing hard, which breaks the grains.

variant_of.differs: The rice is rubbed lightly as it is washed, and the first water is poured away at once, so that it does not soak up the starchy water.

cues.text: Glossy and smooth. A peak stands on the lifted whisk, its tip bending slightly.
The bowl can be tipped without the foam sliding.

technique/whip.does: Beats air into egg whites or cream until they hold a peak.
how: Start with a clean, dry bowl, with no trace of fat or yolk in it.
Whisk slowly at first, until the whites are a loose foam.
Speed up, lifting the whisk through the foam in big circles.
Stop as soon as the foam stands in a peak when the whisk is lifted.

mistakes.fix: Stop at a glossy peak. Whites that have gone grainy cannot be brought back.
mistakes.mistake: Whipping past the peak, so that the foam turns dry and grainy and leaks water.

mistakes.fix: Separate each egg over a small bowl first, and wipe the mixing bowl clean.
mistakes.mistake: A trace of yolk or grease in the bowl, so that the whites never rise.

variant_of.differs: The aim is air. Whisking goes on until the foam holds a peak.

cues.text: No streaks. Beaten eggs are an even yellow that runs off the whisk in a thin stream.

technique/whisk.does: Beats a liquid with a whisk until it is blended and smooth.
how: Use a bowl large enough that nothing slops over.
Tilt the bowl and beat in quick strokes that cross the middle.
Keep going until the mixture is one colour and one texture.

mistakes.fix: Stop as soon as the streaks of white are gone.
mistakes.mistake: Whisking eggs for an omelette until they foam, which makes it spongy.

comes_after.why: The foam is built by steady whisking, so a cook has to know how to whisk first.

cues.text: The foam is pale and thick and leaves a ribbon on its surface when the whisk is lifted.
The whisk meets a light, steady resistance, and the sides of the bowl are warm but not hot.

technique/whisk-over-a-bain-marie.does: Whisks egg yolks, sugar and a sweet wine such as Marsala in a bowl set over barely simmering water, until they swell into a thick, pale, warm foam that holds a ribbon. This is the Italian zabaione, also spelt zabaglione, served warm as it is or chilled and folded into mascarpone cream.
how: Set a heatproof bowl over a pan of water at a bare simmer. The bowl must not touch the water.
Whisk the yolks with the sugar in the bowl until pale, then add the wine.
Keep whisking steadily, scraping the sides and the bottom, as the mixture warms and swells. Lift the bowl off the heat now and then if it gets too hot.
Stop when the foam is thick and holds a ribbon on its surface.
Serve warm at once, or keep whisking over ice until it is cool.

mistakes.fix: Keep the water at a bare simmer and lift the bowl off now and then.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the water boil hard, so that the yolks scramble into lumps.

mistakes.fix: Whisk until it holds a ribbon.
mistakes.mistake: Stopping too soon, so that the foam collapses in the bowl.

mistakes.fix: Whisk without a pause, scraping the sides.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving it still, so that the edges set against the bowl.

variant_of.differs: The yolks are whisked with sugar and Marsala, and the foam is eaten warm as a dessert or folded into cream. It is not taken on to carry butter or to sauce fish.

cues.text: Dark green, glossy and limp, a fraction of the raw heap.

technique/wilt.does: Collapses tender leaves with brief heat, so that they turn soft and dark and lose most of their bulk.
how: Wash the leaves and leave the water that clings to them.
Melt a little fat in a wide pan over medium heat.
Add the leaves by the handful, turning them as they fall.
Take them off the heat as soon as the last leaf has collapsed, and press out the water.

mistakes.fix: Stop the moment they collapse, and drain them.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the leaves on the heat, so that they go on shedding water and turn slimy.

cues.text: The wrapper lies snugly round the food, with the seam underneath and no gaps.
The parcel is firm and holds its shape when it is lifted.

technique/wrap.does: Encloses a filling or a piece of food in a wrapper, such as caul fat, a leaf, a thin omelette or a cloth, and closes it by folding or pulling, so that it keeps its shape and its juices as it cooks.
how: Lay the wrapper out flat and make sure it is soft enough to bend without tearing.
Set the food or the filling in the middle, with a border all round.
Fold the sides over the food, then bring the ends in and over, so that the wrapper meets itself and overlaps a little.
Turn the parcel seam side down, or tie it, so that it stays closed in the heat.

mistakes.fix: Use less filling and leave a border.
mistakes.mistake: Overfilling, so that the wrapper splits when the filling swells.

mistakes.fix: Pull the wrapper snug and set it seam side down, or tie it.
mistakes.mistake: Wrapping loosely, so that the parcel falls open in the pan.

comes_after.why: The nori goes around rice that has already been shaped.

cues.text: The nori is crisp and crackles when it is bitten.
The nori clings to the rice without gaps.

technique/wrap-in-nori.does: Wraps a sheet of dried seaweed around shaped rice just before eating, so that the seaweed stays crisp and does not turn soggy against the moist rice.
how: Cut a sheet of nori into strips or squares, or fold it to fit the rice shape.
Hold the shaped rice in one hand and lay the nori against the rice.
Press it on lightly, so that it clings to the surface.
Wrap it just before it is eaten, or wrap it in a way that keeps part of the nori dry.

mistakes.fix: Wrap it just before eating.
mistakes.mistake: Wrapping long before serving, so that the nori turns damp and chewy.

mistakes.fix: Keep it in a closed container, and crisp it briefly over a flame if needed.
mistakes.mistake: Using nori that has gone soft in the air.

variant_of.differs: The wrapper is a sheet of dried seaweed, put on at the last moment to stay crisp, not a leaf or dough sealed around the food.
